 Q: &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; What are the U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences of exercising my redemption rights? 
 A: &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; The U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences of exercising your redemption rights with respect to your CCXI public shares depend on your particular facts and circumstances. It is possible that you may be treated as selling your shares and, as a result, recognize capital gain or capital loss. It is also possible that the redemption may be treated as a distribution for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes. Whether a redemption of shares qualifies for sale treatment will depend largely on the total number of shares of CCXI public shares you are treated as owning before and after the redemption (including any shares that you constructively own as a result of owning CCXI public warrants and any shares that you directly or indirectly acquire pursuant to the business combination) relative to all of the CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares outstanding both before and after the redemption. U.S.&#160;Holders exercising redemption rights will be subject to the potential tax consequences of the Domestication, including under Section&#160;367 of the Code and potential tax consequences of the U.S.&#160;federal income tax rules relating to PFICs. For a more complete discussion of the U.S.&#160;federal income tax considerations of an exercise of redemption rights, see &#8220; Proposal&#160;No.&#160;1 &#8212;&#160;The Business Combination Proposal&#160;&#8212;&#160;Material U.S.&#160;Federal Income Tax Consequences of the Business Combination to CCXI Shareholders .&#8221; 
 All shareholders considering exercising redemption rights are urged to consult their tax advisors on the tax consequences to them of an exercise of redemption rights, including the applicability and effect of U.S.&#160;federal, state, local and non -U .S.&#160;tax laws. 
 Q. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; What are the U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences of the Merger? 
 A. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Beneficial owners of CCXI public shares who do not exercise their redemption rights will not be selling, exchanging, or otherwise transferring their CCXI public shares in the Merger and will therefore not be subject to any material U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences as a result of the Merger. Each of Agility and CCXI intends for the Merger to qualify as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; pursuant to Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code and based on the terms of the Merger Agreement and the representations and covenants of the parties therein, the Merger should so qualify, although this determination is not free from doubt because there is no authority directly addressing the treatment of all of the particular facts of the Merger for U.S. federal income tax purposes. If the Merger qualifies as a reorganization, then Agility Holders (as defined below) will not recognize gain or loss as a result of the exchange, pursuant to the Merger, of Agility common stock for shares of Post -Closing Company common stock. Regardless of whether the Merger qualifies as a reorganization, Agility and CCXI will not recognize any gain or loss for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes as a result of the Merger. For a more detailed discussion of the U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences of the Merger, please see &#8220; Material U.S.&#160;Federal Income Tax Considerations of the Merger. &#8221; 
 Q. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Do&#160;I have appraisal rights if&#160;I object to the business combination proposal? 
 A. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; CCXI shareholders do not have appraisal rights in connection with the business combination or the Domestication under the Companies Act or under the DGCL.&#160;Please see the section entitled &#8220; Appraisal Rights&#160;&#8212;&#160;Appraisal Rights of CCXI Shareholders. &#8221;

Please see &#8220; Risk Factors&#160;&#8212;&#160;Risk Related to CCXI, the Domestication and the Business Combination&#160;&#8212; &#160; If CCXI is deemed to be an investment company under the Investment Company Act, CCXI may be required to institute burdensome compliance requirements and CCXI&#8217;s activities may be restricted, which may make it difficult for CCXI to complete CCXI&#8217;s initial business combination.&#8221; If we are deemed to be an investment company under the Investment Company Act&#160;of&#160;1940, as amended (the &#8220; Investment Company Act &#8221;), we may be required to institute burdensome compliance requirements and our activities may be restricted, which may make it difficult for us to complete our initial business combination .

 Q. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; What happens to the funds deposited in the trust account after consummation of the business combination?

 Q. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; What happens if a substantial number of CCXI public shareholders vote in favor of the business combination proposal and exercise their redemption rights? 
 A. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; CCXI public shareholders may vote in favor of the business combination and still exercise their redemption rights. Accordingly, the business combination may be consummated even though the funds available from the trust account and the number of CCXI public shareholders are substantially reduced as a result of redemptions by CCXI public shareholders, subject to satisfaction or waiver of the Minimum Cash Condition under the Merger Agreement. 
 Q. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; What happens if the business combination is not consummated? 
 A. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; If CCXI does not complete the business combination for whatever reason, following the termination of the Merger Agreement CCXI would search for another target business with which to complete an initial business combination. If CCXI does not complete an initial business combination with Agility or another target business by the end of the completion window, CCXI must redeem 100% of the outstanding CCXI public shares, at a per share price, payable in cash, equal to the amount then held in the trust account, including interest earned (which interest shall be net of permitted withdrawals and up to $100,000 of interest to pay dissolution expenses and net of taxes payable) divided by the number of outstanding CCXI public shares. The redemption will completely extinguish public shareholders&#8217; rights as shareholders (including the right to receive further liquidating distributions, if any), subject to CCXI&#8217;s obligations under Cayman Islands law to provide for claims of creditors and other requirements of applicable law. The Sponsor and the Insiders have no redemption rights with respect to any CCXI Class&#160;B Ordinary Shares or CCXI private placement shares in the event an initial business combination is not effected in the completion window, and, accordingly, the CCXI Class&#160;B Ordinary Shares and CCXI private placement shares will be worthless. CCXI shareholders may also resolve to amend the CCXI current articles of association to modify the amount of time CCXI has to complete an initial business combination, in which case eligible holders of CCXI public shares will be offered an opportunity to redeem their CCXI public shares. 
 Q. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; How do the Sponsor and the Insiders intend to vote on the proposals?

If you hold your CCXI Ordinary Shares in &#8220;street name,&#8221; which means your shares are held of record by a broker, bank or nominee, you should contact your broker to ensure that votes related to the shares you beneficially own are properly counted. In this regard, you must provide the broker, bank or nominee with instructions on how to vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares or, if you wish to attend the meeting and vote, obtain a proxy card from your broker, bank or nominee. 
 Q. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; If my shares are held in &#8220;street name,&#8221; will my broker, bank or nominee automatically vote my shares for me? 
 A. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Under the rules of various national and regional securities exchanges, your broker, bank or nominee cannot vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares with respect to nonroutine matters unless you provide instructions on how to vote in accordance with the information and procedures provided to you by your broker, bank or nominee. We believe the proposals presented to the shareholders at the extraordinary general meeting will be considered nonroutine and, therefore, your broker, bank or nominee cannot vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares without your instruction on any of the proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting. If you do not provide voting instructions to your broker, bank or other nominee with respect to any of the proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting, your broker, bank or other nominee may deliver a proxy card expressly indicating that it is NOT voting your CCXI Ordinary Shares with respect to those proposals; this indication that a broker, bank or nominee is not voting your shares is referred to as a &#8220;broker non -vote .&#8221; Broker non -votes will be counted for the purposes of determining the existence of a quorum but will not be considered votes cast at the extraordinary general meeting. Your bank, broker or other nominee can vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares only if you provide instructions on how to vote. You should instruct your broker to vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares in accordance with directions you provide. 
 Q. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; How will an abstention or broker non -vote impact the results of each proposal? 
 A. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Abstentions and broker non -votes , while considered present for the purposes of establishing a quorum, will not count as votes cast at the extraordinary general meeting and will not have any effect on the outcome of the proposals. 
 Q. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; May&#160;I change my vote after&#160;I have mailed my signed proxy card? 
 A. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; CCXI shareholders of record may send a later -dated , signed proxy card to CCXI&#8217;s transfer agent at the address set forth at the end of this section so that it is received prior to the vote at the extraordinary general meeting. CCXI shareholders also may revoke their proxy by attending and voting at the extraordinary general meeting or by sending a notice of revocation to CCXI&#8217;s transfer agent, which must be received prior to the vote at the extraordinary general meeting.

 The Parties 
 CCXI 
 Churchill Capital Corp&#160;XI is a blank check company formed in order to effect a merger, amalgamation, share exchange, asset acquisition, stock purchase, reorganization or other similar business combination with one or more businesses. CCXI was incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands on June&#160;4, 2025. 
 On December&#160;18, 2025, CCXI consummated its initial public offering (the &#8220; CCXI IPO &#8221;) of 41,400,000 CCXI public units, including 5,400,000 CCXI public units pursuant to the underwriters&#8217; full exercise of the over -allotment option. The CCXI public units were sold at an offering price of $10.00 per unit, generating gross proceeds to CCXI of $414,000,000. Simultaneously with the consummation of the CCXI IPO and the exercise of the underwriters&#8217; over -allotment option, CCXI consummated the private placement of 500,000 CCXI private placement units to the Sponsor at a price of $10.00 per unit, generating total proceeds of $5,000,000. Transaction costs amounted to $19,618,232, consisting of $3,000,000 of underwriting fees, $15,990,000 of deferred underwriting fees (of which $1,500,000 has been paid and $14,490,000 remains deferred) and $628,232 of other offering costs. 
 A total of $414,000,000 was deposited into the trust account and the remaining net proceeds became available to be used as working capital to provide for business, legal and accounting due diligence on prospective initial business combinations and continuing general and administrative expenses. The CCXI IPO was conducted pursuant to a registration statement on Form&#160;S -1 that became effective on December&#160;16, 2025. As of the close of business on&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;, 2026, the record date for the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders of CCXI (the &#8220; extraordinary general meeting &#8221;), there was approximately $&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;held in the trust account. Each of the CCXI public units, CCXI public shares and CCXI public warrants are each traded on the Global Market tier of Nasdaq under the symbols CCXIU, CCXI and CCXIW, respectively. In connection with the business combination, CCXI will change its name to &#8220;Agility Robotics, Inc.,&#8221; and upon the Closing, CCXI expects that Post -Closing Company common stock and Post -Closing Company warrants will begin trading on Nasdaq under the symbols &#8220;AGLT&#8221; and &#8220;AGLTW,&#8221; respectively. 
 The mailing address of CCXI&#8217;s principal executive office is 640 Fifth Avenue, 14 th Floor, New&#160;York, NY&#160;10019. Its telephone number is (212)&#160;380 -7500 . After the consummation of the business combination, its principal executive office will be that of Agility.

 Agility 
 Agility Robotics, Inc. was formed as a Delaware corporation on November&#160;12, 2015. 
 Agility is a commercial humanoid company. Agility&#8217;s mission is to build robot partners that augment the human workforce, ultimately enabling humans to be more human. Its flagship humanoid robot, Digit, is a multi -purpose , human -centric robot Made for Work&#8482; and currently operating in manufacturing, distribution, and logistics environments to fill physical labor shortages. Through more than a decade of advancing robotics into real -world commercial deployment, Agility has established itself as one of the only humanoid companies with multiple&#160;years of operational experience in real customer environments. 
 The mailing address of Agility&#8217;s principal executive office is 4698 Truax Drive SE, Salem, OR&#160;97317. Its telephone number is (541)&#160;738 -8888 .

 Emerging Growth Company 
 CCXI is an &#8220;emerging growth company,&#8221; as defined in Section&#160;2(a)&#160;of the Securities Act, as modified by the Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act&#160;of&#160;2012 (the &#8220; JOBS Act &#8221;). As such, it is eligible to take advantage of certain exemptions from various reporting requirements that are applicable to other public companies that are not &#8220;emerging growth companies&#8221; including, but not limited to, not being required to comply with the auditor attestation requirements of Section&#160;404 of the Sarbanes -Oxley Act&#160;of&#160;2002 (the &#8220; Sarbanes -Oxley Act &#8221;), reduced disclosure obligations regarding executive compensation in their periodic reports and this proxy statement/prospectus, and exemptions from the requirements of holding a non -binding advisory vote on executive compensation and shareholder approval of any golden parachute payments not previously approved. If some investors find CCXI&#8217;s securities less attractive as a result, there may be a less active trading market for CCXI&#8217;s securities and the prices of its securities may be more volatile. 
 In addition, Section&#160;107 of the JOBS Act also provides that an &#8220;emerging growth company&#8221; can take advantage of the extended transition period provided in Section&#160;7(a)(2)(B)&#160;of the Securities Act for complying with new or revised accounting standards. In other words, an &#8220;emerging growth company&#8221; can delay the adoption of certain accounting standards until those standards would otherwise apply to private companies. CCXI intends to take advantage of the benefits of this extended transition period. 
 CCXI (including the Post -Closing Company) will remain an emerging growth company until the earlier of: (1)&#160;the last&#160;day of the fiscal year (a)&#160;following December&#160;18, 2030, the fifth anniversary of the CCXI IPO, (b)&#160;in which CCXI has total annual gross revenue of at least $1,235,000,000, or (c)&#160;in which CCXI is deemed to be a large accelerated filer, which means the market value of CCXI common stock that is held by non -affiliates exceeds $700,000,000 as of the end of the prior June&#160;30; and (2)&#160;the date on which CCXI has issued more than $1,000,000,000 in nonconvertible debt during the prior three -year period. References herein to &#8220;emerging growth company&#8221; shall have the meaning associated with it in the JOBS Act. 
 Smaller Reporting Company 
 CCXI is also a &#8220;smaller reporting company&#8221; under the Exchange&#160;Act, and may continue to be a smaller reporting company so long as, as of June&#160;30 of the preceding year, (1)&#160;the market value of our Class&#160;A ordinary shares held by non -affiliates , or CCXI&#8217;s public float, is less than $250&#160;million; or (2)&#160;CCXI has annual revenues less than $100&#160;million and our public float is less than $700&#160;million. If the Post -Closing Company is a smaller reporting company at the time it ceases to be an emerging growth company, it may continue to rely on exemptions from certain disclosure requirements that are available to smaller reporting companies. Specifically, as a smaller reporting company the Post -Closing Company may choose to present only the two most recent fiscal&#160;years of audited financial statements in our Annual Report on Form&#160;10 -K and, similar to emerging growth companies, smaller reporting companies have reduced disclosure obligations regarding executive compensation.

 Background of the Transactions 
 CCXI is a blank check company formed to effect a merger, amalgamation, share exchange, asset acquisition, stock purchase, reorganization or other similar business combination with one or more businesses. CCXI was incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands on June 4, 2025. After the CCXI IPO, CCXI commenced an active search for prospective businesses and assets to acquire. 
 In evaluating potential businesses and assets to acquire, CCXI, together with the Sponsor and their advisors, surveyed the landscape of potential acquisition opportunities based on their knowledge of, and familiarity with, the M&amp;A marketplace. CCXI generally sought to identify companies that (i) generate or have the future potential to generate stable free cash -flow , (ii) would benefit uniquely from CCXI&#8217;s capabilities, (iii) are sourced through CCXI&#8217;s proprietary channels, (iv) have a committed and capable management team and (v) have the potential to grow through both organic growth and acquisition opportunities. CCXI also sought to identify companies that it believed would benefit from being a publicly -held entity, particularly with respect to access to capital for both organic growth and for use in acquisitions, with a particular emphasis on opportunities that are primed to unlock disruptive technological advancements. CCXI generally implements these criteria when evaluating potential targets. 
 Starting in December 2025 and continuing through early 2026, following the closing of the CCXI IPO, representatives of Archimedes Advisor Group LLC, CCXI&#8217;s strategic advisor and affiliate of Michael Klein, Chairman of the Board of CCXI (&#8220; Archimedes &#8221;), at the direction of CCXI, and the Sponsor commenced a search for prospective business combination candidates (&#8220; targets &#8221;) for CCXI to partner with in its initial business combination. CCXI, with the assistance of Archimedes, developed a list of approximately a dozen targets leveraging the proprietary sourcing channels described above. Representatives of CCXI were also contacted by potential targets that they had not previously identified through its search process. In certain instances, it was requested by a potential target that CCXI enter into a non -disclosure agreement. CCXI did so on a selective basis, entering into fewer than ten such agreements. Prior to entering into a non -binding letter of intent with Agility, CCXI did not submit a non -binding letter of intent to any prospective target other than Agility. Upon entering into the non -binding letter of intent with Agility, CCXI became subject to an exclusivity provision that precluded CCXI from participating in discussions or negotiations with any other potential target regarding a prospective business combination. 
 For more information, see &#8220; Proposal No. 1. &#8212; The Business Combination Proposal &#8212; Background of the Transactions .&#8221;

 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; by CCXI if the Transactions are not consummated on or before December &#160; 31, 2026 (the &#8220; Termination Date &#8221;), which date may be automatically extended in the event that any action or legal proceeding for specific performance or other equitable relief by any party with respect to the Merger Agreement, any other Transaction Agreement, or otherwise with respect to the Transactions is commenced or pending on or before December &#160; 31, 2026, in which case the Termination Date will be extended until the date that is 30&#160;days following the date on which a final, non -appealable order or judgment has been entered with respect to such action or legal proceeding, provided that CCXI&#8217;s failure to fulfill any obligation under the Merger Agreement is not the primary cause of, or did not primarily result in, the failure of the Closing to occur on or before the Termination Date (as it may be extended); 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; by Agility if the Transactions are not consummated on or before the Termination Date (as it may be extended), provided that Agility&#8217;s failure to fulfill any obligation under the Merger Agreement is not the primary cause of, or did not primarily result in, the failure of the Closing to occur on or before the Termination Date (as it may be extended); and provided, further, that, Agility will use reasonable best efforts to provide written notice to CCXI, in good faith, prior to the Domestication, if Agility believes it has the right to, and intends to, terminate the Merger Agreement prior to the closing of the Transactions; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; by either CCXI or Agility if the other party has breached any of its covenants, agreements, representations or warranties which would cause the conditions to the Closing not to be satisfied and has not cured its breach, if curable, within 30&#160;days of receiving written notice of such breach, provided that the terminating party&#8217;s failure to fulfill any obligation under the Merger Agreement is not the primary cause of, or did not primarily result in, the failure of the Closing to occur on or before such date; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; by either CCXI or Agility if a final, non -appealable governmental order or a statute, rule or regulation permanently enjoins or prohibits consummation of the Merger; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; by either CCXI or Agility if the approval by CCXI shareholders of the proposals voted on at the extraordinary general meeting and required to consummate the Transactions is not obtained at the extraordinary general meeting (subject to any adjournment or postponement thereof), provided that CCXI is not entitled to terminate on these grounds if, at the time of such termination, CCXI is in breach of its obligations under the Merger Agreement with respect to this proxy statement/prospectus and the stockholders&#8217; meeting; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; by CCXI in the event the Agility stockholders holding Agility capital stock sufficient to obtain the Company Stockholder Approval (as defined in the Merger Agreement) fail to deliver the Agility stockholder written consent within 48&#160;hours of the registration statement becoming effective, provided that this right to terminate the Merger Agreement will not be available if the Company Stockholder Approval is obtained prior to CCXI providing notice of its intent to terminate the Merger Agreement on account of a Written Consent Failure (as defined in the Merger Agreement); or 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; by Agility if the CCXI Board changes, withdraws, withholds, qualifies or modifies (or publicly proposes to do so) its recommendation to CCXI shareholders to approve certain matters related to the Transactions. 
 Effect of Termination 
 In the event of proper termination by either CCXI or Agility, the Merger Agreement will become void and have no effect (other than with respect to certain surviving provisions specified in the Merger Agreement), without any liability under the Merger Agreement on the part of any party thereto or its respective affiliates, officers, directors, employees, representatives or stockholders, other than liability of any party thereto for any intentional and willful breach of the Merger Agreement by such party occurring prior to such termination.

 All fees and expenses incurred in connection with the Merger Agreement and the Transactions, except for those fees associated with the filing to obtain clearance pursuant to the HSR Act, will be paid by the party incurring such expenses whether or not the Transactions will be consummated; except that if the Closing occurs, CCXI will bear and pay at or promptly after the Closing:

 provided that all costs of investigation and all defense and attorneys&#8217; and other professional fees and settlement payments related to stockholder actions initiated by or on behalf of any stockholders of Agility, whether borne by CCXI or Agility, will be fully payable by the Post -Closing Company if the closing of the Transactions occurs and not subject to any limitation or cap.  Incentive Plan and ESPP 
 Incentive Plan 
 The CCXI Board will approve the Incentive Plan, subject to the approval of the CCXI shareholders. The Incentive Plan will initially reserve for issuance a number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock equal to 13% of the fully diluted, and as converted, outstanding Post -Closing Company common stock immediately following the consummation of the business combination, subject to certain adjustments and an evergreen provision. The purpose of the Incentive Plan is to provide a means whereby the Post -Closing Company can secure and retain the services of employees, directors and consultants; to provide incentives for such persons to exert maximum efforts for the success of the Post -Closing Company and its affiliates and to provide a means by which such persons may be given an opportunity to benefit from increases in value of the Post -Closing Company common stock through the granting of awards under the Incentive Plan. A copy of the Incentive Plan is included as Annex&#160;E to this proxy statement/prospectus. See the section entitled &#8220; Proposal&#160;No. 6 &#8212;&#160;The Incentive Plan Proposal .&#8221; 
 ESPP 
 The CCXI Board will approve the ESPP, subject to the approval of the CCXI shareholders. The ESPP will initially reserve for issuance a number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock equal to 2% of the fully diluted, and as converted outstanding Post -Closing Company common stock immediately following the consummation of the business combination, subject to certain adjustments and an evergreen provision. The purpose of the ESPP is to provide a means whereby the Post -Closing Company can align the long -term financial interests of its employees with the financial interests of its stockholders. A copy of the ESPP is included as Annex&#160;F to this proxy statement/prospectus. See the section entitled &#8220; Proposal&#160;No. 7 &#8212;&#160;The ESPP Proposal.&#8221;

 Voting Power; CCXI Record Date 
 CCXI shareholders will be entitled to vote or direct votes to be cast at the extraordinary general meeting if they owned CCXI Ordinary Shares at the close of business on &#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; , 2026 (the &#8220; CCXI record date &#8221;), which is the record date for the extraordinary general meeting. CCXI shareholders will have one vote for each share of CCXI Ordinary Shares owned at the close of business on the CCXI record date. If your CCXI Ordinary Shares are held in &#8220;street name&#8221; or are in a margin or similar account, you should contact your broker to ensure that votes related to the shares you beneficially own are properly counted.  Quorum and Vote of CCXI Shareholders 
 A quorum of CCXI shareholders is necessary to hold a valid meeting. A quorum for such meeting will consist of the holders present by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy of shares of CCXI representing at least one -third (1/3) of the paid up voting share capital of CCXI entitled to vote at such meeting. 
 Proxies that are marked &#8220;abstain&#8221; will be treated as shares of CCXI public shares present for purposes of determining the presence of a quorum on all matters. Broker non -votes will be counted for the purposes of determining the existence of a quorum, but will not be considered votes cast at the extraordinary general meeting. 
 The Sponsor owns of record and is entitled to vote &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; % of the outstanding CCXI Ordinary Shares (&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; % of the outstanding CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares and &#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; % of the outstanding CCXI Class&#160;B Ordinary Shares) as of the CCXI record date. Such shares, as well as any shares of CCXI public shares acquired in the aftermarket by the Sponsor, will be voted in favor of the proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting. 
 The proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting will require the following votes: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; the approval of each of the business combination proposal, the advisory organizational documents proposal, the stock issuance proposal, the incentive plan proposal, the ESPP proposal and, if presented, the adjournment proposal require approval by ordinary resolution, being the affirmative vote of a simple majority of the votes cast by holders of outstanding CCXI Ordinary Shares represented at the extraordinary general meeting by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy and entitled to vote at the extraordinary general meeting, voting together as a single class. Accordingly, if a valid quorum is established, a CCXI shareholder&#8217;s failure to vote by proxy or to vote at the extraordinary general meeting with regard to the business combination proposal, the advisory organizational documents proposal, the stock issuance proposal, the incentive plan proposal, the ESPP proposal and, if presented, the adjournment proposal will have no effect on such proposals; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; the approval of the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal require approval by special resolution, being the affirmative vote of holders of at least two -thirds of the CCXI Ordinary Shares represented at the extraordinary general meeting by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy and entitled to vote at the extraordinary general meeting, voting together as a single class. Accordingly, if a valid quorum is established, a CCXI shareholder&#8217;s failure to vote by proxy or to vote at the extraordinary general meeting with regard to the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal will have no effect on such proposals. Under the CCXI current articles of association, CCXI&#8217;s directors have the authority to resolve that CCXI be registered by way of continuation in a jurisdiction outside the Cayman Islands or such other jurisdiction in which it is for the time being incorporated, registered or existing (including, but not limited to, the approval of the organizational documents to be adopted by the Company in such other jurisdiction to the extent applicable). Accordingly, it is not necessary for CCXI to receive shareholder consent to the Domestication, and the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal are therefore being presented to CCXI shareholders on a non -binding advisory basis only; and 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; with respect to the director election proposal, directors are elected by a majority of the votes cast by holders of outstanding CCXI Class&#160;B Ordinary Shares at the extraordinary general meeting by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy and entitled to vote thereon at the extraordinary general meeting. Accordingly, if a valid quorum is established, a CCXI shareholder&#8217;s failure to vote by proxy or to vote at the extraordinary general meeting or a withhold vote with regard to a director nominee named in the director election proposal will have no effect on such proposal. 
 The business combination proposal, the domestication proposal, the organizational documents proposal, the advisory organizational documents proposal, the stock issuance proposal, the incentive plan proposal, the ESPP proposal and the director election proposal are referred to as the &#8220; condition precedent proposals .&#8221; Each condition precedent proposal is conditioned on the approval of each of the condition precedent proposals. Therefore, if any of the condition precedent proposals are not approved at the extraordinary general meeting (or any adjournment or postponement thereof), none of the other condition precedent proposals will have any effect, even if approved by the requisite holders of CCXI Ordinary Shares. It is important for you to note that in the event that any of those proposals are not approved, then unless certain conditions in the Merger Agreement are waived by the applicable parties to the Merger Agreement, the Merger Agreement may be terminated and the business combination may not be consummated.

 Redemption Rights 
 Pursuant to the CCXI current articles of association, a holder of CCXI public shares may demand that CCXI redeem such shares for cash if the business combination is consummated. Such redemption rights are not available to the Sponsor, officers or directors. Eligible holders of CCXI public shares will be entitled to receive cash for these shares only if they demand in writing that CCXI redeem their CCXI public shares for cash no later than the Redemption Deadline by delivering their shares and requesting in writing that CCXI redeem such CCXI public shares for cash to Continental Stock Transfer&#160;&amp; Trust Company, CCXI&#8217;s transfer agent. If the business combination is not completed, the CCXI public shares will not be redeemed. If an eligible holder of CCXI public shares properly exercises their redemption rights and the business combination is consummated, CCXI will redeem such shares for cash in an amount equal to their pro rata portion of the funds in the trust account, calculated as of two&#160;business days prior to the consummation of the business combination and net of certain permitted withdrawals. As of the CCXI record date, this would amount to approximately $ &#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; per share. In such case, such holder of CCXI public shares will be exchanging their shares for cash and will no longer own such shares. Please see the section entitled &#8220; Extraordinary General Meeting of CCXI&#160;&#8212;&#160;Redemption Rights &#8221; for a detailed description of the procedures to be followed if you wish to redeem your CCXI public shares for cash. 
 Notwithstanding the foregoing, a holder of CCXI public shares, together with any affiliate of such holder or any other person with whom such holder is acting in concert or as a &#8220;group&#8221; (as defined in Section&#160;13(d)(3)&#160;of the Exchange&#160;Act), will be restricted from seeking redemption with respect to more than 15% of the CCXI public shares. 
 Accordingly, all CCXI public shares in excess of 15% held by a CCXI public shareholder, together with any affiliate of such holder or any other person with whom such holder is acting in concert or as a &#8220;group,&#8221; will not be redeemed without the prior consent of our directors. 
 Pursuant to the Sponsor Agreement, the Sponsor and the Insiders have agreed to waive their redemption rights with respect to all of their CCXI Ordinary Shares in connection with the consummation of the business combination and, because of this, such CCXI Ordinary Shares are excluded from the pro rata calculation used to determine the per share redemption price. As is customary in transactions of this type, the Sponsor and the Insiders did not receive any consideration for waiving their redemption rights.

 Regulatory Matters 
 Under the HSR Act and the rules that have been promulgated thereunder by the Federal Trade Commission (the &#8220; FTC &#8221;), certain transactions may not be consummated unless information has been furnished to the Antitrust Division of the Department of Justice (the &#8220; Antitrust Division &#8221;) and the FTC and certain waiting period requirements have been satisfied. The Transactions are subject to these requirements and may not be completed until the expiration of a 
 

 18 
 Table of Contents 

 
 30 -day waiting period following the filing of the required Notification and Report Forms with the Antitrust Division and the FTC or until early termination is granted. If the FTC or the Antitrust Division issues a Request for Additional Information or Documentary Material (a &#8220; Second Request &#8221;) within the initial 30 -day waiting period, the waiting period with respect to the Transactions will be extended for an additional period of 30 calendar&#160;days, which will begin on the date on which the filing parties each certify compliance with the Second Request. The parties may also enter into a timing agreement with the Antitrust Division or FTC to not consummate the Transactions for a specified period of time. Complying with a Second Request can take a significant period of time. 
 Each of CCXI and Agility filed a Notification and Report Form&#160;with the FTC and the Antitrust Division in connection with the Transactions on July&#160;9, 2026. The initial 30 -day waiting period will expire at 11:59&#160;p.m., Eastern time, on August&#160;10, 2026, which waiting period may be shortened, restarted or extended. 
 At any time before or after consummation of the Transactions, notwithstanding termination of the waiting period under the HSR Act, the applicable competition authorities could take such action under applicable antitrust laws as each deems necessary or desirable in the public interest, including seeking to enjoin the consummation of the Transactions. Private parties may also seek to take legal action under the antitrust laws under certain circumstances. There is no assurance that the Antitrust Division, the FTC, any state attorney general, or any other government authority will not attempt to challenge the Transactions on antitrust grounds, and, if such a challenge is made, we cannot assure you as to its result. 
 Neither CCXI nor Agility is aware of any material regulatory approvals or actions that are required for completion of the Transactions other than the expiration or early termination of the waiting period under the HSR Act. It is presently contemplated that if any such additional regulatory approvals or actions are required, those approvals or actions will be sought. There can be no assurance, however, that any additional approvals or actions will be obtained. 
 Summary Risk Factors 
 Agility&#8217;s business is subject to a number of risks of which you should be aware before making a decision to invest in our securities. These risks include, among others, the following: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Agility&#8217;s business plans require a significant amount of capital. Agility&#8217;s future capital needs may require Agility to sell additional equity or debt securities that may dilute its stockholders or introduce covenants that may restrict its operations or its ability to pay dividends. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Agility has very limited experience commercializing its products and may not be able to do so efficiently or effectively. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Agility relies on a limited number of customers for a significant portion of potential revenue, and the loss of any one of these customers may adversely affect Agility&#8217;s business, financial condition and results of operations. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Agility operates in a competitive industry that is subject to rapid technological change, and Agility expects competition to increase. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; It is possible that the unit economics of Agility&#8217;s humanoid robot solutions do not materialize as expected, which could significantly hinder Agility&#8217;s ability to generate a commercially viable product at scale and adversely affect Agility&#8217;s business prospects. See the section entitled &#8220; Unaudited Prospective Unit Economics Information &#8221; for more information. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Agility relies on global supply chains and disruptions could delay production, increase costs, and limit Agility&#8217;s ability to fulfill customer orders. Changes in trade policy, including tariffs and &#8220;Buy American&#8221; requirements, could further disrupt Agility&#8217;s supply chain and raise input costs. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Design flaws, defects, software errors, or unintended AI -driven behaviors could result in product recalls, injury to co -located workers, product liability claims, and significant litigation expenses. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; The regulatory framework for robotics, AI -enabled products, and humanoid robots operating in shared workspaces is rapidly evolving. Failure to comply with new or changing regulations&#160;&#8212;&#160;including evolving AI -governance laws, industrial safety standards, and privacy requirements&#160;&#8212;&#160;could lead to product withdrawal, increased costs, or restrictions on deployment.

 Table of Contents 

 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Agility&#8217;s success depends in part on its ability to obtain and maintain protection for the intellectual property relating to or incorporated into its products. Agility may be subject to intellectual property infringement claims or misappropriation claims, which may be time -consuming and expensive and, if adversely determined, could limit Agility&#8217;s ability to commercialize its products. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Agility is subject to cybersecurity risks to operational systems, security systems, infrastructure, integrated software and partners&#8217; and customers&#8217; data processed by Agility or third -party vendors or suppliers and any material failure, weakness, interruption, cyber event, incident or breach of security may prevent Agility from effectively operating its business. Further, issues relating to Agility&#8217;s use of AI, combined with an uncertain legal and regulatory environment, may adversely affect Agility&#8217;s business, financial condition and results of operations. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; The issuance of shares of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s securities in connection with private placement will dilute the voting power of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s shareholders. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Churchill and Agility will incur significant transaction costs in connection with the business combination, and the incurrence of these costs will reduce the amount of cash available to be used for other corporate purposes by Churchill if the business combination is not completed. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; The consummation of the business combination is subject to several conditions and if those conditions are not satisfied or waived, the business combination may not be completed. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Agility is highly dependent on the services of its senior management and other key employees and, if Agility is unable to attract and retain a sufficient number of qualified employees, its ability to design, manufacture and launch its products, operate its business and compete could be harmed. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; If a significant number of Churchill&#8217;s Ordinary Shares are elected to be redeemed in connection with the business combination, the stock ownership of the Post -Closing Company will be highly concentrated, which will reduce the public &#8220;float&#8221; and may have a negative effect on the market price of the common stock of the Post -Closing Company. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Churchill&#8217;s shareholders will experience dilution as a consequence of the issuance of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s common stock as consideration in the business combination. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; The benefits of the business combination may not be realized to the extent currently anticipated by Agility and Churchill, or at all. If the business combination&#8217;s benefits do not meet the expectations of investors or securities analysts, the market price of Churchill&#8217;s securities or, following the consummation of the business combination, the value of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s securities may decline. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; After the closing of the business combination, sales of a substantial number of shares of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s stock in the public market by existing shareholders could cause the stock price to decline. Further, after the closing of the business combination, a significant number of shares of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s stock will be subject to issuance upon exercise of outstanding warrants, which may result in dilution to the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s shareholders. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; There is no assurance that the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s securities will be approved for listing on Nasdaq or that the Post -Closing Company will be able to comply with the continued listing standards of Nasdaq. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Some of Churchill&#8217;s officers and directors and its Sponsor may have conflicts of interest that may influence or have influenced them to support or approve the business combination. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Legal proceedings in connection with the business combination, the outcomes of which are uncertain, could delay or prevent the completion of the business combination. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Changes in laws or regulations, or a failure to comply with any laws and regulations, may adversely affect Agility and the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s business and ability to consummate the business combination. Further, Agility expects to incur significantly increased costs as a result of and devote substantial management time to operating as a public company.

 Selected Unaudited Pro Forma Condensed Combined Financial Information 
 The following selected unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial information (the &#8220; selected pro forma data &#8221;) give effect to the business combination and other events contemplated by the Merger Agreement as described in the section entitled &#8220; Unaudited Pro Forma Condensed Combined Financial Information .&#8221; 
 The business combination will be accounted for as a reverse recapitalization, with no goodwill or other intangible assets recorded, in accordance with GAAP.&#160;Under this method of accounting, CCXI, which is the legal acquirer, will be treated as the accounting acquiree for financial reporting purposes and Agility, which is the legal acquiree, will be treated as the accounting acquirer for financial reporting purposes. Accordingly, the consolidated assets, liabilities and results of operations of Agility will become the historical financial statements of the Post -Closing Company, and CCXI&#8217;s assets, liabilities and results of operations will be consolidated with Agility&#8217;s beginning on the acquisition date. For accounting purposes, the financial statements of the Post -Closing Company will represent a continuation of the financial statements of Agility with the business combination being treated as the equivalent of Agility issuing stock for the net assets of CCXI, accompanied by a recapitalization. The selected unaudited pro forma condensed combined balance sheet data as of June&#160;30, 2026 gives effect to the business combination and financing activities described above as if they had occurred on June&#160;30, 2026. The selected unaudited pro forma condensed combined statement of operations data for the six&#160;months ended June&#160;30, 2026 and for the year ended December&#160;31, 2025 give effect to the business combination and financing activities described above as if they had occurred on January&#160;1, 2025. 
 The selected pro forma data have been derived from, and should be read in conjunction with, the more detailed unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial information (the &#8220; Pro Forma Financial Information &#8221;) of Agility and CCXI appearing elsewhere in this proxy statement/prospectus and the accompanying notes to the Pro Forma Financial Information. In addition, the Pro Forma Financial Information were based on, and should be read in conjunction with, the historical consolidated financial statements and related notes of the entities for the applicable periods included in this proxy statement/prospectus. The selected unaudited pro forma data have been presented for informational purposes only and are not necessarily indicative of what the combined financial position or results of operations actually would have been had the business combination been completed as of the dates indicated. The unaudited pro forma condensed combined financial information does not give effect to any anticipated synergies, operating efficiencies or cost savings that may be associated with the business combination. In addition, the selected unaudited pro forma data does not purport to project the future financial position or operating results of Agility and CCXI subsequent to the close of the business combination.

 Shareholders should carefully consider the following risk factors, together with all of the other information included in this proxy statement/prospectus, before they decide whether to vote or instruct their vote to be cast to approve the proposals described in this proxy statement/prospectus. Investing in the Post -Closing Company common stock involves a high degree of risk. The following risk factors apply to the business and operations of CCXI and Agility and will also apply to the business and operations of the Post -Closing Company following the completion of the business combination. The occurrence of one or more of the events or circumstances described in these risk factors, alone or in combination with other events or circumstances, may have an adverse effect on the ability to complete or realize the anticipated benefits of the business combination, and may adversely affect the business, cash flows, financial condition, and results of operations of the Post -Closing Company. In that case, the trading price of Post -Closing Company common stock may decline, and you may lose all or part of your investment. You should also carefully consider the following risk factors in addition to the other information included in this proxy statement/prospectus, including matters addressed in the section entitled &#8220;Cautionary Note&#160;Regarding Forward -Looking Statements.&#8221; CCXI or Agility may face additional risks and uncertainties that are not presently known to CCXI and Agility, or that CCXI and Agility currently deem immaterial, which may also impair CCXI&#8217;s or Agility&#8217;s business or financial condition. The following discussion should be read in conjunction with the financial statements and notes to the financial statements included herein. 
 Risks Related to Agility 
 Unless the context otherwise requires, references in this subsection to &#8220;Agility,&#8221; &#8220;the Company,&#8221; &#8220;we,&#8221; &#8220;us&#8221; or &#8220;our&#8221; refer to the business of Agility and its subsidiaries prior to the consummation of the business combination, which will be the business of the Post -Closing Company and its subsidiaries following the business combination. 
 Risks Related to Our Industry 
 Humanoid robots are an emerging category of robotics, and customer adoption of Agility&#8217;s humanoid robot, Digit, and similar humanoid systems may be slower than anticipated relative to fixed industrial robots, autonomous mobile robots (&#8220;AMRs&#8221;) or other warehouse automation solutions that have longer track records and more established customer acceptance. If potential customers choose proven conventional automation over humanoid robots, Agility&#8217;s revenue growth and market penetration could be materially adversely affected. 
 Humanoid robots represent an entirely new category of robotic systems that have not yet achieved broad commercial deployment or widespread customer acceptance. Unlike fixed industrial robots and AMRs, which have decades of proven track records in manufacturing and warehouse environments, humanoid bipedal robots such as Digit are unproven at scale and customers may be reluctant to adopt them over established automation solutions. Potential customers may perceive humanoid robots as unproven technology, lack confidence in Agility&#8217;s business model, or prefer the demonstrated reliability and lower perceived risk of conventional automation. The market for our products may not develop as expected, or may develop more slowly than anticipated, due to customer hesitancy, long evaluation cycles, or a preference for incremental automation solutions with which their workforces and operations teams are already familiar. If potential customers choose conventional automation&#160;&#8212;&#160;including AMRs, collaborative robots, or fixed material -handling equipment&#160;&#8212;&#160;over humanoid robots, or if customer adoption is slower than we anticipate, Agility&#8217;s ability to generate revenue and achieve profitability could be materially adversely affected. 
 The robotics and warehouse automation industry is characterized by rapid technological change, evolving industry standards, and intensifying competition from a range of established and emerging players. If Agility is unable to keep pace with technological developments&#160;&#8212;&#160;including advances in machine learning, computer vision and bipedal locomotion&#160;&#8212;&#160;or to differentiate its Digit humanoid robot and future products effectively, its competitive position and operating results could be materially adversely affected. 
 The robotics and warehouse automation industry is subject to rapid technological change, and Agility expects competition to intensify in the future. Agility&#8217;s product offerings compete in a broad competitive landscape that includes developers of humanoid robots, autonomous mobile robots, collaborative robots, fixed industrial automation systems, and traditional material -handling equipment. Agility also faces potential competition from diversified technology companies and robotic solution suppliers that do not have directly competing products today but could become competitors through organic development or acquisitions; such companies often have existing customer relationships and distribution channels that could enable them to emerge as formidable threats. Developments in alternative technologies,

 such as advances in AI, machine learning, computer vision, and bipedal locomotion by competitors, may materially and adversely affect Agility&#8217;s business in ways it does not currently anticipate. Any failure by Agility to successfully react to changes in existing technologies or to develop new or enhanced technologies could materially harm its competitive position and growth prospects. Agility&#8217;s competitors may respond more quickly to new or emerging technologies, undertake more extensive marketing campaigns, have greater financial, manufacturing and other resources, or be more successful in attracting potential customers, employees and strategic partners. If Agility is not able to compete effectively, its business, prospects, financial condition and operating results will be negatively impacted. 
 Competition in the humanoid and robotics market is intensifying, including from well-funded market participants, many of which have significantly greater financial, technical and marketing resources than Agility. If these competitors bring competing humanoid and robotics products to market more quickly or at lower cost, or if they secure more favorable customer relationships, Agility&#8217;s competitiveness could be materially adversely affected. 
 Competition in the humanoid and robotics market is intensifying rapidly, with well -funded entrants including Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Apptronik, Figure AI, 1X Technologies, Sanctuary AI, Hexagon, and NEURA Robotics, among others, actively developing competing humanoid systems. Many of these competitors have significantly greater brand recognition, customer relationships, and financial, technical, manufacturing, and other resources than Agility. They may be able to deploy greater resources to the design, development, manufacturing, distribution, promotion, sales, marketing, and support of their humanoid robotics programs. Additionally, these competitors may have longer operating histories, larger sales forces, broader customer and industry relationships, and other tangible and intangible resources that provide them with competitive advantages. Some competitors may decide to operate solely with a traditional sales model that may be viewed more favorably by potential customers, or may bundle their humanoid products with complementary offerings at lower effective prices. If any of these competitors bring competing humanoid products to market more quickly, at lower cost, with superior performance, or with more favorable customer terms, Agility&#8217;s competitiveness could be materially adversely affected. 
 The market for humanoid robots designed to work alongside humans in warehouse, logistics and manufacturing environments is nascent and unproven. Important assumptions about the total addressable market for Agility&#8217;s humanoid robot, Digit, and future products, pricing under Agility&#8217;s Robots-as-a-Service subscription model (&#8220;RaaS&#8221;) and direct-sale models, customer adoption rates, and the length of sales and deployment cycles may prove to be inaccurate. If the market for humanoid robots does not develop as anticipated, or develops more slowly than expected, Agility&#8217;s business, financial condition, and results of operations would be materially and adversely affected. 
 The market for humanoid robots designed to work alongside humans in warehouse, logistics, and manufacturing environments is nascent and largely unproven. Important assumptions about the total addressable market for Digit and future products, pricing under Agility&#8217;s RaaS subscription model and direct -sale models, customer adoption rates, anticipated future labor shortages and the length of sales and deployment cycles are based on management estimates that may prove inaccurate. Given the evolving nature of the markets in which Agility operates, it is difficult to predict customer demand or adoption rates for its products or the future growth of the markets it expects to target. If one or more of the targeted markets experience a shift in customer or prospective customer demand or new solutions that better address customer needs, Agility&#8217;s products may not compete as effectively, if at all. Agility&#8217;s expectations with respect to its total potential addressable market may differ from those of third parties, including investors or securities analysts. If demand does not develop as expected or if Agility cannot accurately forecast pricing, adoption rates, and sales cycle for its products, its business, results of operations, and financial condition will be adversely affected. 
 The benefits offered by Agility&#8217;s humanoid robot, Digit, and future products could be supplanted by advances in competing technologies that may match or exceed the capabilities of humanoid robots at lower cost or with less operational complexity. If alternative automation technologies emerge that render humanoid robots less competitive or obsolete for warehouse, logistics and manufacturing applications, demand for Agility&#8217;s products could decline materially. 
 The benefits offered by Agility&#8217;s humanoid robot, Digit, and future products could be supplanted by advances in autonomous mobile robots, fixed warehouse automation systems, AI -driven software solutions, or other competing technologies that may match or exceed the capabilities of humanoid robots at lower cost or with less operational complexity. Although Agility believes that its humanoid robots will be superior to alternative automation technologies in addressing tasks requiring human -like dexterity and mobility in unstructured environments, alternative technologies may match or exceed the benefits introduced by its products or be more cost effective. The development of any

 alternative technology that can compete with or supplant humanoid robots may materially and adversely affect Agility&#8217;s business, prospects, financial condition, and operating results in ways Agility does not currently anticipate. Successful commercialization of competing automation approaches&#160;&#8212;&#160;including further advances in AMRs, AI -powered pick -and-place systems, or fully integrated warehouse automation platforms&#160;&#8212;&#160;may prove more cost effective or appealing to the warehouse, logistics, and manufacturing markets, potentially reducing market demand for Digit and future humanoid products. Any failure by Agility to develop new or enhanced technologies or processes, or to react to changes in existing technologies, could materially delay its development and introduction of new products, which could result in decreased revenue and a loss of market share. 
 Adverse macroeconomic conditions, including inflation, rising interest rates, and tighter credit markets, could reduce customer capital spending on automation and robotics. During periods of economic uncertainty, Agility&#8217;s customers may delay, reduce, or cancel planned deployments of robotic systems, which would adversely affect Agility&#8217;s revenue, backlog, and growth prospects. 
 Agility&#8217;s business is sensitive to general economic conditions and customer capital spending cycles. Adverse macroeconomic conditions, including inflation, rising interest rates, tighter credit markets, potential recession, and global trade uncertainty, could reduce customer capital spending on automation and robotics. During periods of economic uncertainty, customers in the warehouse, logistics, and manufacturing sectors may delay, reduce, or cancel planned deployments of robotic systems, extend evaluation and procurement timelines, or prioritize spending on core operations rather than new technology adoption. Agility&#8217;s RaaS subscription model, while designed to reduce customer upfront capital requirements, may still be viewed as discretionary spending during economic downturns. In addition, economic uncertainty may reduce the willingness of customers to commit to long -term subscription or deployment agreements. Any delay or reduction in customer spending would adversely affect Agility&#8217;s revenue, backlog, growth prospects, and ability to achieve profitability. 
 Adoption of Agility&#8217;s humanoid robot, Digit, and future products in warehouse and logistics environments may be limited by employee resistance, organized labor concerns, and negative public perception regarding humanoid robots displacing human workers. Employee discomfort with or resistance to humanoid co-workers may be more pronounced with Digit as compared to conventional automation because Digit is designed to work alongside humans in shared workspaces, which could limit commercial acceptance and slow revenue growth. 
 Even if Agility successfully markets its products, the purchase or subscription, adoption, and use of its humanoid robots may be materially and negatively impacted if the employees of Agility&#8217;s customers resist the use and adoption of the products. Agility&#8217;s customer&#8217;s employees may resist the adoption of humanoid robots for several reasons, including a perception that the benefit of using the products does not outweigh the perceived difficulties or discomfort associated with working alongside humanoid co -workers , resistance by labor unions, fear of job displacement, workplace discomfort with humanoid form factors, and safety concerns. Employee discomfort with or resistance to humanoid co -workers may be more pronounced with Digit than with conventional automation because Digit is designed to work alongside humans in shared workspaces and approximates human appearance and movement, which could create unease among workers. In addition, negative public perception regarding humanoid robots displacing human workers may lead to organized opposition, media criticism, political pressure or regulatory developments that constrain customer willingness to deploy Digit. If the employees of Agility&#8217;s customers resist adoption of Digit, or if negative public perception limits customer willingness to deploy humanoid robots, Agility&#8217;s business, prospects, financial condition, and operating results could be materially and adversely affected. 
 Agility operates in an industry highly dependent on global supply chains for semiconductors, batteries, sensors, actuators, and specialty alloys. Disruptions to these supply chains&#160;&#8212;&#160;whether caused by geopolitical events, natural disasters, pandemics, or other factors&#160;&#8212;&#160;could delay production, increase costs, and materially impact Agility&#8217;s ability to fulfill customer orders on a timely basis. 
 Agility relies on third -party suppliers for the provision and development of many key components and materials used in its products, including semiconductors, batteries, sensors, actuators, computing hardware, and specialty alloys. Some of the components used in Digit may have to be purchased from a single source or limited number of sources. If Agility&#8217;s suppliers are unable to supply key components and materials at the required volume, quality, or cost, Agility&#8217;s production schedules, sales, revenues, and profitability will likely be adversely affected. Agility and its suppliers may experience increases in the cost of and interruptions in the supply or shortage of materials due to geopolitical events, natural disasters, pandemics, trade restrictions, or other factors beyond Agility&#8217;s control. Due to

 the complexity of its products, each Digit unit is expected to contain thousands of components, and difficulty securing any critical component could result in production delays that may be compounded if components require redesign or reengineering. Substantial increases in the prices for materials, such as battery cells, semiconductors, or specialty alloys, would increase Agility&#8217;s operating costs and could reduce its margins if the increased costs cannot be recouped through increased pricing. Any sustained supply interruption or shortage could prevent or delay the commercialization of Agility&#8217;s products and materially and negatively impact its business, prospects, financial condition, and operating results. 
 Tariffs, trade restrictions, and &#8216;Buy American&#8217; requirements may increase Agility&#8217;s costs or limit its ability to source critical components and sell into certain markets. Changes in trade policy or the imposition of new tariffs could disrupt Agility&#8217;s supply chain, raise input costs, and reduce the competitiveness of its products in both domestic and international markets. 
 Agility is subject to risks relating to tariffs, trade restrictions, and government procurement requirements that may increase its costs or limit its ability to source critical components. The United&#160;States administration has imposed, and may continue to impose, tariffs on goods imported from other countries, and certain of these countries have imposed retaliatory tariffs. Changes in trade policy, the imposition of new tariffs, or the expansion of existing tariffs could increase the cost of components sourced internationally, disrupt established supply relationships, and reduce the competitiveness of Agility&#8217;s products in both domestic and international markets. In addition, &#8216;Buy American&#8217; or other similar requirements imposed on government contractors may limit Agility&#8217;s ability to source components from the most cost -effective suppliers and may require Agility to establish domestic supply chains that are more expensive. If Agility cannot effectively mitigate the impact of tariffs and trade restrictions through alternative sourcing, supply chain restructuring, or other measures, its margins, production timelines, and competitive position could be materially adversely affected. 
 Negative publicity, adverse events, product defects, or accidents involving competing humanoid robots or similar robotic products could harm public perception of the humanoid robotics market and adversely affect demand for Agility&#8217;s products. 
 The humanoid robotics industry is in its early stages, and adverse events involving competitors&#8217; products could harm public perception of the entire product category. High -profile accidents, product defects, malfunctions, or controversies involving humanoid robots or similar robotic products developed by Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Apptronik, Figure AI, 1X Technologies, or other companies could damage public and customer confidence in humanoid robotics generally, regardless of whether such incidents involve Agility&#8217;s products. Because Agility operates in a new and evolving market, a single widely publicized safety incident&#160;&#8212;&#160;even one entirely unrelated to Agility&#160;&#8212;&#160;could set back industry -wide customer adoption and regulatory acceptance, result in new or more restrictive safety regulations, and reduce the willingness of warehouse, logistics, manufacturing, and other customers to deploy humanoid robots in their facilities. Negative media coverage or heightened regulatory scrutiny of humanoid robots as a category could reduce customer demand for Agility&#8217;s humanoid robot, Digit, and our other products by association, slow market adoption for all industry participants, and materially harm our business, reputation, and growth prospects. 
 The market for humanoid and general-purpose robots is highly dependent on continued advances in AI, foundation models and computer vision, and Agility&#8217;s ability to integrate or develop competitive AI capabilities is critical to the performance and commercial viability of its humanoid robot, Digit, and future products. If the pace of AI development slows, if key AI technologies become unavailable or prohibitively expensive to license, or if competitors achieve superior AI integration, Agility&#8217;s products could become less competitive and its business could be materially adversely affected. 
 The commercial viability of Agility&#8217;s humanoid robot, Digit, and future products is critically dependent on continued advances in AI, foundation models, and computer vision technologies. Agility relies on AI and machine learning capabilities to enable Digit to navigate complex warehouse environments, manipulate objects, and interact safely with human co -workers . If the pace of AI development slows, if key AI technologies become unavailable or prohibitively expensive to license, or if access to large -scale computing infrastructure necessary for AI model training becomes constrained, Agility&#8217;s ability to improve and maintain the performance of its products could be materially impaired. In addition, if competitors&#160;&#8212;&#160;including large technology companies with substantially greater resources&#160;&#8212;&#160;achieve superior AI integration in their humanoid or robotic products, Agility&#8217;s competitive position could be weakened. Full utilization of Agility&#8217;s products may also depend on third -party software, models, and

 Risks Related to Our Business 
 Agility is an early-stage company with a history of net losses, and it expects to incur significant expenses and continuing losses for the foreseeable future. Agility has devoted substantially all of its resources to research, development, and commercialization of its humanoid robot, Digit, and the build-out of its RoboFab manufacturing facility in Salem, Oregon, and has not yet generated sufficient revenue to offset its operating expenses. There can be no assurance that Agility will achieve or sustain profitability. 
 Agility has incurred net losses since inception and expects to continue to incur operating and net losses for the foreseeable future. Agility has devoted substantially all of its resources to research, development, and commercialization of its humanoid robot, Digit, and the build -out of its RoboFab manufacturing facility in Salem, Oregon, and has not yet generated sufficient revenue to offset its operating expenses. Agility expects the rate at which it will incur losses may be higher in future periods as it continues to design, develop, manufacture, and commercialize its existing and future products, or if Agility expands its production capabilities at RoboFab, builds up inventories of parts and components, develops its maintenance and servicing capacity; increases its sales and marketing activities and develops its distribution infrastructure, and/or increases its general and administrative functions to support growing operations and to operate as a public company. Because Agility will incur the costs and expenses from these efforts before it receives any incremental revenues with respect thereto, its losses in future periods will be significant. In addition, Agility may find that these efforts are more expensive than it currently anticipates or that these efforts may not result in revenues, which would further increase its losses. Agility&#8217;s potential profitability is dependent upon the successful development and successful commercial introduction and acceptance of its humanoid robotic systems, which may not occur. There can be no assurance that Agility will achieve or sustain profitability. 
 Agility has yet to achieve positive operating cash flow and, given its projected funding needs, its ability to generate positive cash flow is uncertain. 
 Agility has had negative cash flow from operating activities since inception. Agility expects to continue to have negative cash flow from operating and investing activities as it incurs research and development, sales and marketing, and general and administrative expenses, and makes capital expenditures in its efforts to increase sales, engage in development work, and ramp up manufacturing operations at its RoboFab facility. Agility&#8217;s business will at times require significant amounts of working capital to build inventory and support the growth of its product lines. An inability to generate positive cash flow for the near term may adversely affect Agility&#8217;s ability to raise needed capital on reasonable terms, diminish supplier or customer willingness to enter into transactions with Agility, and have other adverse effects that may decrease its long -term viability. There can be no assurance that Agility will achieve positive operating cash flow in the near future or at all.

 The Post-Closing Company&#8217;s ability to use Agility&#8217;s net operating losses and certain other tax attributes to offset future taxable income may be limited. 
 Agility currently has substantial U.S.&#160;federal net operating loss (&#8220; NOL &#8221;) carry forward and other state tax attributes. The Post -Closing Company&#8217;s ability to use these tax attributes to reduce its future U.S.&#160;federal and state income tax obligations depends on many factors, including its future taxable income, the timing of which is uncertain. In addition, the use of these attributes may be subject to significant limitations under Section&#160;382 and Section&#160;383 of the Code, respectively, and similar provisions of state law, including limitations that may result from the consummation of the business combination. Under those sections of the Code, if a corporation undergoes an &#8220;ownership change,&#8221; the corporation&#8217;s ability to use its pre -change net operating loss carryforwards and other pre -change attributes, such as research tax credits, to offset its post -change income or tax may be limited. In general, an &#8220;ownership change&#8221; will occur if there is a cumulative change in ownership by &#8220;5 -percent shareholders&#8221; that exceeds 50 percentage points over a rolling three -year period. Similar rules may apply under state tax laws. Agility has not yet determined whether the business combination will give rise to an &#8220;ownership change&#8221; for purposes of Section&#160;382 and Section&#160;383 of the Code. Furthermore, Agility may have experienced ownership changes in the past and the Post -Closing Company may experience ownership changes in the future as a result of subsequent shifts in stock ownership (some of which shifts are outside of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s control). As a result, the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s ability to use federal NOLs and other tax attributes to offset future taxable income and taxes could be subject to limitations. For these reasons, the Post -Closing Company may be unable to use a material portion of Agility&#8217;s NOLs and other tax attributes, which could adversely affect its future net income and cash flows.
