 Our Customer Acceleration Program May Not Result in Commercial Deployments or Revenue, and We May Expend Significant Time and Resources Pursuing Program Participants Without a Corresponding Return 
 We established the Customer Acceleration Program (&#8220;CAP&#8221;) in late 2025 to move customers from initial evaluation to scaled deployment of Digit through a proof of technology, an on -site proof of concept and a commercial Robot -as-a-Service deployment. Participation in the CAP requires customers to pay a program fee of approximately $500,000 to Agility, reflecting a meaningful commercial commitment to evaluating deployment of Digit within their operations. As of May 2026, Agility signed four new customers to the CAP program and were engaged with more than 30 prospective customers. Our other current commercial deployments predate the program. Participation in CAP requires us to devote substantial engineering, deployment, and hardware resources to each prospective customer over an extended multi -month period, often before we have any binding commitment that the customer will proceed to a commercial deployment or generate revenue. There can be no assurance that CAP participants will elect to proceed to a commercial deployment on the timeline or at the scale we anticipate, and we may invest significant time and resources pursuing customers through CAP that never result in revenue, which could adversely affect our operating results and cash flows. Because CAP is a relatively new program with a limited track record, our assumptions regarding expected conversion rates and resource requirements may prove inaccurate, and our actual results could differ materially from our current expectations.

 If Agility&#8217;s RaaS model or other recurring revenue models for Digit, including without limitation, any recurring revenue models related to Agility Arc, fail to gain commercial acceptance or generate profitable unit economics at scale, Agility&#8217;s growth, margins, cash flow and path to profitability may be materially adversely affected. 
 Agility&#8217;s ability to generate recurring revenue depends in part on its ability to successfully market its RaaS subscription model and build a base of ongoing customers. The market for humanoid robot -as-a-service offerings is nascent, and there can be no assurance that customers will prefer a subscription model over outright purchase of robotic systems, conventional automation alternatives or manual labor, or that Agility will be able to price its offerings at levels sufficient to achieve profitability. 
 Agility&#8217;s RaaS model has not yet demonstrated profitability at scale. Returns under the model depend on factors that remain unproven, including the useful life and durability of Digit units in warehouse, logistics and manufacturing environments, maintenance and repair costs, customer renewal rates and Agility&#8217;s ability to achieve favorable unit economics over the contract lifecycle. Because Agility retains ownership of deployed Digit units, it is exposed to risks of deterioration, damage or theft, higher servicing costs and earlier -than-expected replacement needs. The RaaS model also requires significant upfront capital investment before subscription revenue is received over time, which may strain Agility&#8217;s cash flow and working capital. If the RaaS model fails to gain commercial acceptance, customers do not renew contracts at anticipated rates, servicing costs exceed expectations, Digit units require more frequent maintenance or replacement than currently anticipated or deployed units have a shorter useful life than anticipated, Agility&#8217;s growth, margins, cash flow and path to profitability could be materially adversely affected.

 Risks Related to Legal and Regulatory Concerns 
 Agility may seek to derive a substantial portion of its revenue from sales to U.S.&#160;federal, state, and foreign government entities, which are subject to budgetary cycles, continuing resolution periods, termination for convenience, audits, investigations, and other risks unique to government contracting. Reductions in government budgets or priorities, or the loss of key government contracts, could materially reduce Agility&#8217;s revenue and harm its financial condition. 
 Sales to government entities are subject to a number of risks unique to government contracting. Selling to government entities can be highly competitive, expensive, and time -consuming , often requiring significant upfront time and expense without any assurance that these efforts will generate a sale. Government demand and payment for Agility&#8217;s products may be impacted by public sector budgetary cycles, continuing resolution periods, and funding authorizations, with funding reductions or delays adversely affecting demand. Government entities may have statutory, contractual, or other legal rights to terminate contracts for convenience or default.  Agility&#8217;s business relies on AI technologies that are subject to a rapidly evolving and fragmented regulatory landscape across multiple jurisdictions, and failure to comply with new or changing AI laws could result in enforcement actions, significant fines, litigation, and restrictions on Agility&#8217;s ability to develop, deploy, or commercialize its products. 
 We use AI and machine learning, including proprietary AI and machine learning algorithms and models, as well as third -party generative AI tools used internally to support software development and business operations (collectively, &#8220;AI Technologies&#8221;) throughout our business, and are making significant investments in this area. For example, we use AI Technologies to develop proprietary AI models that run onboard our robots to perform perception and motion control, and we use third -party generative AI tools internally to support software development and business operations. 
 The regulatory framework for AI Technologies is rapidly evolving. Already, certain existing legal regimes (e.g., relating to data privacy) regulate certain aspects of AI Technologies, and many federal, state and foreign government bodies and agencies have enacted or are currently considering additional laws and regulations governing AI.&#160;Additionally, existing laws and regulations may be enjoined in judicial proceedings, or may be interpreted or enforced in ways that would affect the operation and use of our AI Technologies, or could be rescinded or amended as new administrations take differing approaches to evolving AI Technologies. As a result, implementation standards and enforcement practices are likely to remain uncertain for the foreseeable future, and we cannot predict the impact future laws, regulations, or standards, or the market perception of their requirements, may have on our business or how we will respond to these laws or regulations. 
 In the United&#160;States, the regulatory framework for AI Technologies faces significant uncertainty. At the federal level, Congress has yet to enact meaningful AI legislation. Instead, federal policy on AI has been shaped by a series of executive orders that have shifted priorities and requirements substantially depending on the administration in power. In the absence of federal AI legislation, states have filled the void by enacting laws regulating different aspects of AI Technologies. For example, California has enacted laws and regulations related to AI safety protocols, reporting and transparency, among other AI -related topics. In addition, Utah&#8217;s Artificial Intelligence Policy Act establishes disclosure requirements and accountability measures for the use of generative AI in certain consumer interaction, and the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act prohibits the development and deployment of AI systems for certain purposes while establishing a regulatory sandbox. 
 Numerous other states have enacted, passed, or are considering AI -focused legislation, creating a patchwork of regulations and a complex compliance challenge. However, the durability of these laws and the potential of additional state -level legislative activity faces uncertainty following President Trump&#8217;s December&#160;2025 Executive Order &#8220;Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence.&#8221; This Executive Order establishes a federal policy favoring a uniform national AI regulatory framework designed to promote innovation and U.S.&#160;global competitiveness. The order directs federal agencies to identify, challenge, and potentially pre -empt state and local AI laws that are viewed as inconsistent with or burdensome to this national approach. It remains to be seen how agencies will effectuate this directive, and how states will approach AI legislation moving forward. Any or all of the foregoing regulatory developments could affect our use of AI and our ability to provide, improve or commercialize our services, require changes to our operations and processes, and materially adversely affect our business, results of operations, and financial condition. Further, any failure or perceived failure by us to comply with existing or newly enacted laws, regulations and other requirements relating to AI Technologies could result in legal claims or proceedings (including class actions), regulatory investigations or enforcement actions. 
 In Europe, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (the &#8220; EU AI Act &#8221;) has entered into force, and establishes a comprehensive, risk -based governance framework for AI in the EU market. The EU AI Act&#8217;s obligations are being phased in over time: while certain obligations have applied since February 2025, obligations for high -risk AI systems were originally scheduled to apply from August 2026 (or August 2027, for systems covered by harmonization legislation listed in Annex I), but these deadlines are expected to be extended pursuant to a political agreement among the EU institutions. These increased costs and administrative burdens of operating as a public company could have a material adverse effect on the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s business, prospects, financial condition, and operating results, particularly given the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s early stage of operations and limited administrative resources.

 Short sellers may engage in manipulative activity intended to drive down the market price of the Post-Closing Company&#8217;s common stock, which could also result in related regulatory and governmental scrutiny, among other effects. 
 Short selling is the practice of selling securities that the seller does not own but rather has borrowed or intends to borrow from a third party with the intention of later buying lower priced identical securities to return to the lender. Accordingly, it is in the interest of a short seller of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s common stock for the price to decline. At any time, short sellers may publish, or arrange for the publication of, opinions or characterizations that are intended to create negative market momentum. Issuers, like the Post -Closing Company, whose securities have historically had limited trading history or volumes and/or have been susceptible to relatively high volatility levels

 The provisions of the Proposed Certificate of Incorporation requiring exclusive forum in the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware and the federal district courts of the United&#160;States for certain types of lawsuits may have the effect of discouraging certain lawsuits, including derivative lawsuits and lawsuits against our directors and officers, by limiting plaintiffs&#8217; ability to bring a claim in a judicial forum that they find favorable. 
 The Post -Closing Company&#8217;s proposed certificate of incorporation (the &#8220; Proposed Certificate of Incorporation &#8221;) provides that, to the fullest extent permitted by law, and unless the Post -Closing Company consents in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware (or, if and only if the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware lacks subject matter jurisdiction, any state court located within the State of Delaware or, if and only if all such state courts lack subject matter jurisdiction, the federal district court for the District of Delaware) and any appellate court therefrom will be the sole and exclusive forum for (i)&#160;any derivative claim or cause of action brought on behalf of the Post -Closing Company, (ii)&#160;any claim or cause of action for breach of a fiduciary duty owed by any current or former director, officer or other employee of the Post -Closing Company to the Post -Closing Company or the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s stockholders, (iii)&#160;any claim or cause of action against the Post -Closing Company or any current or former director, officer or other employee of the Post -Closing Company arising out of or

The enforceability of similar choice of forum provisions in other companies&#8217; certificates of incorporation or bylaws has been challenged in legal proceedings, and it is possible that, in connection with any applicable action brought against the Post -Closing Company, a court could find the choice of forum provisions contained in the Proposed Certificate of Incorporation to be inapplicable or unenforceable in such action. 
 While the Delaware courts have determined that such choice of forum provisions are facially valid, a stockholder may nevertheless seek to bring a claim in a venue other than those designated in the exclusive forum provisions, and there can be no assurance that such provisions will be enforced by a court in those other jurisdictions.  Following the business combination, the Post-Closing Company is expected to be an &#8220;emerging growth company&#8221; and a &#8220;smaller reporting company&#8221; within the meaning of the Securities Act, and to the extent that the Post-Closing Company takes advantage of certain exemptions from disclosure requirements available to emerging growth companies or smaller reporting companies, this could make the Post-Closing Company&#8217;s securities less attractive to investors and may make it more difficult to compare the Post-Closing Company&#8217;s performance with other public companies. 
 Following the business combination, the Post -Closing Company is expected to be an &#8220;emerging growth company&#8221; within the meaning of the Securities Act, as modified by the JOBS Act, and the Post -Closing Company may take advantage of certain exemptions from various reporting requirements that are applicable to other public companies that are not emerging growth companies including, but not limited to, not being required to comply with the auditor attestation requirements of Section&#160;404 of the Sarbanes -Oxley Act, reduced disclosure obligations regarding executive compensation in the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s periodic reports and proxy statements, and exemptions from the requirements of holding a nonbinding advisory vote on executive compensation and shareholder approval of any golden parachute payments not previously approved. As a result, the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s stockholders may not have access to certain information they may deem important. Neither CCXI nor Agility can predict whether investors will find the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s securities less attractive because the Post -Closing Company will rely on these exemptions. If some investors find the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s securities less attractive as a result of its reliance on these exemptions, the trading prices of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s securities may be lower than they otherwise would be, there may be a less active trading market for the securities and the trading prices of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s securities may be more volatile. 
 Further, Section&#160;102(b)(1)&#160;of the JOBS Act exempts emerging growth companies from being required to comply with new or revised financial accounting standards until private companies (that is, those that have not had a Securities Act registration statement declared effective or do not have a class of securities registered under the Exchange&#160;Act) are required to comply with the new or revised financial accounting standards. The JOBS Act provides that a company can elect to opt out of the extended transition period and comply with the requirements that apply to non -emerging growth

 companies but any such election to opt out is irrevocable.  Agility and CCXI will incur significant transaction costs, which could be higher than currently anticipated, and these transaction costs add risk to the Post-Closing Company&#8217;s ability to be a going concern and/or act on the Post-Closing Company&#8217;s business plan. 
 Both CCXI and Agility have incurred and expect to continue to incur significant, non -recurring costs in connection with consummating the Transactions.  Without consideration of the proposed business combination transaction, Agility has concluded there is substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern, which could materially adversely affect the Post-Closing Company&#8217;s business, financial condition, and the value of your investment. 
 Agility&#8217;s historical financial statements have been prepared under the assumption that Agility will continue as a going concern. Agility has incurred operating losses since its inception and that management expects operating losses and negative cash flows to continue for the foreseeable future, which raises substantial doubt about Agility&#8217;s ability to continue as a going concern that Agility concluded could not be overcome by management&#8217;s plans as of the date of financials statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, which did not consider the proposed business combination transaction. In addition, Grant Thornton LLP, Agility&#8217;s independent registered public accounting firm, has issued a report on Agility&#8217;s audited financial statements for the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024 that includes an explanatory paragraph stating that substantial doubt exists about Agility&#8217;s ability to continue as a going concern. The going concern basis of presentation assumes that, from the date the financial statements are issued, Agility will continue in operation, realize its assets and satisfy its liabilities in the normal course of business for a minimum of one year. 
 Based on Agility&#8217;s current operating plan and forecasted cash flows, which did not consider the proposed business combination transaction, management has determined that existing cash and cash equivalents will not be sufficient to fund operations and satisfy obligations as they become due for at least one year from the date the financial statements are issued. Accordingly, substantial doubt exists regarding Agility&#8217;s ability to continue as a going concern within one year after the date the financial statements are issued. The accompanying financial statements do not include any adjustments relating to the recoverability and classification of recorded asset amounts or the amounts and classification of liabilities that might result from the outcome of this uncertainty. 
 Agility is an early -stage growth company in the development stage that has incurred net losses since inception and expects to continue to incur operating and net losses for the foreseeable future. Agility has devoted substantially all of its resources to research, development, and commercialization of its humanoid robot, Digit, and the build -out of its RoboFab manufacturing facility in Salem, Oregon, and has not yet generated sufficient revenue to offset its operating expenses. Agility has had negative cash flow from operating activities since inception, and expects to continue to have negative cash flow from operating and investing activities as it incurs research and development, sales and marketing, and general and administrative expenses, and makes capital expenditures in its efforts to increase sales and ramp up manufacturing operations. 
 Management&#8217;s plans to alleviate these conditions include pursuing additional equity financing opportunities and strategic transactions, including the proposed business combination. During 2025, Agility completed multiple closings associated with its Series C financing and received aggregate net proceeds of approximately $162,385,117, and from January 1, 2026 through the date the financial statements were issued, received approximately $5,004,410 of additional proceeds associated with subsequent Series C closings. In addition, in July 2026, Agility raised $100 million of additional financing through the issuance and sale of simple agreements for future equity (&#8220;SAFEs&#8221;). However, the consummation of the proposed business combination is not fully within Agility&#8217;s control and are not considered probable of being effectively implemented under ASC 205 -40 , management has concluded that these plans do not alleviate the substantial doubt regarding Agility&#8217;s ability to continue as a going concern. 
 The consummation of the business combination is expected to provide Agility with access to additional capital, which Agility expects will help fund its operations and business plan. However, there can be no assurance that the business combination will be completed or, if completed, that the proceeds therefrom will be sufficient to fund Agility&#8217;s operations for at least one year or to otherwise alleviate the conditions that raise substantial doubt about Agility&#8217;s ability to continue as a going concern. If Agility is not able to obtain additional equity or debt financing on reasonable terms,

 Risks Related to CCXI, the Domestication and the Business Combination 
 The consummation of the proposed business combination is subject to a number of conditions and, if those conditions are not satisfied or waived, the definitive agreements relating to the proposed business combination, including the Merger Agreement, may be terminated in accordance with such definitive agreement&#8217;s terms and the proposed business combination may not be completed. 
 The proposed business combination is subject to certain conditions as outlined in the Merger Agreement. If the conditions are not met, there is a risk that the business combination may not occur as planned. Even if the Merger Agreement is approved by the shareholders of CCXI, specified conditions must be satisfied or waived before the parties to the Merger Agreement are obligated to complete the proposed business combination. CCXI does not control the satisfaction of all such conditions. For a summary of the conditions that must be satisfied or waived prior to completion of the business combination, please see the section entitled &#8220; Proposal&#160;No.&#160;1 &#8212;&#160;The Business Combination Proposal&#160;&#8212;&#160;Certain Agreements Related to the Business Combination&#160;&#8212;&#160;Merger Agreement&#160;&#8212;&#160;Conditions to Closing General Conditions .&#8221; If the closing conditions are not satisfied or waived, the proposed business combination will not occur, or will be delayed pending later satisfaction or waiver, and such delay may cause CCXI and Agility to each lose some or all of the intended benefits of the proposed business combination and this could have a significant material impact for each of our businesses. 
 The ability of CCXI&#8217;s shareholders to exercise redemption rights with respect to a large number of outstanding CCXI public shares may prevent CCXI from completing the proposed business combination or optimizing its capital structure. 
 CCXI does not know how many CCXI public shareholders will ultimately exercise their redemption rights in connection with the business combination. 
 As such, the business combination is structured based on certain assumptions as to the number of shares that will be submitted for redemption. If a higher number of shares are ultimately submitted for redemption, including as a result of an extension of the combination period, if any, CCXI may need to restructure the transaction to reserve a greater portion of the cash in the trust account or arrange for additional third -party financing. As of&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;, 2026, there was $&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;in the trust account. 
 The Merger Agreement provides that the consummation of the business combination is conditioned upon CCXI having at least $200&#160;million of Available Closing SPAC Cash. There can be no assurances that CCXI will be able to retain all of the cash in the trust account. 
 Raising additional financing, or increasing the equity portion of the aggregate consideration to be paid to Agility equityholders, in either case, if so authorized by Agility, may involve dilutive equity issuances or the incurrence of indebtedness at higher than desirable levels. These considerations may limit CCXI&#8217;s ability to complete the business combination or optimize the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s capital structure. 
 CCXI&#8217;s Sponsor and the Insiders have agreed to vote in favor of the business combination, regardless of how CCXI&#8217;s public shareholders vote.

 The National Securities Markets Improvement Act&#160;of&#160;1996, which is a federal statute, prevents or preempts the states from regulating the sale of certain securities, which are referred to as &#8220;covered securities.&#8221; Because CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares are listed on Nasdaq, CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares qualify as covered securities under such statute. Although the states are preempted from regulating the sale of CCXI securities, the federal statute does allow the states to investigate companies if there is a suspicion of fraud, and, if there is a finding of fraudulent activity, then the states can regulate or bar the sale of covered securities in a particular case. While CCXI is not aware of a state having used these powers to prohibit or restrict the sale of securities issued by blank check companies, other than the State of Idaho, certain state securities regulators view blank check companies unfavorably and might use these powers, or threaten to use these powers, to hinder the sale of securities of blank check companies in their states.  Because CCXI is incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands, in the event the business combination is not completed, you may face difficulties in protecting your interests, and your ability to protect your rights through the U.S.&#160;federal courts may be limited. 
 Because CCXI is currently incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands, you may face difficulties in protecting your interests and your ability to protect your rights through the U.S.&#160;federal courts may be limited prior to the Domestication. CCXI is currently an exempted company under the laws of the Cayman Islands. As a result, it may be difficult for investors to effect service of process within the United&#160;States upon members of the CCXI Board or CCXI&#8217;s executive officers, or enforce judgments obtained in the U.S.&#160;courts against members of the CCXI Board or CCXI&#8217;s officers. 
 Until the Domestication is effected, CCXI&#8217;s corporate affairs are governed by the CCXI current articles of association, the Companies Act and the common law of the Cayman Islands. CCXI is also subject to the federal securities laws of the United&#160;States. The rights of shareholders to take action against members of the CCXI Board, actions by minority shareholders and the fiduciary responsibilities of members of the CCXI Board to CCXI under the laws of the Cayman Islands are to a large extent governed by the common law of the Cayman Islands. The common law in the Cayman Islands is derived in part from comparatively limited judicial precedent in the Cayman Islands and from English common law. Appeals from the Cayman Islands Courts to the Privy Council (which is the final Court of Appeal for British overseas territories such as the Cayman Islands) are binding on a court in the Cayman Islands. Decisions of the English courts, and particularly the Supreme Court and the Court of Appeal are generally of persuasive authority but are not binding in the courts of the Cayman Islands. Decisions of courts in other Commonwealth jurisdictions are similarly of persuasive but not binding authority. The rights of CCXI&#8217;s shareholders and the fiduciary responsibilities of members of the CCXI Board under Cayman Islands law are different from what they would be under statutes or judicial precedent in some jurisdictions in the United&#160;States. In particular, the Cayman Islands has a different body of securities laws as compared to the United&#160;States, and certain states, such as Delaware, may have more fully developed and judicially interpreted bodies of corporate law. In addition, Cayman Islands companies may not have standing to initiate a shareholders derivative action in a federal court of the United&#160;States. 
 CCXI has been advised by Ogier (Cayman) LLP, its Cayman Islands legal counsel, that the courts of the Cayman Islands are unlikely (1)&#160;to recognize or enforce against CCXI judgments of courts of the United&#160;States predicated upon the civil liability provisions of the federal securities laws of the United&#160;States or any state; and (2)&#160;in original actions brought in the Cayman Islands, to impose liabilities against CCXI predicated upon the civil liability provisions of the federal securities laws of the United&#160;States or any state, so far as the liabilities imposed by those provisions are penal in nature. In those circumstances, although there is no statutory enforcement in the Cayman Islands of judgments obtained in the United&#160;States, the courts of the Cayman Islands will recognize and enforce a foreign money judgment of a foreign court of competent jurisdiction without retrial on the merits based on the principle that a judgment of a competent foreign court imposes upon the judgment debtor an obligation to pay the sum for which judgment has been given provided certain conditions are met. For a foreign judgment to be enforced in the Cayman Islands, such judgment must be final and conclusive and for a liquidated sum, and must not be in respect of taxes or a fine or penalty, inconsistent with a Cayman Islands judgment in respect of the same matter, impeachable on the grounds of fraud or obtained in a manner, or be of a kind the enforcement of which is, contrary to natural justice or the public policy of the Cayman Islands (awards of punitive or multiple damages may well be held to be contrary to public policy). A Cayman Islands court may stay enforcement proceedings if concurrent proceedings are being brought elsewhere.

 The Domestication may result in adverse tax consequences for holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares or CCXI Warrants. 
 CCXI intends for the Domestication to qualify as a reorganization within the meaning of Section&#160;36 8(a)(1)(F) of the Code, i.e., an F Reorganization (and is not otherwise treated as a reorganization within the meaning of Section&#160;368(a)(1)&#160;of the Code). If the Domestication fails to qualify as an F Reorganization (and does not otherwise qualify as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; within the meaning of Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code), a U.S.&#160;Holder generally would recognize gain or loss with respect to its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares or CCXI Warrants in an amount equal to the difference, if any, between the sum of the fair market value of the corresponding CCXI common stock or CCXI Warrants received in the Domestication and the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares or CCXI Warrants surrendered. U.S.&#160;Holders exercising redemption rights will be subject to the potential tax consequences of the Domestication. Additionally, Non -U .S.&#160;Holders generally will become subject to withholding tax on any amounts treated as dividends paid on Agility common stock after the Domestication. 
 Assuming that the Domestication qualifies as an F Reorganization, subject to the PFIC rules discussed below, U.S.&#160;Holders generally will be subject to Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code in connection with the Domestication, and, as a result: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; a U.S.&#160;Holder who is a 10% U.S.&#160;Shareholder on the date of the Domestication generally will be required to include in income as a deemed dividend deemed paid by CCXI the &#8220;all earnings and profits amount&#8221; (as defined in the Treasury Regulations under Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code) attributable to the CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares held directly by such U.S.&#160;Holder; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; a U.S.&#160;Holder whose CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares have a fair market value of $50,000 or more on the date of the Domestication and who, on the date of the Domestication, is not a 10% U.S.&#160;Shareholder generally will recognize gain (but not loss) with respect to its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares as if such U.S.&#160;Holder exchanged its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares for CCXI common stock in a taxable transaction, unless such U.S.&#160;Holder elects in accordance with applicable Treasury Regulations to include in income as a deemed dividend deemed paid by CCXI the &#8220;all earnings and profits amount&#8221; (as defined in the Treasury Regulations under Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code) attributable to such U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares; and 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; a U.S.&#160;Holder whose CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares have a fair market value of less than $50,000 on the date of the Domestication and who, on the date of the Domestication, is not a 10% U.S.&#160;Shareholder, generally will not recognize any gain or loss or include any part of CCXI&#8217;s earnings and profits in income under Section&#160;367 of the Code in connection with the Domestication. 
 Additionally, even if the Domestication qualifies as an F Reorganization, proposed Treasury Regulations promulgated under Section&#160;1291(f)&#160;of the Code and certain other PFIC rules (which have retroactive proposed effective dates) generally require that a U.S.&#160;person who disposes of stock of a PFIC (including for this purpose, under a proposed Treasury Regulation that generally treats an &#8220;option&#8221; to acquire the stock of a PFIC as stock of the PFIC, exchanging CCXI Warrants for newly issued CCXI Delaware Warrants in the Domestication) must recognize gain equal to the excess of the fair market value of such PFIC stock over its adjusted tax basis, notwithstanding any other provision of the Code. CCXI believes that it is likely classified as a PFIC for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes. As a result, these proposed Treasury Regulations, if finalized in their current form, would generally require a U.S.&#160;Holder of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares to recognize gain under the PFIC rules on the exchange of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares for CCXI common stock pursuant to the Domestication unless such U.S.&#160;Holder has made certain tax elections with respect to such U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares. The proposed Treasury Regulations provide coordinating rules with other sections of the Code, including Section&#160;367(b), which affect the manner in which the rules under such other sections apply to transfers of PFIC stock. These proposed Treasury Regulations, if finalized in their current form, would also apply to a U.S.&#160;Holder who exchanges CCXI Warrants for newly issued CCXI Delaware Warrants; under current law, however, the elections mentioned above do not apply to CCXI Warrants. Any gain recognized from the application of the PFIC rules described above would be taxable income with no corresponding receipt of cash. The tax on any such gain would be imposed at the rate applicable to ordinary income and an interest charge would apply based on complex rules designed to offset the tax deferral to such U.S.&#160;Holder on the undistributed earnings,

 if any, of CCXI.&#160;It is not possible to determine at this time whether, in what form, and with what effective date, final Treasury Regulations under Section&#160;1291(f)&#160;of the Code may be adopted or how any such Treasury Regulations would apply.  CCXI&#8217;s shareholders may be held liable for claims by third parties against CCXI to the extent of distributions received by them upon redemption of their shares. 
 If CCXI is forced to enter into an insolvent liquidation, any distributions received by shareholders could be viewed as an unlawful payment if it were proved that immediately following the date on which the distribution was made, CCXI was unable to pay their debts as they fall due in the ordinary course of business. As a result, a liquidator could seek to recover some or all amounts received by their shareholders. Furthermore, the CCXI Board may be viewed as having breached their fiduciary duties to their creditors or as having acted in bad faith, exposing themselves and CCXI to claims, by paying public shareholders from the trust account prior to addressing the claims of creditors. The claims may be brought against CCXI for these reasons. The CCXI Board and the CCXI officers who knowingly and willfully authorized or permitted any distribution to be paid out of the share premium account while CCXI was unable to pay their debts as they fall due in the ordinary course of business would be guilty of an offense and may be liable for a fine of $18,293 and imprisonment for five&#160;years in the Cayman Islands. 
 Activities taken by CCXI, the Sponsor and/or existing CCXI shareholders to increase the likelihood of approval of the business combination proposal and the other proposals described in this proxy statement/prospectus could have a negative effect on the CCXI Ordinary Shares. 
 At any time prior to the extraordinary general meeting, during a period when they are not then aware of any material nonpublic information regarding CCXI or its securities, the Sponsor, directors, officers, advisors or any of their respective affiliates may purchase shares from institutional and other investors who vote, or indicate an intention to vote, against the business combination proposal, or execute agreements to purchase such shares from such investors in the future, or they may enter into transactions with such investors and others to provide them with incentives to acquire shares of CCXI Ordinary Shares or vote their shares in favor of the business combination proposal. While the exact nature of any such transactions, if any, has not been determined, the purpose of such share purchases and other transactions would be to decrease the number of redemptions to increase the likelihood of satisfaction of the requirements to consummate the Transactions. Entering into any such arrangements may have a negative effect on the market price of CCXI Ordinary Shares. For example, as a result of these arrangements, an investor or holder may have the ability to effectively purchase shares at a price lower than market and may therefore be more likely to sell the shares they own, either prior to or immediately after the extraordinary general meeting. Further, the public &#8220;float&#8221; of the public shares and the number of beneficial holders of CCXI&#8217;s securities may be reduced as a result of such purchases, possibly making it difficult to obtain or maintain the quotation, listing or trading of CCXI&#8217;s securities

 The estimated net cash per share of CCXI Ordinary Shares that will be contributed to the Post-Closing Company in the business combination is less than the redemption price. 
 Each CCXI public unit sold in the CCXI IPO at an offering price of $10.00 per CCXI public unit consisted of one CCXI public share and one -tenth of one CCXI public warrant. As a result, CCXI public shareholders who own CCXI&#8217;s public shares on a redemption date can anticipate receiving the redemption price in connection with a redemption for each CCXI public share that they choose to redeem. 
 There can be no assurance that, after the business combination, the CCXI public shareholders would be able to sell their shares in the post -business combination company for the redemption price, or any higher price. In recent&#160;years, the share prices of many post -business combination companies have fallen following a business combination. As a result, if the CCXI public shareholders continue to hold shares in the post -business combination company following the business combination, CCXI cannot assure CCXI&#8217;s shareholders that the trading price of such shares will be greater than the redemption price.

 CFIUS or other regulatory agencies may modify, delay or prevent the business combination. 
 CFIUS has authority to review direct and indirect foreign acquisitions of and certain foreign investments in U.S.&#160;businesses. Whether CFIUS has jurisdiction to review a transaction depends on, among other factors, the nature and structure of the transaction (including the level of the foreign counterparty&#8217;s beneficial ownership interest and the nature of the foreign counterparty&#8217;s information or governance rights with respect to the U.S.&#160;business), and the nature of the U.S.&#160;business&#8217;s technology and operations (e.g., data collection practices). 
 

 81 
 Table of Contents 

 
 All transactions that could result in foreign &#8220;control&#8221; of a U.S.&#160;business as that term is defined in the CFIUS regulations are subject to CFIUS jurisdiction. Transactions with foreign counterparties involving a U.S.&#160;businesses that has a qualifying nexus to &#8220;critical technology,&#8221; &#8220;critical infrastructure,&#8221; or &#8220;sensitive personal data&#8221; are subject to a lower CFIUS jurisdiction threshold that is triggered when a foreign investor will not &#8220;control&#8221; the U.S.&#160;business, but will be afforded certain information or governance rights with respect to the U.S.&#160;business&#160;&#8212;&#160;including board representation or observer rights, access to certain nonpublic technical information, or the right to involvement in certain company decision making. 
 When a foreign acquisition or investment transaction is subject to CFIUS jurisdiction (a &#8220; Covered Transaction &#8221;), the CFIUS regulations may require the parties thereto to submit pre -closing filings seeking CFIUS approval to close the transaction at issue. In the absence of such &#8220;mandatory&#8221; filing requirements, and if the parties forego a &#8220;voluntary&#8221; CFIUS filing, CFIUS may initiate a review of the covered transaction post -closing on its own initiative. If during the course of a review of a covered transaction CFIUS determines that the transaction gives rise to national security concerns, CFIUS may prohibit, unwind, or place restrictions on the transaction. 
 If the business combination were to fall within CFIUS&#8217;s jurisdiction, CFIUS may inquire about, intervene in, prohibit, or unwind the transaction or parts thereof before or after the closing. For example, CFIUS may decide to modify the transaction by limiting certain foreign shareholder rights, or to delay the business combination to address perceived national security concerns therewith. If CFIUS determines that it is unable to address perceived national security issues with the transaction by modifying the terms thereof, CFIUS may request the President of the United&#160;States to prohibit the business combination before closing, or unwind the transaction or parts thereof after closing&#160;&#8212;&#160;including by requiring certain foreign investors to divest of some or all of their ownership interest in CCXI.&#160;Should CFIUS inquire about the business combination or require a formal review thereof, the time necessary for the completion of such inquiry or review may prevent the business combination from occurring within the applicable time period required under CCXI&#8217;s certificate of incorporation. These risks may limit the attractiveness of, delay or prevent CCXI from pursuing the business combination. 
 Any foreign direct investment regulatory review, whether by CFIUS or otherwise, could be lengthy, and CCXI has limited time to complete the business combination. If CCXI is unable to consummate the business combination within the applicable time period required under CCXI&#8217;s certificate of incorporation, CCXI will be required to wind up, redeem and liquidate. If CCXI is required to wind up, redeem and liquidate, CCXI shareholders will miss the opportunity to benefit from an investment in a target company, the CCXI Warrants will expire worthless and the appreciation in value of such investment through a business combination. 
 Legal proceedings in connection with the business combination, the outcomes of which are uncertain, could delay or prevent the completion of the business combination. 
 Lawsuits may be filed against CCXI or its directors and officers in connection with the Transactions.  CCXI may amend the terms of the CCXI public warrants in a manner that may be adverse to holders of CCXI public warrants with the approval by the holders of at least 50% of the then-outstanding CCXI public warrants.  In order not to be regulated as an investment company under the Investment Company Act, unless CCXI can qualify for an exclusion, CCXI must ensure that CCXI is engaged primarily in a business other than investing, reinvesting or trading in securities and that CCXI&#8217;s activities do not include investing, reinvesting, owning, holding or trading &#8220;investment securities&#8221; constituting more than 40% of CCXI&#8217;s total assets (exclusive of U.S.&#160;government securities and cash items) on an unconsolidated basis. CCXI&#8217;s business is to identify and complete a business combination and thereafter to operate the post -transaction business or assets for the long term. CCXI does not plan to buy businesses or assets with a view to resale or profit from their resale. CCXI does not plan to buy unrelated businesses or assets or to be a passive investor. 
 It is possible that a claim could be made that CCXI has been operating as an unregistered investment company. If CCXI is deemed to be an investment company for purposes of the Investment Company Act, we might be forced to abandon CCXI&#8217;s efforts to complete an initial business combination and instead be required to liquidate CCXI.&#160;If we are required to liquidate CCXI, CCXI&#8217;s investors would not be able to realize the benefits of owning stock in a successor operating business, including the potential appreciation in the value of CCXI&#8217;s shares following such a transaction. 
 CCXI does not believe that CCXI&#8217;s principal activities currently subject CCXI to the Investment Company Act. To this end, from the time beginning with the consummation of the CCXI IPO, the proceeds held in the trust account have been invested only in United&#160;States &#8220;government securities&#8221; within the meaning of Section&#160;2(a)(16)&#160;of the Investment Company Act having a maturity of 185&#160;days or less, in money market funds meeting certain conditions under Rule&#160;2a -7 promulgated under the Investment Company Act which invest only in direct U.S.&#160;government treasury obligations or cash. Pursuant to the trust agreement, the trustee is not permitted to invest in other securities or assets. By restricting the investment of the proceeds to these instruments and by subsequently holding all funds in the trust account in cash, which may include demand deposit accounts (as described in the following paragraph), and by having a business plan targeted at acquiring and growing businesses for the long -term (rather than on buying and selling businesses in the manner of a merchant bank or private equity fund), CCXI does not believe CCXI is an &#8220;investment company&#8221; within the meaning of the Investment Company Act. 
 The CCXI IPO was not intended for persons seeking a return on investments in government securities or investment securities. The trust account is intended as a holding place for funds pending the earliest to occur of: (1)&#160;the completion of CCXI&#8217;s primary business objective, which is a business combination; (2)&#160;the redemption of any public shares properly submitted in connection with a shareholder vote to amend the CCXI current articles of association (a)&#160;to modify the substance or timing of CCXI&#8217;s obligation to redeem 100% of the public shares if CCXI has not consummated an initial business combination within the completion window, or (b)&#160;with respect to any other provision of the articles relating to the rights of holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares or pre -initial business combination activity; and (3)&#160;the redemption of CCXI&#8217;s public shares if CCXI has not completed an initial business combination within the completion window. Because CCXI has invested only in permitted instruments, CCXI believes CCXI is not an investment company. If CCXI is deemed to be subject to the Investment Company Act, compliance with these additional regulatory burdens would require additional expenses for which CCXI has not allotted funds and may hinder CCXI&#8217;s ability to consummate CCXI&#8217;s initial business combination. If CCXI is unable to complete the initial business combination within the completion window CCXI&#8217;s public shareholders may receive only approximately $10.00 per share on the liquidation of CCXI&#8217;s trust account. In certain circumstances, CCXI&#8217;s public shareholders may receive less than $10.00 per share on the redemption of their shares if CCXI is unable to complete CCXI&#8217;s initial business combination within the completion window. 
 To mitigate the risk of being deemed to have been operating as an unregistered investment company (including under the subjective test of Section&#160;3(a)(1)(A)&#160;of the Investment Company Act&#160;of&#160;1940, as amended), all funds in the trust account are held and will be held in cash (which may include demand deposit accounts) until the earlier of consummation of CCXI&#8217;s initial business combination or liquidation. 
 Furthermore, such cash (which may include demand deposit accounts) is held in bank accounts that exceed federally insured limits as guaranteed by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (the &#8220; FDIC &#8221;). While CCXI has only placed CCXI&#8217;s trust account deposits with Continental Stock Transfer&#160;&amp; Trust Company, only a small portion of the funds in CCXI&#8217;s trust account will be guaranteed by the FDIC.

 The Post-Closing Company may be subject to a 1% U.S.&#160;federal excise tax in connection with redemptions of the Post-Closing Company common stock. 
 On August&#160;16, 2022, President Biden signed into law the Inflation Reduction Act&#160;of&#160;2022, which, among other things, imposes a 1% excise tax on the fair market value of stock repurchased by &#8220;covered corporations&#8221; beginning in 2023, with certain exceptions (the &#8220; Excise Tax &#8221;).&#160;The Excise Tax is imposed on the repurchasing corporation itself, not its stockholders from whom or which the stock is repurchased.&#160;Because the Post -Closing Company is domesticating and continuing as a Delaware corporation and CCXI&#8217;s securities will continue to trade on Nasdaq, we believe that we are a &#8220;covered corporation&#8221; for this purpose, however, we expect that we will not be subject to material excise tax payments in connection with redemptions, either because redemptions will occur prior to the Domestication or because such redemptions will be offset by other share issuances made by us during the same taxable year.&#160;The amount of the Excise Tax is generally 1% of the fair market value of the shares repurchased at the time of the repurchase. 
 However, for purposes of calculating the Excise Tax, repurchasing corporations are permitted to net the fair market value of certain new stock issuances (such as the shares of Post -Closing Company common stock being issued in the business combination) against the fair market value of stock repurchases during the same taxable year.&#160;In addition, certain exceptions apply to the Excise Tax. 
 Any redemption or other repurchase that the Post -Closing Company makes after the Domestication may be subject to the Excise Tax.&#160;Whether and to what extent the Post -Closing Company would be subject to the Excise Tax would depend on a number of factors, including (1)&#160;the fair market value of the redemptions and repurchases in connection with the business combination, (2)&#160;the nature and amount of any equity issuances in connection with the business combination, including the business combination and any PIPE Investment, and (3)&#160;the content of regulations and other guidance from the U.S.&#160;Department of Treasury.&#160;Prior to the consummation of the business combination, funds in the trust account, including any interest thereon, will not be used to pay for any Excise Tax.&#160;If the business combination is consummated, any Excise Taxes from redemptions of shares of CCXI public shares in connection with the business combination would reduce the funds available to Agility for working capital following the business combination. 
 If the Merger does not qualify as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes, Agility U.S.&#160;Holders will be required to recognize gain or loss for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes upon the exchange of their Agility common stock for Post-Closing Company common stock in the Merger. 
 The U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences of the Merger to Agility U.S.&#160;Holders generally will depend on whether the Merger qualifies as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes.&#160;If the Merger fails to qualify as a reorganization within the meaning of Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code, an Agility U.S.&#160;Holder generally would recognize gain or loss for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes on each share of Agility capital stock surrendered in the Merger for Post -Closing Company common stock.&#160;For a more complete discussion of the material U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences of the Merger, please carefully review the information set forth in the section entitled &#8220; Material U.S. &#160; Federal Income Tax Considerations of the Merger &#8221; in this proxy statement/prospectus.&#160;Each Agility U.S.&#160;Holder should consult its own tax advisor to determine the particular tax consequences to it in light of its own particular circumstances if the Merger fails to qualify as a reorganization for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes. 
 Risks Related to the Redemption 
 You must tender your CCXI public shares in order to validly exercise your redemption rights. 
 In connection with tendering your shares for redemption, you must request in writing that CCXI redeem your CCXI public shares for cash and elect either to physically tender your share certificates to CCXI&#8217;s transfer agent or to deliver your shares to the transfer agent electronically using The Depository Trust Company&#8217;s DWAC System, which election would likely be determined based on the manner in which you hold your shares, in each case, by two&#160;business days prior to the initially scheduled vote on the business combination proposal or such later date as CCXI&#8217;s directors may determine. The requirement for physical or electronic delivery by two&#160;business days prior to the initially scheduled vote on the business combination proposal or such later date as CCXI&#8217;s directors may determine ensures that a redeeming holder&#8217;s election to redeem is irrevocable once the business combination is approved. Any failure to observe these procedures will result in your loss of redemption rights in connection with the vote on the business combination.  Public shareholders, together with any affiliates of theirs or any other person with whom they are acting in concert or as a &#8220;group,&#8221; will be restricted from seeking redemption with respect to more than 15% of the public shares. 
 The CCXI current articles of association provides that a public shareholder, together with any affiliate of such shareholders or any other person with whom such stockholder is acting in concert or as a &#8220;group&#8221; (as defined under Section&#160;13(d)&#160;of the Exchange&#160;Act), will be restricted from redeeming in the aggregate his, her or its shares or, if part of such a group, the group&#8217;s shares, in excess of 15% of the CCXI public shares unless such shareholder first obtains CCXI&#8217;s prior consent (the &#8220; Excess Shares &#8221;). Your inability to redeem Excess Shares will reduce your influence over CCXI&#8217;s ability to consummate the business combination and you could suffer a material loss on your investment in CCXI if you sell such excess shares in open market transactions. 
 Additionally, you will not receive redemption distributions with respect to such excess shares if CCXI consummates the business combination. As a result, you will continue to hold that number of shares aggregating to more than 15% of the shares sold in the CCXI IPO and, in order to dispose of such excess shares, would be required to sell your shares in open market transactions, potentially at a loss. CCXI cannot assure you that the value of such excess shares will appreciate over time following the business combination or that the market price of CCXI public shares will exceed the per share redemption price. Notwithstanding the foregoing, shareholders may challenge CCXI&#8217;s determination as to whether a shareholder is acting in concert or as a group with another shareholder in a court of competent jurisdiction. 
 However, CCXI&#8217;s shareholders&#8217; ability to vote all of their shares (including Excess Shares) for or against the business combination is not restricted by this limitation on redemption. 
 There is no guarantee that a shareholder&#8217;s decision whether to redeem its shares for a pro rata portion of the trust account will put the shareholder in a better future economic position. 
 CCXI can give no assurance as to the price at which a shareholder may be able to sell its public shares in the future following the completion of the business combination or any alternative business combination. Certain events following the consummation of any initial business combination, including the business combination, may cause an increase in CCXI&#8217;s share price, and may result in a lower value realized now than a shareholder of CCXI might realize in the future had the shareholder not redeemed its shares.  Risks if the Adjournment Proposal&#160;Is Not Approved 
 If the adjournment proposal is not approved, and an insufficient number of votes have been obtained to authorize the consummation of the business combination, the CCXI Board will not have the ability to adjourn the extraordinary general meeting to a later date in order to solicit further votes, and, therefore, the business combination will not be approved. 
 If, at the extraordinary general meeting, the CCXI Board determines that it would be in the best interest of CCXI to adjourn the extraordinary general meeting to give CCXI more time to consummate the business combination for whatever reason (such as if the business combination proposal is not approved, or if additional time is needed to fulfill other closing conditions), the CCXI Board will seek approval to adjourn the extraordinary general meeting to a later date or dates. If the adjournment proposal is not approved, the CCXI Board will not have the ability to adjourn the extraordinary general meeting to a later date and, therefore, the business combination would not be completed.

 CCXI is furnishing this proxy statement/prospectus to CCXI shareholders (&#8220; you &#8221;) as part of the solicitation of proxies by the CCXI Board for use at the extraordinary general meeting of CCXI shareholders (the &#8220; extraordinary general meeting &#8221;) to be held on&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;, and at any adjournment or postponement thereof.  The extraordinary general meeting will be held via live webcast at &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; a.m. Eastern Time, on&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; .  Voting Power; CCXI Record Date 
 CCXI shareholders will be entitled to vote or direct votes to be cast at the extraordinary general meeting if they owned CCXI Ordinary Shares at the close of business on &#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; , 2026 (the &#8220; CCXI record date &#8221;), which is the record date for the extraordinary general meeting. CCXI shareholders will have one vote for each share of CCXI Ordinary Shares owned at the close of business on the CCXI record date. If your CCXI Ordinary Shares are held in &#8220;street name&#8221; or are in a margin or similar account, you should contact your broker to ensure that votes related to the shares you beneficially own are properly counted. On the CCXI record date, there were 55,700,000 CCXI Ordinary Shares outstanding, of which 41,900,000 were CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares and 13,800,000 were CCXI Class&#160;B Ordinary Shares. 
 Quorum 
 A quorum of CCXI shareholders is necessary to hold a valid meeting. A quorum for such meeting will consist of the holders present by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy of CCXI Ordinary Shares representing at least one -third (1/3) of the paid up voting share capital of CCXI entitled to vote at such meeting. The Sponsor owns&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;% of the outstanding CCXI Ordinary Shares (&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;% of the outstanding CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares and&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;% of the outstanding CCXI Class&#160;B Ordinary Shares) as of the CCXI record date, which will count towards this quorum. As a result, as of the CCXI record date, in addition to shares of the Sponsor,&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;CCXI Ordinary Shares held by CCXI public shareholders would be required to be present at the extraordinary general meeting to achieve a quorum. Proxies that are marked &#8220;abstain&#8221; will be treated as shares of CCXI public shares present for purposes of determining the presence of a quorum on all matters. Broker non -votes will be counted for the purposes of determining the existence of a quorum, but will not be considered votes cast at the extraordinary general meeting. 
 Effect of Abstentions and Broker Non-Votes 
 As a matter of Cayman Islands law, abstentions will not constitute votes cast at the CCXI extraordinary general meeting and therefore will have no effect on the approval of the proposals. 
 Under the rules of various national and regional securities exchanges, your broker, bank or nominee cannot vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares with respect to nonroutine matters unless you provide instructions on how to vote in accordance with the information and procedures provided to you by your broker, bank or nominee. We believe the proposals presented to the shareholders at the extraordinary general meeting will be considered nonroutine and, therefore, your broker, bank or nominee cannot vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares without your instruction on any of the proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting. If you do not provide voting instructions to your broker, bank or other nominee with respect to any of the proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting, your broker, bank or other nominee may deliver a proxy card expressly indicating that it is NOT voting your CCXI Ordinary Shares with respect to those proposals; this indication that a broker, bank or nominee is not voting your shares is referred to as a &#8220;broker non -vote .&#8221; 
 Broker non -votes will be counted for the purposes of determining the existence of a quorum, but will not be considered votes cast at the extraordinary general meeting. Your bank, broker or other nominee can vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares only if you provide instructions on how to vote. You should instruct your broker to vote your CCXI Ordinary Shares in accordance with directions you provide. 
 Broker non -votes will not have any effect on the outcome of the proposals. 
 Vote Required for Approval 
 The Sponsor owns of record and is entitled to vote &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; % of the outstanding CCXI Ordinary Shares (&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; % of the outstanding CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares and&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; % of the outstanding CCXI Class&#160;B Ordinary Shares) as of the CCXI record date. Such shares, as well as any CCXI Ordinary Shares acquired in the aftermarket by the Sponsor, will be voted in favor of the proposals presented at the extraordinary general meeting. Accordingly, the business combination proposal does not require the approval of a majority of the unaffiliated holders of CCXI. 
 

 96 
 Table of Contents 

 
 The approval of each of the business combination proposal, stock issuance proposal, incentive plan proposal, ESPP proposal, director election proposal, advisory organizational documents proposal, and, if necessary, the adjournment proposal requires an ordinary resolution, being the affirmative vote of a simple majority of the votes cast by holders of outstanding CCXI Ordinary Shares represented at the extraordinary general meeting by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy and entitled to vote at the extraordinary general meeting, voting together as a single class. Accordingly, if a valid quorum is established, a CCXI shareholder&#8217;s failure to vote by proxy or to vote at the extraordinary general meeting with regard to the business combination proposal, stock issuance proposal, incentive plan proposal, ESPP proposal, director election proposal and, if necessary, the adjournment proposal, will have no effect on such proposals. Prior to the closing of an initial business combination, the CCXI current articles of association prescribe that only holders of CCXI Class&#160;B Ordinary Shares are entitled to appoint and remove directors. This provision of the CCXI current articles of association may only be amended if approved by a special resolution passed by at least 90% (or, where such amendment is proposed in respect of the consummation of CCXI&#8217;s initial business combination, two -thirds ) of the CCXI Ordinary Shares voting at the applicable general meeting, voting together as a single class. Accordingly, the director election proposal is being voted on by CCXI shareholders on a non -binding advisory basis only. 
 The approval of the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal requires a special resolution, being the affirmative vote of holders of at least two -thirds of the CCXI Ordinary Shares represented at the extraordinary general meeting by attendance via the virtual meeting website, in person or by proxy and entitled to vote at the extraordinary general meeting, voting together as a single class. Accordingly, if a valid quorum is established, a CCXI shareholder&#8217;s failure to vote by proxy or to vote at the extraordinary general meeting with regard to the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal will have no effect on such proposals. Under the CCXI current articles of association, CCXI&#8217;s directors have the authority to resolve that CCXI be registered by way of continuation in a jurisdiction outside the Cayman Islands or such other jurisdiction in which it is for the time being incorporated, registered or existing (including, but not limited to, the approval of the organizational documents to be adopted by the Company in such other jurisdiction to the extent applicable). Accordingly, it is not necessary for CCXI to receive shareholder consent to the domestication, and the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal are therefore being presented to CCXI shareholders on a non -binding advisory basis only. 
 Consummation of the business combination is conditioned on the approval of each of the condition precedent proposals. If any of those proposals are not approved, at the extraordinary general meeting (or any adjournment or postponement thereof) then unless certain conditions in the Merger Agreement are waived by the applicable parties to the Merger Agreement, the Merger Agreement may be terminated and the business combination may not be consummated.

 Redemption Rights 
 Pursuant to the CCXI current articles of association, any holder of CCXI public shares who is not the Sponsor or a CCXI officer or director may, contemporaneously with the vote on the business combination proposal, request to redeem all or a portion of its CCXI public shares for cash, regardless of whether it votes &#8220;for&#8221; or &#8220;against&#8221; the business combination proposal. Any such CCXI shareholder holding CCXI public shares as of the CCXI record date may demand that CCXI redeem such shares for cash in an amount equal to their pro rata portion of the funds held in the trust account net of permitted withdrawals (which, for illustrative purposes, was approximately $ &#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; per share as of the CCXI record date), calculated as of two&#160;business days prior to the anticipated consummation of the business combination. If a holder of CCXI public shares properly exercises its redemption rights as described in this section and the business combination is consummated, CCXI will redeem such holder&#8217;s shares for a pro rata portion of funds held in the trust account and the holder will no longer own CCXI public shares following the business combination. 
 Notwithstanding the foregoing, (1)&#160;a holder of CCXI public shares, together with any affiliate of such holder or any other person with whom such holder is acting in concert or as a &#8220;group&#8221; (as defined in Section&#160;13(d)(3)&#160;of the Exchange&#160;Act), will be restricted from seeking redemption with respect to more than 15% of the CCXI public shares. Accordingly, all CCXI public shares in excess of 15% held by a CCXI public shareholder, together with any affiliate of such holder or any other person with whom such holder is acting in concert or as a &#8220;group,&#8221; will not be redeemed for cash and (2)&#160;a holder of CCXI public shares that holds CCXI public shares beneficially through a nominee must identify itself to CCXI in connection with any redemption election in order to validly redeem such CCXI public shares. Moreover, pursuant to the terms of the Sponsor Agreement, the Sponsor and the Insiders have each agreed to waive any redemption rights with respect to any CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares they own in connection with the consummation of the business combination. 
 Holders of CCXI public shares may demand redemption by delivering their shares, either physically or electronically using Depository Trust Company&#8217;s DWAC System, and requesting in writing that CCXI redeem such CCXI public shares for cash to Continental Stock Transfer&#160;&amp; Trust Company, CCXI&#8217;s transfer agent, at least two&#160;business days prior to the initially scheduled vote at the extraordinary general meeting (the &#8220; Redemption Deadline &#8221;). If you hold the shares of CCXI in street name, you will have to coordinate with your broker to have your shares certificated or delivered electronically. Certificates that have not been tendered (either physically or electronically) in accordance with these procedures will not be redeemed for cash. There is a nominal cost associated with this tendering process and the act of certificating the shares of CCXI public shares or delivering them through the DWAC System. The transfer

 agent will typically charge the tendering broker $100 and it would be up to the broker whether or not to pass this cost on to the redeeming shareholder. In the event the business combination is not consummated, this may result in an additional cost to CCXI shareholders for the return of their shares. 
 The Redemption Deadline may occur prior to the Domestication, but the redemption will be with respect to Post -Closing Company common stock that an electing holder of CCXI public shares holds after the Domestication. For the purposes of the CCXI current articles of association, the exercise of redemption rights will be treated as an election to have such CCXI public shares redeemed for cash, and references in this proxy statement/prospectus to &#8220;redemption&#8221; or &#8220;redeeming&#8221; will be interpreted accordingly. Immediately following the Domestication and the Closing, the Post -Closing Company will satisfy the exercise of redemption rights by redeeming the corresponding shares of Post -Closing Company common stock issued to the CCXI public shareholders that validly exercised their redemption rights. 
 If the business combination is not approved or completed for any reason, then holders of CCXI public shares that elected to exercise their redemption rights will not be entitled to redeem their CCXI public shares for cash in an amount equal to their pro rata portion of the funds held in the trust account, as applicable. In such case, CCXI will promptly return any CCXI public shares delivered by shareholders. 
 The closing price of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares on the CCXI record date was $ &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; per share. The cash held in the trust account on such date was approximately $&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; ($&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; per CCXI public share outstanding as of the record date). Prior to exercising redemption rights, CCXI shareholders should verify the market price of CCXI public shares as they may receive higher proceeds from the sale of their shares in the public market than from exercising their redemption rights if the market price per share is higher than the redemption price. CCXI cannot assure its shareholders that they will be able to sell their CCXI public shares in the open market, even if the market price per share is higher than the redemption price stated above, as there may not be sufficient liquidity in its securities when CCXI shareholders wish to sell their shares. 
 If a holder of CCXI public shares properly exercises their redemption rights and the business combination is consummated, then they will be exchanging their CCXI public shares for cash and will no longer own those shares. They will be entitled to receive cash for their CCXI public shares only if they properly exercise their redemption rights no later than the Redemption Deadline by delivering their share certificate (either physically or electronically) to CCXI&#8217;s transfer agent prior to the Redemption Deadline. 
 Pursuant to the Sponsor Agreement, the Sponsor and the Insiders have agreed to waive their redemption rights with respect to all of their CCXI Ordinary Shares in connection with the consummation of the business combination and, because of this, such CCXI Ordinary Shares are excluded from the pro rata calculation used to determine the per share redemption price. As is customary in transactions of this type, the Sponsor and the Insiders did not receive any consideration for waiving their redemption rights.
