 Purchases of Shares 
 The Sponsor and/or its affiliates may purchase shares in privately negotiated transactions or on the open market either prior to or following the completion of the business combination, although they are under no obligation to do so. Such a purchase may include a contractual acknowledgement that such shareholder, although still the record holder of our shares, is no longer the beneficial owner thereof and therefore agrees not to exercise its redemption rights. In the event shares are purchased in privately negotiated transactions from public shareholders who have already elected to exercise their redemption rights, such selling shareholders would be required to revoke their prior elections to redeem their shares. The purpose of such purchases would be to reduce the number of shares of CCXI public shares that may be redeemed in connection with the business combination, and may include a business decision to increase such purchaser&#8217;s ownership at an attractive price. In addition, the Sponsor and/or its affiliates may purchase CCXI public shares on the open market prior to the extraordinary general meeting and separate from the redemption process conducted in connection with the business combination (&#8220; Open Market Purchases &#8221;). The Sponsor and/or its respective affiliates shall only make Open Market Purchases to the extent the price per share of CCXI public shares so acquired is no higher than the redemption price that would be available in connection with the redemption procedures described in this proxy statement/prospectus. In addition, the Sponsor and/or its affiliates will waive any redemption rights with respect to any CCXI public shares purchased in Open Market Purchases and will not vote any CCXI public shares purchased in Open Market Purchases in favor of the proposals. While the exact nature of any such arrangements has not been determined as of the date of this proxy statement/prospectus, they might include, without limitation, arrangements to protect such investors or holders against potential loss in value of their shares, including the granting of put options and, with Agility&#8217;s consent, the transfer to such investors or holders of shares owned by the Sponsor for nominal value. 
 Entering into any such arrangements may have a negative effect on the market price of CCXI Ordinary Shares. For example, as a result of these arrangements, an investor or holder may have the ability to effectively purchase shares at a price lower than market and may therefore be more likely to sell the shares such person owns, either prior to or immediately after the extraordinary general meeting. 
 If such transactions are effected, the consequence could be to cause the business combination to be approved in circumstances where such approval could not otherwise be obtained. Purchases of shares by the persons described above would allow them to exert more influence over the approval of the Agility business combination proposal and other proposals and would likely increase the chances that such proposals would be approved. 
 No agreements dealing with the above arrangements or purchases have been entered into as of the date of this proxy statement/prospectus by the Sponsor or any of its affiliates. CCXI will file a Current Report on Form&#160;8 -K to disclose arrangements entered into, or significant purchases made by, any of the aforementioned persons that would affect the vote on the business combination proposal or the satisfaction of any closing conditions. Any such report will include descriptions of any arrangements entered into or significant purchases by any of the aforementioned persons.

 (4) &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Includes 500,000 CCXI private placement shares held by the Sponsor and 13,800,000 CCXI Founder Shares held by the Sponsor. 
 (5) &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Pursuant to the terms of the PIPE Subscription Agreements, as described above, CCXI has agreed to issue and sell to the PIPE Investors, and the PIPE Investors have agreed to buy, 20,102,500 Subscribed Shares at a purchase price of $10.00 per share for an aggregate commitment of $201.0&#160;million. 
 CCXI Deferred Underwriting Fees 
 $1.5&#160;million of the underwriting fee payable in connection with the CCXI IPO was deferred and conditioned upon the announcement by CCXI that it has entered into a definitive business combination agreement, which amount was paid to Citi, the underwriter in the CCXI IPO, on July&#160;7, 2026. An additional approximately $14.5&#160;million of the underwriting fee payable in connection with the CCXI IPO was deferred and conditioned upon completion of an initial business combination. As of the date of this proxy statement/prospectus, Citi has waived any claim to the Deferred Underwriting Fee payable to it pursuant to the Underwriting Agreement, dated December&#160;16, 2025, between CCXI and Citi, subject to its receipt of the $7.0&#160;million Capital Markets Advisory Fee payable upon the Closing. CCXI and Citi have entered into an engagement letter under which Citi will provide capital markets advisory services to CCXI in connection with the business combination, and the Capital Markets Advisory Fee will be payable upon the Closing and Citi shall be eligible for an additional incentive fee of up to $3.0&#160;million payable solely at the discretion of CCXI.

 Background of the Transactions 
 CCXI is a blank check company formed to effect a merger, amalgamation, share exchange, asset acquisition, stock purchase, reorganization or other similar business combination with one or more businesses. CCXI was incorporated under the laws of the Cayman Islands on June&#160;4, 2025. The business combination is the result of extensive work by CCXI, leveraging the Sponsor&#8217;s global network and the investing, operating and transaction experience of CCXI&#8217;s management team and members of the CCXI Board. The terms of the business combination are the result of arm&#8217;s -length negotiations between representatives of CCXI and representatives of Agility. The following is a brief discussion of the background of these negotiations, the Merger Agreement and the business combination. 
 On December&#160;16, 2025, CCXI completed its initial public offering. Prior to the consummation of the CCXI IPO, neither CCXI, nor anyone on its behalf, contacted any prospective target business or held any substantive discussions, formal or otherwise, with respect to a transaction with CCXI.&#160;After the CCXI IPO, CCXI commenced an active search for prospective businesses and assets to acquire. 
 In evaluating potential businesses and assets to acquire, CCXI, together with the Sponsor and their advisors, surveyed the landscape of potential acquisition opportunities based on their knowledge of, and familiarity with, the M&amp;A marketplace. In general, CCXI looked for acquisition targets that were of a size relevant to the public marketplace and positioned, operationally and financially, to be successful as a public company. CCXI further looked for those transactions that it believed, if entered, would be well received by the public markets. In particular, CCXI generally sought to identify companies that (i)&#160;generate or have the future potential to generate stable free cash -flow , (ii)&#160;would benefit uniquely from CCXI&#8217;s capabilities, (iii)&#160;are sourced through CCXI&#8217;s proprietary channels, (iv)&#160;have a committed and capable management team and (v)&#160;have the potential to grow through both organic growth and acquisition opportunities. CCXI also sought to identify companies that it believed would benefit from being a publicly -held entity, particularly with respect to access to capital for both organic growth and for use in acquisitions, with a particular emphasis on opportunities that are primed to unlock disruptive technological advancements. CCXI generally implements these criteria when evaluating potential targets. 
 Central to CCXI&#8217;s strategy was to originate an investment opportunity sourced through its proprietary channels. CCXI&#8217;s selection process leveraged the Sponsor&#8217;s network of industry, venture capital sponsor and private equity sponsor relationships as well as relationships with management teams of public and private companies, investment bankers, attorneys and accountants. 
 Starting in December 2025 and continuing through early 2026, following the closing of the CCXI IPO, representatives of Archimedes Advisor Group LLC, CCXI&#8217;s strategic advisor and affiliate of Michael Klein, Chairman of the Board of CCXI (&#8220; Archimedes &#8221;), at the direction of CCXI, and the Sponsor commenced a search for prospective business combination candidates (&#8220; targets &#8221;) for CCXI to partner with in its initial business combination. CCXI, with the assistance of Archimedes, developed a list of approximately a dozen targets leveraging the proprietary sourcing channels described above. Representatives of CCXI were also contacted by potential targets that they had not previously identified through its search process. In certain instances, it was requested by a potential target that CCXI enter into a non -disclosure agreement. CCXI did so on a selective basis, entering into fewer than ten such agreements. Prior to entering into a non -binding letter of intent with Agility, CCXI did not submit a non -binding letter of intent to any prospective target other than Agility. Upon entering into the non -binding letter of intent with Agility, CCXI became subject to an exclusivity provision that precluded CCXI from participating in discussions or negotiations with any other potential target regarding a prospective business combination.

 On January 7, 2026, Mr. Klein held a videoconference call with Agility&#8217;s Chief Executive Officer, Ms. Margaret &#8220;Peggy&#8221; Johnson. Ms. Johnson shared that Agility was experiencing strong momentum in its business and was interested in evaluating potential options to become the first publicly traded pure -play humanoid robotics company. During the call, Mr. Klein provided his perspective on the state of the equity capital markets and an overview of CCXI. Mr. Klein and Ms. Johnson discussed the merits of exploring a potential business combination between CCXI and Agility.

During the remainder of February until the execution of the LOI on March&#160;15, 2026, the representatives of CCXI and Agility continued discussions and conducted due diligence on the humanoid industry, Agility&#8217;s technology and customer base as well as the broader market opportunity.

 On March&#160;2, 2026, CCXI sent an initial non -binding LOI to Agility&#8217;s advisor, BTIG.&#160;The initial proposal contemplated a business combination between CCXI and Agility whereby Agility would combine with CCXI in a transaction ascribing a&#160;pre -money &#160;equity value for Agility of $2,500 - $3,000&#160;million, together with detailed further transaction terms. In establishing the pre -money equity value range set forth above, CCXI considered the approximately $2,000 million post -money equity value ascribed to Agility in its Series C3 financing round. CCXI indicated to Agility that the preliminary pre -money equity value was subject to additional due diligence and that CCXI would require a fairness opinion from an independent third -party valuation firm before entering into a transaction with Agility. Prior to submission of the LOI, CCXI and Agility had not previously discussed the pre -money equity value range

 proposed by CCXI. CCXI and Agility did not agree on a precise equity value until, as further described below, the parties agreed to a $2,500 million equity value in connection with engaging prospective PIPE Investors beginning on May 7, 2026. 
 The initial letter of intent from CCXI provided that the consideration to be paid in the business combination with Agility would consist entirely of newly issued shares of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s common stock valued at the price per share of funds held in the trust account as of the Closing. The proposal further contemplated a post -Closing lock -up for the Sponsor and Agility&#8217;s shareholders, restricting the transfer of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock to be received in the business combination, with 100% of the share consideration being locked up for 180&#160;days post -Closing , subject to early release based on stock price performance. Included in the proposal letter was a mutual&#160;45 -day &#160;exclusivity period to allow CCXI to complete its due diligence and to allow the parties to negotiate and finalize definitive documentation. The initial proposal also contemplated that prior to the execution of the business combination, the parties would work together to obtain binding written commitments from institutional investors for an aggregate of $200&#160;million in gross proceeds in a private placement of equity securities of the surviving Post -Closing Company (the &#8220;PIPE&#8221;). The LOI included a request by CCXI that Agility secure from its existing equityholders participation in the PIPE. 
 From March&#160;2, 2026 through March&#160;15, 2026, Agility, with the assistance of its advisors, Latham&#160;&amp; Watkins LLP (&#8220; Latham &#8221;) and BTIG&#8217;s M&amp;A advisory team, negotiated the non -binding LOI with CCXI.&#160;On March&#160;13, 2026, Agility responded to CCXI&#8217;s initial proposal, accepting the&#160;pre -money &#160;equity valuation range, lock -up terms, and target PIPE size of $200 million. Agility revised the PIPE provisions to provide that it would use reasonable best efforts to obtain participation from its existing equityholders and also introduced a minimum cash condition, without specifying a minimum cash amount. 
 On March 15, 2026, CCXI sent a revised proposal to Agility that accepted Agility&#8217;s proposed revisions to the PIPE provisions, while providing for a target of at least $50 million of participation from Agility&#8217;s existing equityholders. CCXI also accepted the concept of a minimum cash condition and proposed a threshold of $200 million, consisting of the funds remaining in CCXI&#8217;s Trust Account after giving effect to all pre -Closing redemptions, but before payment of any Transaction Expenses or unpaid Sponsor loans, plus the proceeds from the PIPE or any Company Bridge Financing. CCXI also proposed revisions to select certain other non -material provisions of the LOI.

Later that&#160;day, the Agility Board met, together with representatives of Archimedes and BTIG, to consider the final LOI.&#160;The LOI was agreed and executed on March&#160;15, 2026.

 Reasons for Approval of the Transactions 
 The CCXI Board, in evaluating the Transactions, consulted with CCXI&#8217;s management and financial, technical and legal advisors. In (1)&#160;resolving that it is fair to and in the best interests of CCXI and its shareholders, and declaring it advisable, to enter into the Merger Agreement, the related agreements to which CCXI is a party and the Transactions, (2)&#160;approving the Merger Agreement, the related agreements to which CCXI is a party and the Transactions, including the Merger, on the terms and subject to the conditions of the Merger Agreement, and (3)&#160;adopting a resolution recommending the business combination proposal be approved by CCXI shareholders, the CCXI Board considered and evaluated a number of factors, including the factors discussed below. The CCXI Board did not consider it practicable to, and did not attempt to, quantify or otherwise assign relative weights to the specific factors it considered in reaching its determination. In addition, individual directors may have given different weight to different factors. The CCXI Board viewed its decision as being based on all of the information available and the factors presented to and considered by it. This explanation of CCXI&#8217;s reasons for the Transactions and all other information presented in this section is forward -looking in nature and, therefore, should be read in light of the factors discussed in the section entitled &#8220; Cautionary Note&#160;Regarding Forward -Looking Statements .&#8221;

 The CCXI Board considered a number of factors pertaining to the Transactions as generally supporting its decision to enter into the Merger Agreement, the related agreements to which CCXI is a party, and the Transactions, including but not limited to, the following material factors: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Reasonableness of Aggregate Consideration .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;Following a review of the financial data provided to CCXI, including Agility&#8217;s historical financial statements and certain unaudited prospective financial information, CCXI&#8217;s due diligence review of Agility&#8217;s business and the views of CCXI&#8217;s financial advisor (which supported CCXI management&#8217;s view regarding valuation), the CCXI Board considered the aggregate consideration to be paid and determined that the aggregate consideration was reasonable in light of such data and financial information. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Business and Financial Condition and Prospects .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;After conducting extensive due diligence, the CCXI Board and CCXI&#8217;s management team obtained a better understanding of Agility&#8217;s business, financial condition, management team and future growth prospects. The CCXI Board considered the results of the due diligence review of Agility&#8217;s business, as further described in &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Background of the Transactions, &#8221; as well as Agility&#8217;s management team&#8217;s experience. The CCXI Board considered how these factors will enhance Agility&#8217;s ability to scale effectively and to execute upon and achieve its business plan. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Financings and Minimum Cash Condition.&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; The CCXI Board considered the fact that Agility would need additional financing to pursue its business plan in setting the Minimum Cash Condition, and in that regard considered Agility&#8217;s active pursuit of additional equity financing opportunities and strategic transactions, including Agility SAFEs and the potential to raise a PIPE Investment, together which were expected to be sufficient to satisfy the Minimum Cash Condition, as further described in &#8220;&#8212; Background of the Transactions.&#8221; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Experienced and Committed Management Team .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;The CCXI Board considered that the Post -Closing Company is expected to continue to be led by Agility&#8217;s senior management team, whose collective experience includes the development of humanoid robotics and physical AI technologies, the commercialization of enterprise technology products, and the scaling of technology businesses. The CCXI Board also considered that the senior management team has led Agility&#8217;s evolution from technology development to commercial deployment with leading customers and is expected to remain with the Post -Closing Company in the capacity of officers and/or directors, providing continuity in executing the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s business strategy. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Opinion of CCXI&#8217;s Financial Advisor .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;The CCXI Board took into account the financial presentation, orally presented to the CCXI Board on June &#160; 22, 2026, and the written opinion, dated as of June &#160; 23, 2026, of Ocean Tomo to the CCXI Board as to the fairness, from a financial point of view and as of the date of the opinion, of the Purchase Price to CCXI&#8217;s shareholders (other than the Sponsor), which opinion was based on and subject to the matters considered, the procedures followed, the assumptions made and various limitations of and qualifications to the review undertaken as more fully described under the section entitled &#8220; &#8212;&#160;Opinion of CCXI&#8217;s Financial Advisor &#8221; below. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Commitment of Agility&#8217;s Owners .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;The CCXI Board considered the fact that Agility&#8217;s Chief Executive Officer and other key executives, together with all of the other shareholders of Agility, are not selling any of their current shareholdings of Agility in the Transaction, which the CCXI Board believed reflects such shareholders&#8217; belief in and commitment to the continued growth prospects of Agility going forward. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Other Alternatives .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;CCXI raised $414,000,000 in 2025 with the objective of consummating an attractive business combination. Since that time, as more fully described in &#8220; &#8212;&#160;Background of the Transactions ,&#8221; CCXI has evaluated a number of businesses but has been most impressed by the Agility business. The CCXI Board believed that, based upon the terms of the Transactions, the Transactions provide the best available opportunity to maximize value for CCXI shareholders. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Terms of the Merger Agreement and the Related Agreements .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;The CCXI Board considered the terms and conditions of the Merger Agreement and the related agreements and the transactions contemplated thereby, including the Merger, each party&#8217;s representations, warranties and covenants, the conditions to each party&#8217;s obligation to consummate the transactions contemplated thereby and the termination provisions, as well as the strong commitment by both Agility and CCXI to complete the Transactions.

 Agility&#8217;s Reasons for Engaging in the Transactions 
 In evaluating the Transactions, the Agility board considered a number of factors pertaining to the Transactions, including the following principle purposes: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Access to Public Capital Markets .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;Agility is an early -stage technology company that has funded its operations to date through private capital raises. The Agility Board considered that becoming a publicly traded company on a major U.S. stock exchange through the business combination would provide Agility with access to the U.S. public capital markets, enabling Agility to raise additional capital to support the commercialization and large -scale manufacturing of Digit, scale operations, execute its long -term growth strategy and provide Agility with greater financial flexibility and a broader range of capital -raising alternatives than are typically available to a privately held company. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Immediate Capital Infusion &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; The Transactions, together with the PIPE Investment of up to $201,025,000, and the potential availability of cash from the CCXI trust account, are expected to provide Agility with a substantial capital infusion at the Closing to support its commercialization, manufacturing scale -up and operating needs. The Agility Board considered this an important advantage over other paths to public listing that may not provide a concurrent capital raise of comparable certainty and magnitude. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Enhanced Visibility and Brand Awareness .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;Becoming a publicly traded company would enhance Agility&#8217;s visibility and brand recognition in the market, which may support commercial adoption of Agility&#8217;s humanoid robotics and physical AI solutions, strengthen customer confidence, and facilitate strategic partnerships with leading companies. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Talent Attraction and Retention.&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; The Agility Board considered that the business combination would enhance Agility&#8217;s ability to attract, incentivize and retain high -quality talent by enabling the company to offer employees and prospective hires equity -based compensation in the form of publicly traded securities, which the Agility Board believes would increase the attractiveness and perceived value of such awards and strengthen Agility&#8217;s ability to compete for talent in a highly competitive market. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Ability to Use Equity as Currency .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;As a public company, Agility would have the ability to use its publicly traded common stock as consideration for potential future acquisitions and strategic investments, which the Agility Board believes would enhance Agility&#8217;s flexibility in pursuing strategic transactions and support its long -term growth objectives.

 Benefits and Detriments of the Business Combination 
 Stakeholder &#160; Benefits &#160; Detriments CCXI &#160; The completion of the business combination avoids the liquidation of the trust account and is expected to create value for CCXI and its shareholders. &#160; By pursuing the business combination, CCXI could have potentially forgone opportunities to identify a target that may have a more optimal risk/return profile than Agility. Sponsor&#160;&amp; affiliates &#160; The completion of the business combination avoids the liquidation of the trust account, in which case the Sponsor would not be entitled to rights to liquidating distributions from the trust account with respect to any CCXI Founder Shares or CCXI private placement units it holds, and is expected to create value for CCXI and its shareholders. In addition, see &#8220; Proposal&#160;No.&#160;1&#160;&#8212;&#160;The Business Combination Proposal&#160;&#8212;&#160;Interests of Certain CCXI Persons in the Business Combination&#160;&#8212;&#160;Sponsor and Affiliates Compensation &#8221; for more information about the Sponsor and its affiliates&#8217; compensation. &#160; By pursuing the business combination, CCXI could have potentially forgone opportunities to identify a target that may have a more optimal risk/return profile than Agility. Unaffiliated security holders &#160; If the market were to recognize the valuation and potential of Agility, the price of Post -Closing Company common stock may increase following the Closing from the per share trust account balance of approximately $10.16 per share as of June&#160;30, 2026, which will benefit the unaffiliated security holders. &#160; For non -redeeming &#160;shareholders, if the market does not recognize the valuation and potential of Agility, either as a result of a general market downturn or risks specific to Agility, the price of Post -Closing Company common stock may decrease following the Closing from the per share trust account balance of approximately $10.16 as of June&#160;30, 2026, which may result in a loss to such shareholders as compared to if they had exercised their redemption rights prior to the closing. Agility &#160; The completion of the business combination will result in Agility becoming a publicly traded company on a major U.S.&#160;stock exchange. As a U.S.&#160;public company, Agility and, therefore, Agility&#8217;s legacy stockholders, are expected to benefit from increased visibility in the capital markets, which may enhance awareness of the Agility brand and support commercial adoption of its humanoid robotics and physical AI solutions. In addition, Agility will have access to the U.S.&#160;public capital markets, providing the ability to raise additional capital to support commercialization, scale operations, and execute its long -term growth strategy. &#160; Agility&#8217;s management has invested substantial time and effort to complete the business combination; the benefits sought to be achieved by the business combination might not be fully achieved or may not be achieved within the expected timeframe; and the completion of the business combination is conditioned on the satisfaction of certain closing conditions that are not within Agility&#8217;s control.

 (3) &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Reflects the amount of time before RaaS payment subscription fees received by Agility exceed the total Bill -of-Materials (&#8220; BOM &#8221;) for Digit.

Cumulative cost under both models includes upfront Digit BOM, one -time deployment costs of approximately $15k, and annual costs of delivery for software and maintenance provided by Agility of approximately $15k. Excludes corporate SG&amp;A and R&amp;D costs. 
 (5) &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Immediate payback given upfront purchase price of Digit is greater than the Digit BOM.

 Summary of Financial Analyses 
 In preparing the Opinion, Ocean Tomo utilized two valuation approaches to determine the implied value of Agility, specifically the Discounted Cash Flow (&#8220; DCF &#8221;) method of the income approach and the market approach (as described in further detail below). For purposes of its financial analyses, Ocean Tomo assumed that the Purchase Price set forth in the Merger Agreement had a value equal to $2.5&#160;billion. The financial and other terms of the business combination were determined pursuant to negotiations between the parties to the Merger Agreement and were not determined by or pursuant to any recommendation from Ocean Tomo. The following is a summary of the financial analyses performed by Ocean Tomo in connection with the preparation of the Opinion presented to CCXI.&#160;For each valuation approach, Ocean Tomo considered four possible scenarios. The four scenarios were based on the Financial Disclosures provided by CCXI and Agility with sensitivities around a) delays in the Deployment Schedule, b) cost reductions related to the robot bill of materials (&#8220; BOM &#8221;), c) pricing adjustments to both sold robots (&#8220; CapEx &#8221;) and RaaS offerings, and d) reductions in deployment volumes. 
 The following is a summary of the scenarios considered by Ocean Tomo in connection with the preparation of the Opinion and presented to the CCXI Board on June&#160;22, 2026: 
 1. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Base Case: &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;Uses the Financial Disclosures and unit economics provided by CCXI and Agility as presented (&#8220; Base Case &#8221;). 
 2. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Scenario 2: &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;Assumes that the initial deployment assumptions included in Financial Disclosures and unit economics provided by CCXI and Agility are delayed by one year and that the 2030 BOM cost reduction is not fully achieved and is only reduced to $100,000 per robot (&#8220; Scenario 2 &#8221;). 
 3. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Scenario 3: &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;Assumes the same sensitivity from Scenario 2 with the additional assumption of a 10% reduction in CapEx and RaaS robot pricing (&#8220; Scenario 3 &#8221;). 
 4. &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Scenario 4: &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;Assumes the same sensitivities from Scenario 3 with the addition of (a) 20% reduction in both CapEx and RaaS pricing and (b) a 10% general reduction in the deployment volumes (&#8220; Scenario 4 &#8221;). 
 Discounted Cash Flow Analysis 
 The DCF method of the income approach estimates the value of a company as the present value of expected future cash flows that a business can be expected to generate. The DCF method begins with an estimation of the annual cash flows the subject business is expected to generate over a discrete projection period (e.g., a fifteen -year period). The estimated cash flows for each of the&#160;years in the discrete projection period are then converted to their present value equivalents using a discount rate appropriate for the risk of achieving the projected cash flows. The present value of the estimated discrete period cash flows is then added to the present value equivalent of the residual/terminal value of the business at the end of the discrete projection period to arrive at an estimate of total value. The terminal value is the value of a business beyond the explicit forecast period and represents the future cash flows expected to be generated by the business into perpetuity. 
 The DCF analyses performed by Ocean Tomo incorporated both the Gordon Growth Model and Exit Multiples Approach in estimating terminal value for each scenario to ensure a robust and balanced assessment of long -term value. 
 The Gordon Growth Model estimates terminal value by capitalizing projected cash flows assuming a constant perpetual growth rate beyond the explicit forecast period. This approach reflects the expectation that, at maturity, the subject company will generate stable and predictable cash flows that grow at a normalized long -term rate. 
 

 137 
 Table of Contents 

 
 The Exit Multiples Approach, by contrast, estimates terminal value based on observable public market valuation benchmarks. Under this method, enterprise value (&#8220; EV &#8221;) multiples are derived from comparable companies by relating their market values to key financial performance indicators, most commonly revenue or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (&#8220; EBITDA &#8221;). These observed EV/Revenue and EV/EBITDA multiples are then applied to the subject company&#8217;s projected financial metrics at the end of the discrete forecast period to arrive at an undiscounted indication of the terminal value. 
 Ocean Tomo&#8217;s DCF analyses of Agility forecasted the discrete period from fiscal year ending (&#8220; FYE &#8221;) December&#160;31, 2026, through FYE 2040. Ocean Tomo arrived at each indication of value by adding both the present value of the discrete period cash flows and a terminal value. Forecasted unlevered free cash flow assumptions were developed by Ocean Tomo based on the Financial Disclosures (as described in the section entitled &#8220; Financial Disclosures &#8221;), interviews with Agility management, other relevant business and financial documentation provided by CCXI and Agility, and its industry expertise. 
 The risk inherent in each scenario was reflected in Ocean Tomo&#8217;s selected discount rate, which was developed using the Capital Asset Pricing Model (&#8220; CAPM &#8221;) framework, supplemented by a qualitative risk assessment and benchmarking against venture capital and private equity rates of return for companies at similar stages of development and commercialization. The resulting range of discount rates was derived using the weighted average cost of capital methodology and incorporated considerations such as published studies on discount rates and observed industry capital costs. 
 In evaluating the risk associated with the Deployment Schedule, Ocean Tomo considered both the probability -weighted deployment as well as the Company&#8217;s broader opportunity pipeline. The pipeline data provided additional context regarding the risk of the Deployment Schedule. Ocean Tomo noted that the Deployment Schedule represents a risk -adjusted , significantly reduced subset of the broader opportunity pipeline. Consideration of both the unadjusted opportunity pipeline and the Deployment Schedule, together with observed market indications of value which imply lower required returns for investments of this nature, supported the selected discount rate range. The unadjusted opportunity pipeline estimates a total of approximately 28,000 robots deployed by 2030. In contrast, the Deployment Schedule estimates used by Ocean Tomo considered only a total of approximately 7,000 robots deployed. Additionally, the Deployment Schedule only considers the low -risk and already demonstrated robot capability of goods movement via totes. The unadjusted opportunity considers 26 additional capabilities for future generation robots currently under development. 
 In determining an appropriate EV/Revenue and EV/EBITDA exit multiple for purposes of estimating a terminal value, Ocean Tomo conducted a detailed review of financial and market data for a set of selected companies with publicly traded equity securities that were deemed relevant benchmarks. These companies consisted of mature diversified manufacturing companies engaged in the manufacture and sale of industrial robotics and related equipment. The selected benchmarks were chosen to reflect the anticipated mature operating profile, scale, and risk characteristics of Agility in the terminal year of 2040 (the &#8220; Selected Mature Industrial Robotics and Equipment Publicly Traded Companies &#8221;). The selected companies and resulting median, mean, and quartile data included the following:

 For purposes of estimating the terminal value under the Gordon Growth Model, Ocean Tomo calculated terminal values for each scenario using a 10% long -term growth rate. This assumption reflects analyst expectations that the robotics industry will continue to exhibit sustained growth at or above this level beyond the 2040 terminal year. Ocean Tomo applied a terminal year discount rate of 15% to reflect the lower, stabilized risk profile associated with a mature operating business at exit in 2040. Ocean Tomo then discounted the terminal value back to present&#160;day at a discount rate of 18%, consistent with the risk identified in the CAPM approach. 
 Under the Exit Multiple Approach, Ocean Tomo utilized an EV/Revenue multiple of 4.5x and an EV/EBITDA multiple of 23.3x, representing the median observed multiples of the selected mature public company benchmarks identified above. These multiples reflect normalized valuation levels for scaled, commercially mature industrial robotics and equipment companies. Terminal values derived under this approach were also discounted to present value using an 18% discount rate consistent with the risk identified in the CAPM framework. Both terminal value methodologies assume a normalization of growth, margins, and risk at the point of exit for each scenario. 
 Based on the application of these assumptions and methodologies, the DCF analysis yielded an average implied enterprise value of $3.8&#160;billion with an implied enterprise value range of approximately $1.7&#160;billion to $7.3&#160;billion across the evaluated scenarios.  Market Approach 
 The market approach estimates EV by applying valuation multiples derived from comparable market evidence to relevant financial metrics of the subject company. These valuation multiples are informed by observable data from actively traded public companies, including market pricing and historical financial performance. In addition, Ocean Tomo considered consensus equity analyst estimates of forward looking financial results, as well as valuation indications implied by prices paid in completed mergers, acquisitions, or other transaction precedents. 
 Ocean Tomo conducted four separate market approaches. As part of the forward multiples approach, Ocean Tomo applied revenue multiples derived from humanoid and non -humanoid robotics guideline public companies (see below) to Agility&#8217;s future revenues (&#8220; Forward Multiples Approach &#8221;). Specifically, Ocean Tomo identified five publicly traded humanoid and non -humanoid robotics companies as benchmarks for the Forward Multiples Approach (the &#8220; Selected Humanoid&#160;&amp; Non -Humanoid Robotics Publicly Traded Companies &#8221;). These are companies that have historically been, and currently are, primarily engaged in the manufacture and sale of non -humanoid industrial robots, but have publicly announced strategic initiatives to develop and deploy humanoid robotics solutions. Ocean Tomo selected these companies based on the relative comparability of their products, underlying technologies, and business models. 
 

 139 
 Table of Contents 

 
 Ocean Tomo estimated enterprise value by applying forward revenue multiples, based on consensus projections for the next three&#160;years of the Selected Humanoid&#160;&amp; Non -Humanoid Robotics Publicly Traded Companies to Agility&#8217;s corresponding projected revenues for each respective year. Each resulting indication of value was then discounted to present value using an 18% discount rate, consistent with the risk profile identified through the CAPM analysis. The overall enterprise value indication for each scenario was calculated as the average of the discounted values across the three forward projection&#160;years. 
 Notwithstanding the analytical framework described above, Ocean Tomo considered, but ultimately did not rely upon and gave no weight to, the Forward Multiples Approach. Ocean Tomo determined that forward revenue multiples derived from the selected companies could not be meaningfully applied to the Company, as Agility has limited current and near -term revenue against which such multiples could be applied, whereas the selected guideline public companies from which the forward multiples were derived were established operating companies with current or near -term revenue. Accordingly, Ocean Tomo did not place direct reliance on the valuation indications derived from the Forward Multiples Approach in its overall assessment of value. 
 The second market approach analysis conducted by Ocean Tomo involved a review of value indications implied by precedent transactions. Ocean Tomo analyzed 25 historical funding rounds and merger and acquisition transactions within the robotics sector. However, Ocean Tomo determined that this approach could not be applied quantitatively as sufficient financial data for the identified transactions was not publicly available to establish reliable valuation multiples. Further, many of the precedent transactions were more than 5 years old and not reflective of current market conditions. Given the difference in market conditions between the precedent transaction dates and the current date; and the lack of available or reliable financial data, Ocean Tomo did not rely upon the precedent transactions analysis to arrive at its conclusions of value. 
 The third market approach analysis conducted by Ocean Tomo evaluated the impact of changes in market multiples on Agility&#8217;s value between its June&#160;25, 2025, Series&#160;C -3 funding round, and the Opinion Date ( &#8220;Multiple Expansion Approach&#8221; ). As of the Series&#160;C -3 financing, Agility was valued at approximately $1.985&#160;billion. Under this approach, Ocean Tomo analyzed the change in forward looking EV/Revenue multiples of the Selected Humanoid&#160;&amp; Non -Humanoid Robotics Publicly Traded Companies over the intervening period and applied the observed multiple expansion to Agility&#8217;s prior implied valuation. 
 The fourth market approach conducted by Ocean Tomo assessed changes in the overall market values of the Selected Humanoid&#160;&amp; Non -Humanoid Robotics Publicly Traded Companies between the date of Agility&#8217;s Series&#160;C -3 financing on June&#160;25, 2025, and the Opinion Date (the &#8220; Value Growth Approach &#8221;). Under this approach, Ocean Tomo evaluated the implied change in Agility&#8217;s enterprise value by analyzing observed increases in key market -based indicators for the selected companies over the relevant period, including 1) market capitalization, 2) enterprise value, and 3) stock price. 
 In applying this methodology, Ocean Tomo calculated the implied current value of Agility based on the lowest and most conservative of these measures, changes in stock price, observed across the Selected Humanoid&#160;&amp; Non -Humanoid Robotics Publicly Traded Companies over the period from the Series&#160;C -3 to the Opinion Date.

 Implied Value Per Share Calculation 
 In addition to the enterprise valuation, Ocean Tomo performed a post -Closing pro forma implied value per share calculation to determine the implied pro forma value per share for the shareholders of CCXI at Closing under various redemption scenarios. For the purposes of its calculation, Ocean Tomo utilized the average of all its DCF and market approach enterprise valuations for each of the four different valuation scenarios described above. The average EV from each scenario was then adjusted for the expected cash in the trust account at Closing (assuming both no redemptions by CCXI public stockholders and the Maximum Redemptions Scenario in which redemptions by CCXI public stockholders result in $0 in the trust account at Closing). The average EV from each scenario was then divided by two different post -Closing outstanding share counts, which were based on the two aforementioned redemption scenarios provided by CCXI.&#160;This analysis resulted in the ranges of implied pro forma values per share of CCXI Class&#160;A common stock shown in the table below. Ocean Tomo compared these ranges to the illustrative redemption value for a CCXI public share of $10.10. All of the pro forma implied values of the Class&#160;A shares were in excess of the illustrative redemption value of $10.10.

 Conclusion 
 Ocean Tomo estimated the range of enterprise values for Agility to be $1.7&#160;billion to $7.3&#160;billion based on four different scenarios and approaches as noted above. Additionally, based on Ocean Tomo&#8217;s post -Closing pro forma implied value per share analysis, Ocean Tomo estimated the range of pro forma implied value per share for CCXI Class&#160;A common stock to be $11.39 to $16.69 based on the different scenarios noted above. Based upon and subject to the foregoing, Ocean Tomo is of the opinion that, as of the Opinion Date, the Purchase Price pursuant to the Merger Agreement is fair, from a financial perspective, to the shareholders of CCXI.

 Recommendation of the CCXI Board to CCXI Shareholders 
 After careful consideration, the CCXI Board has unanimously determined that the business combination proposal is fair to, and in the best interests of, CCXI and its shareholders and unanimously recommends that you vote or give instruction to vote &#8220;FOR&#8221; the business combination proposal. 
 Satisfaction of the 80% Test 
 It is a requirement under the CCXI current articles of association that any business acquired by CCXI have a fair market value equal to at least 80% of the balance of the funds in the trust account (excluding net of amounts disbursed to management for working capital purposes, if applicable, taxes payable on interest income earned from the trust account and the deferred underwriting fees at the time of the execution of a definitive agreement for an initial business combination). As of June&#160;24, 2026, the date of the execution of the Merger Agreement, the balance of the funds in the trust account was approximately $404,533,968.07 (excluding up to $15.9&#160;million of deferred underwriting fees) and 80% thereof represents approximately $323,627,174.46. In reaching its conclusion on the 80% asset test, the CCXI Board used as a fair market value the $2,500,000,000 equity value for Agility, which was implied based on the terms of the Transactions agreed to by the parties in negotiating the Merger Agreement. 
 The CCXI Board also considered qualitative factors such as Agility&#8217;s business and financial condition and prospects, the experience and commitment of Agility&#8217;s management team, as well as valuations and trading of publicly traded companies in similar and adjacent sectors. The CCXI Board determined that the consideration being paid in the Merger, which amount was negotiated at arm&#8217;s -length , was fair to, and in the best interests of, CCXI and its shareholders and appropriately reflected Agility&#8217;s value. 
 The CCXI Board believes that, because of the financial skills and background of its directors, it was qualified to conclude that the acquisition of Agility met the 80% requirement. Based on the fact that the $2.5&#160;billion fair market value of Agility as described above is in excess of the threshold of approximately $323,627,174.46, representing 80% of the balance of the funds in the trust account (excluding net of amounts disbursed to management for working capital purposes, if applicable, taxes payable on interest income earned from the trust account and the deferred underwriting fees), the CCXI Board determined that the fair market value of Agility was substantially in excess of 80% of the funds in the trust account and that the 80% test was met.

 Redemption Rights 
 Pursuant to the CCXI current articles of association, eligible CCXI public shareholders may seek to redeem their CCXI public shares for cash, regardless of whether they vote &#8220;for&#8221; or &#8220;against&#8221; the business combination proposal. Eligible shareholders holding CCXI public shares as of the record date may demand that CCXI redeem such shares for cash in an amount equal to their pro rata portion of the funds held in the trust account net of permitted withdrawals (which, for illustrative purposes, was approximately $ &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; per share as of the close of business on&#160;&#160;&#160; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; , 2026, the record date for the extraordinary general meeting), calculated as of two&#160;business days prior to the anticipated Closing Date. If a holder of CCXI public shares properly exercises its redemption rights as described in this section and the business combination is consummated, CCXI will redeem such holder&#8217;s shares for a pro rata portion of funds held in the trust account net of permitted withdrawals, and the holder will no longer own CCXI public shares following the business combination. Such redemption rights are not available to our Sponsor, officers or directors. 
 Notwithstanding the foregoing, a holder of CCXI public shares, together with any affiliate of such holder or any other person with whom such holder is acting in concert or as a &#8220;group&#8221; (as defined in Section&#160;13(d)(3)&#160;of the Exchange&#160;Act), will be restricted from seeking redemption with respect to more than 15% of the CCXI public shares. Accordingly, all CCXI public shares in excess of 15% held by a CCXI public shareholder, together with any affiliate of such holder or any other person with whom such holder is acting in concert or as a &#8220;group,&#8221; will not be redeemed for cash. Moreover, pursuant to the terms of the Sponsor Agreement, the Sponsor and the Insiders have each agreed to waive any redemption rights with respect to any CCXI Ordinary Shares they own in connection with the consummation of the business combination. 
 Holders may demand redemption by delivering their shares, either physically or electronically using Depository Trust Company&#8217;s DWAC System and requesting in writing that CCXI redeem such shares for cash to Continental Stock Transfer&#160;&amp; Trust Company, CCXI&#8217;s transfer agent, at least two&#160;business days prior to initially scheduled vote at the extraordinary general meeting. If you hold the CCXI Ordinary Shares in street name, you will have to coordinate with your broker to have your shares certificated or delivered electronically. Certificates that have not been tendered (either 
 

 145 
 Table of Contents 

 
 physically or electronically) in accordance with these procedures will not be redeemed for cash. There is a nominal cost associated with this tendering process and the act of certificating the CCXI Ordinary Shares or delivering them through the DWAC System. CCXI&#8217;s transfer agent will typically charge the tendering broker $100 and it would be up to the broker whether or not to pass this cost on to the redeeming shareholder. In the event the business combination is not consummated, this may result in an additional cost to CCXI shareholders for the return of their shares. 
 Any request to redeem such shares, once made, may be withdrawn at any time up to the vote on the business combination proposal. Furthermore, if a holder of CCXI public shares delivered their certificate in connection with an election of their redemption and subsequently decides prior to the applicable date not to elect to exercise such rights, they may simply request that the transfer agent return the certificate (physically or electronically). 
 If the business combination is not approved or completed for any reason, then CCXI public shareholders that elected to exercise their redemption rights will not be entitled to redeem their shares for cash in an amount equal to their pro rata portion of the funds held in the trust account net of permitted withdrawals, as applicable. In such case, CCXI will promptly return any CCXI public shares delivered by shareholders.

 CCXI cannot assure its shareholders that they will be able to sell CCXI public shares in the open market, even if the market price per share is higher than the redemption price stated above, as there may not be sufficient liquidity in its securities when its shareholders wish to sell their shares. 
 If a holder of CCXI public shares properly exercises its redemption rights and the business combination is consummated, then they will be exchanging their CCXI public shares for cash and will no longer own those shares. They will be entitled to receive cash for their CCXI public shares only if they properly exercise their redemption rights no later than the Redemption Deadline by delivering their certificate (either physically or electronically) to CCXI&#8217;s transfer agent prior to the Redemption Deadline.

 Because the components of a CCXI Unit are generally separable at the option of the holder, the holder of a CCXI Unit generally should be treated, for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes, as the owner of the underlying CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Share and CCXI Warrant components of the CCXI Unit, and the discussion below with respect to actual Holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares and CCXI Warrants also should apply to holders of CCXI Units&#160;(as the deemed owners of the underlying CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares and CCXI Warrants that constitute the CCXI Units).  Tax Treatment of the Domestication 
 Subject to the limitations set forth herein, the Domestication should qualify as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; within the meaning of Section&#160;368(a)(1)(F)&#160;of the Code. A transaction qualifies as a reorganization within the meaning of Section&#160;368(a)&#160;(1)(F)&#160;of the Code if it is a &#8220;mere change in identity, form, or place of organization of one corporation, however effected&#8221; (an &#8220; F Reorganization &#8221;). 
 Pursuant to the Domestication, CCXI will change its jurisdiction of incorporation from the Cayman Islands to Delaware, and, in connection with the Closing of the Merger, will be renamed &#8220;Agility Robotics, Inc.&#8221;

 Tax Effects of the Domestication to U.S.&#160;Holders 
 Generally 
 Assuming the Domestication qualifies as an F Reorganization, U.S.&#160;Holders of CCXI Securities generally should not recognize gain or loss for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes in connection with the Domestication, except as provided below under the sections entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Effects of Section&#160;367 to U.S.&#160;Holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares &#8221; and &#8220;&#8212;&#160; PFIC Considerations .&#8221; 
 Subject to the discussion below under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; PFIC Considerations ,&#8221; if the Domestication fails to qualify as an F Reorganization (and does not otherwise qualify as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; within the meaning of Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code), a U.S.&#160;Holder of CCXI Securities generally would recognize gain or loss with respect to its CCXI Securities in an amount equal to the difference, if any, between the fair market value of the corresponding CCXI Delaware Securities received in the Domestication and the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in its CCXI Securities surrendered. 
 U.S.&#160;Holders exercising redemption rights will be subject to the potential tax consequences of the Domestication. All U.S.&#160;Holders considering exercising redemption rights with respect to CCXI public shares are urged to consult with their tax advisors with respect to the potential tax consequences to them of the Domestication and exercise of redemption rights. 
 Basis and Holding Period Considerations 
 Assuming the Domestication qualifies as an F Reorganization, subject to the discussion below under the section entitled &#8220; &#8212;&#160;PFIC Considerations &#8221;: (1)&#160;the tax basis of a share of CCXI common stock or CCXI Delaware Warrant received by a U.S.&#160;Holder in the Domestication will equal the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in the CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Share or CCXI Warrant surrendered in exchange therefor, increased by any amount included in the income of such U.S.&#160;Holder as a result of Section&#160;367 of the Code (as discussed below) and (2)&#160;the holding period for a share of CCXI common stock or CCXI Delaware Warrant received by a U.S.&#160;Holder will include such U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for the CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Share or CCXI Warrant surrendered in exchange therefor.

 Effects of Section&#160;367 to U.S.&#160;Holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares 
 Section&#160;367 of the Code applies to certain transactions involving foreign corporations, including a domestication of a foreign corporation in a transaction that qualifies as an F Reorganization. Subject to the discussion below under the section entitled &#8220; &#8212;&#160;PFIC Considerations ,&#8221; Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code and the Treasury Regulations promulgated thereunder impose U.S.&#160;federal income tax on certain U.S.&#160;persons in connection with transactions that would otherwise be tax -deferred . Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code will generally apply to U.S.&#160;Holders on the date of the Domestication, including any such U.S.&#160;Holders exercising redemption rights. 
 U.S.&#160;Holders Who Own 10% or More (By Vote or Value) of CCXI Shares 
 Subject to the discussion below under the section entitled &#8220; &#8212;&#160;PFIC Considerations, &#8221; a 10% U.S.&#160;Shareholder on the date of the Domestication must include in income as a deemed dividend deemed paid by CCXI the &#8220;all earnings and profits amount&#8221; attributable to the CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares it directly owns within the meaning of Treasury Regulations under Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code. A U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s ownership of CCXI Warrants will be taken into account in determining whether such U.S.&#160;Holder is a 10% U.S.&#160;Shareholder. Complex attribution rules apply in determining whether a U.S.&#160;Holder is a 10% U.S.&#160;Shareholder and all U.S.&#160;Holders are urged to consult their tax advisors with respect to these attribution rules. 
 A 10% U.S.&#160;Shareholder&#8217;s &#8220;all earnings and profits amount&#8221; with respect to its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares is the net positive earnings and profits of CCXI attributable to such CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares (each as determined under Treasury Regulations under Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code) but without regard to any gain that would be realized on a sale or exchange of such CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares. Treasury Regulations under Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code provide that the &#8220;all earnings and profits amount&#8221; attributable to a shareholder&#8217;s stock is determined according to the principles of Section&#160;1248 of the Code. In general, Section&#160;1248 of the Code and the Treasury Regulations under the Code provide that the amount of earnings and profits attributable to a block of stock (as defined in Treasury Regulations under Section&#160;1248 of the Code) in a foreign corporation is the ratably allocated portion of the foreign corporation&#8217;s earnings and profits generated during the period the shareholder held the block of stock. 
 CCXI does not expect to have significant, if any, cumulative net earnings and profits on the date of the Domestication. If CCXI&#8217;s cumulative net earnings and profits through the date of the Domestication are less than or equal to zero, then a 10% U.S.&#160;Shareholder should not be required to include in gross income an &#8220;all earnings and profits amount&#8221; with respect to its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares. However, the determination of earnings and profits is complex and may be impacted by numerous factors (including matters discussed in this proxy statement/prospectus). It is possible that the amount of CCXI&#8217;s cumulative net earnings and profits could be positive through the date of the Domestication, in which case a 10% U.S.&#160;Shareholder would be required to include its &#8220;all earnings and profits amount&#8221; in income as a deemed dividend deemed paid by CCXI under Treasury Regulations under Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code as a result of the Domestication. Any such deemed dividend is expected to be treated as foreign -source income for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes, and is not expected to be eligible for preferential tax rates because CCXI is expected to be treated as a PFIC. 
 U.S.&#160;Holders Who Own Less Than 10% (By Vote or Value) of CCXI Shares 
 Subject to the discussion below under the section entitled &#8220; &#8212;&#160;PFIC Considerations, &#8221; a U.S.&#160;Holder who, on the date of the Domestication, is not a 10% U.S.&#160;Shareholder and whose CCXI common stock has a fair market value of $50,000 or more on the date of the Domestication will recognize gain (but not loss) with respect to the CCXI common stock received in the Domestication or, in the alternative, may elect to recognize the &#8220;all earnings and profits amount&#8221; attributable to such U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares as described below.

 The election must be attached by an electing U.S.&#160;Holder to such U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s timely filed U.S.&#160;federal income tax return (including extensions, if any) for the taxable year in which the Domestication occurs, and the U.S.&#160;Holder must send notice of making the election to CCXI or CCXI Delaware no later than the date such tax return is filed. In connection with this election, CCXI Delaware may reasonably endeavor to cooperate with U.S.&#160;Holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares, upon written request, to make available to such requesting U.S.&#160;Holders information regarding CCXI&#8217;s earnings and profits, but there is no assurance that CCXI or the Post -Closing Company will timely provide such required information. 
 CCXI does not expect to have significant, if any, cumulative earnings and profits through the date of the Domestication and if that proves to be the case, U.S.&#160;Holders who make this election are not expected to have a significant income inclusion under Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code, provided that the U.S.&#160;Holder properly executes the election and complies with the applicable notice requirements. However, as noted above, if it were determined that CCXI had positive earnings and profits through the date of the Domestication, a U.S.&#160;Holder that makes the election described in this proxy statement/prospectus could have an &#8220;all earnings and profits amount&#8221; with respect to its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares, and thus could be required to include that amount in income as a deemed dividend deemed paid by CCXI under applicable Treasury Regulations as a result of the Domestication. Any such deemed dividend is expected to be treated as foreign -source income for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes, and is not expected to be eligible for preferential tax rates because CCXI is expected to be treated as a PFIC. 
 Each U.S.&#160;Holder is urged to consult its tax advisor regarding the consequences to it of making an election to include in income the &#8220;all earnings and profits amount&#8221; attributable to its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares under Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code and the appropriate filing requirements with respect to such election.

 PFIC Considerations 
 Regardless of whether the Domestication qualifies as an F Reorganization (and, if the Domestication qualifies as an F Reorganization, in addition to the discussion above under the section entitled &#8220; &#8212;&#160;Effects of Section&#160;367 to U.S.&#160;Holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares &#8221;), the Domestication could be a taxable event to U.S.&#160;Holders under the PFIC provisions of the Code if CCXI is considered a PFIC. 
 Definition of a PFIC 
 A foreign (i.e., non -United &#160;States) corporation will be classified as a PFIC for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes if either (1)&#160;at least 75% of its gross income in a taxable year, including its pro rata share of the gross income of any corporation in which it is considered to own at least 25% of the shares by value, is passive income or (2)&#160;at least 50% of its assets in a taxable year (generally determined based on fair market value and averaged quarterly over the year), including its pro rata share of the assets of any corporation in which it is considered to own at least 25% of the shares by value, are held for the production of, or produce, passive income. Passive income generally includes dividends, interest, rents and royalties (other than rents or royalties derived from the active conduct of a trade or business received from unrelated persons) and gains from the disposition of passive assets. The determination of whether a foreign corporation is a PFIC is made annually. Pursuant to a &#8220;startup exception,&#8221; a foreign corporation will not be a PFIC for the first taxable year the foreign corporation has gross income (the &#8220; startup year &#8221;) if (1)&#160;no predecessor of the foreign corporation was a PFIC; (2)&#160;the foreign corporation satisfies to the IRS that it will not be a PFIC for either of the first two taxable&#160;years following the startup year; and (3)&#160;the foreign corporation is not in fact a PFIC for either of those&#160;years. 
 PFIC Status of CCXI 
 Based upon the composition of its income and assets, and upon a review of its financial statements, CCXI believes that it likely will not be eligible for the startup exception and therefore likely has been a PFIC since its first taxable year and will likely be considered a PFIC for each taxable year thereafter, including the taxable year which ends as a result of the Domestication. 
 Effects of PFIC Rules on the Domestication 
 Even if the Domestication qualifies as an F Reorganization, Section&#160;1291(f)&#160;of the Code requires that, to the extent provided in Treasury Regulations, a U.S.&#160;person who disposes of stock of a PFIC (including for this purpose, under a proposed Treasury Regulation that generally treats an &#8220;option&#8221; (which would generally include a CCXI Warrant) to acquire the stock of a PFIC as stock of the PFIC, exchanging warrants of a PFIC for newly issued warrants in connection with a domestication transaction) recognizes gain notwithstanding any other provision of the Code. No final Treasury Regulations are currently in effect under Section&#160;1291(f)&#160;of the Code. However, proposed Treasury 
 

 152 
 Table of Contents 

 
 Regulations under Section&#160;1291(f)&#160;of the Code have been proposed with a retroactive proposed effective date. If finalized in their current form, those proposed Treasury Regulations would require gain recognition to U.S.&#160;Holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares and CCXI Warrants as a result of the Domestication if: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; CCXI were classified as a PFIC at any time during such U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period in such CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares or CCXI Warrants; and 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; the U.S.&#160;Holder had not timely made (1)&#160;a QEF Election (as defined below) for the first taxable year in which the U.S.&#160;Holder owned such CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares or in which CCXI was a PFIC, whichever is later (or a QEF Election along with a purging election), or (2)&#160;an MTM Election (as defined below) with respect to such CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares. Under current law, neither a QEF Election nor an MTM Election can be made with respect to warrants (including CCXI Warrants). 
 The tax on any such recognized gain would be imposed based on a complex set of computational rules designed to offset the tax deferral with respect to the undistributed earnings of CCXI.&#160;Under these rules (the &#8220; excess distributions regime &#8221;): 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s gain will be allocated ratably over the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for such U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares or CCXI Warrants; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; the amount of gain allocated to the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s taxable year in which the U.S.&#160;Holder recognized the gain, or to the period in the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period before the first&#160;day of the first taxable year in which CCXI was a PFIC, will be taxed as ordinary income; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; the amount of gain allocated to other taxable&#160;years (or portions of such taxable&#160;years) of the U.S.&#160;Holder and included in such U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period would be taxed at the highest tax rate in effect for that year and applicable to the U.S.&#160;Holder; and 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; an additional tax equal to the interest charge generally applicable to underpayments of tax will be imposed on the U.S.&#160;Holder in respect of the tax attributable to each such other taxable year (described in the third bullet above) of such U.S.&#160;Holder. 
 The proposed Treasury Regulations provide coordinating rules with Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code, whereby, if the gain recognition rule of the proposed Treasury Regulations applied to a disposition of PFIC stock that results from a transfer with respect to which Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code requires the U.S.&#160;Holder to recognize gain or include an amount in income as a deemed dividend deemed paid by CCXI, the gain realized on the transfer is taxable as an excess distribution under the excess distribution regime, and the excess, if any, of the amount to be included in income under Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code over the gain realized under the excess distribution regime is taxable as provided under Section&#160;367(b)&#160;of the Code. See the discussion above under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Effects of Section&#160;367 to U.S.&#160;Holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares .&#8221; 
 It is difficult to predict whether, in what form and with what effective date, final Treasury Regulations under Section&#160;1291(f)&#160;of the Code may be adopted or how any such final Treasury Regulations would apply. Therefore, U.S.&#160;Holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares that have not made a timely and effective QEF Election (or a QEF Election along with a purging election) or an MTM Election (each as defined below) may, pursuant to the proposed Treasury Regulations, be subject to taxation under the PFIC rules on the Domestication with respect to their CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares and CCXI Warrants under the excess distribution regime in the manner set forth above. A U.S.&#160;Holder that made a timely and effective QEF Election (or a QEF Election along with a purging election) or an MTM Election with respect to its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares is referred to in this proxy statement/prospectus as an &#8220; Electing Shareholder &#8221; and a U.S.&#160;Holder that is not an Electing Shareholder is referred to in this proxy statement/prospectus as a &#8220; Non -Electing Shareholder .&#8221; 
 As discussed above, proposed Treasury Regulations issued under the PFIC rules generally treat an &#8220;option&#8221; (which would include a CCXI Warrant) to acquire the stock of a PFIC as stock of the PFIC, while final Treasury Regulations issued under the PFIC rules provide that neither a QEF Election nor an MTM Election (as defined below) may be made with respect to options. Therefore, it is possible that the proposed Treasury Regulations, if finalized in their current form, would apply to cause gain recognition on the exchange of CCXI Warrants for CCXI Delaware Warrants pursuant to the Domestication.
