 Any gain recognized by a Non -Electing Shareholder of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares or a U.S.&#160;Holder of CCXI Warrants as a result of the Domestication pursuant to the PFIC rules would be taxable income to such U.S.&#160;Holder and taxed under the excess distribution regime in the manner set forth above, with no corresponding receipt of cash. 
 As noted above, if CCXI is considered a PFIC, the Domestication could be a taxable event under the PFIC rules regardless of whether the Domestication qualifies as an F Reorganization, and, absent a QEF Election (or a QEF Election along with a purging election) or an MTM Election, a U.S.&#160;Holder would be taxed under the excess distribution regime in the manner set forth above. 
 All U.S.&#160;Holders are urged to consult their tax advisors regarding the effects of the PFIC Rules on the Domestication, including the impact of any proposed or final Treasury Regulations. 
 QEF Election and Mark-to-Market Election 
 The impact of the PFIC rules on a U.S.&#160;Holder of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares will depend on whether the U.S.&#160;Holder has made a timely and effective election to treat CCXI as a &#8220;qualified electing fund&#8221; under Section&#160;1295 of the Code for the taxable year that is the first year in the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares during which CCXI qualified as a PFIC (a &#8220; QEF Election &#8221;) or, if in a later taxable year, the U.S.&#160;Holder made a QEF Election along with a purging election. One type of purging election creates a deemed sale of the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares at their then fair market value and requires the U.S.&#160;Holder to recognize gain pursuant to such purging election, subject to the excess distribution regime described above. As a result of any such purging election, the U.S.&#160;Holder would increase the adjusted tax basis in its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares by the amount of the gain recognized and, solely for purposes of the PFIC rules, would have a new holding period in its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares. U.S.&#160;Holders are urged to consult their tax advisors as to the application of the rules governing purging elections to their particular circumstances. 
 A U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s ability to make a timely and effective QEF Election (or a QEF Election along with a purging election) with respect to its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares is contingent upon, among other things, the provision by CCXI of a &#8220;PFIC Annual Information Statement&#8221; to such U.S.&#160;Holder. 
 CCXI or the Post -Closing Company (as applicable) will reasonably endeavor to provide a requesting U.S.&#160;Holder such information the IRS may require, including a PFIC Annual Information Statement, for making or maintaining a QEF Election (or making a QEF Election along with a purging election) for CCXI&#8217;s taxable year that ends on the date of the Domestication (and prior taxable&#160;years), but there is no assurance that CCXI or the Post -Closing Company will timely provide such required information. As discussed above, a U.S.&#160;Holder is not able to make a QEF Election with respect to CCXI Warrants under current law. An Electing Shareholder generally would not be subject to the excess distribution regime discussed above with respect to their CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares. As a result, an Electing Shareholder generally should not recognize gain or loss as a result of the Domestication except to the extent described under &#8220; &#8212;&#160;Effects of Section&#160;367 to U.S.&#160;Holders of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares ,&#8221; and subject to the discussion above under &#8220; &#8212;&#160;Tax Effects of the Domestication to U.S.&#160;Holders ,&#8221; but rather would include annually in gross income its pro rata share of the ordinary earnings and net capital gain of CCXI, whether or not such amounts are actually distributed. 
 The impact of the PFIC rules on a U.S.&#160;Holder of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares may also depend on whether the U.S.&#160;Holder has made a mark -to-market election under Section&#160;1296 of the Code (an &#8220; MTM Election &#8221;). U.S.&#160;Holders who hold (actually or constructively) stock of a foreign corporation that is classified as a PFIC may elect to mark such stock to its market value each taxable year if such stock is &#8220;marketable stock,&#8221; generally, stock that is regularly traded on a stock exchange that is registered with the SEC, including Nasdaq and the New&#160;York Stock Exchange. No assurance can be given that CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares are considered to be marketable stock for purposes of the MTM Election for any taxable year or whether the other requirements of this election are satisfied. If such an election is available and has been made, such Electing Shareholder generally would not be subject to the excess distributions regime discussed above with respect to their CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares in connection with the Domestication. Instead, in general, such Electing Shareholder will include as ordinary income each year the excess, if any, of the fair market value of its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares at the end of its taxable year over its adjusted tax basis in its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares. The Electing Shareholder also will recognize an ordinary loss in respect of the excess, if any, of its adjusted tax basis in its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares over the fair market value of its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares at the end of its taxable year (but only to the extent of the net amount of previously included income as a result of the MTM Election). The Electing Shareholder&#8217;s tax basis in its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares will be adjusted to reflect any such income or loss amounts, and any further gain recognized on a sale or other taxable disposition of 
 

 154 
 Table of Contents 

 
 its CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares will be treated as ordinary income (and any further loss recognized on such sale or disposition in excess of the net amount previously included in income as a result of the MTM Election would be capital loss). However, if the MTM Election is not made by a U.S.&#160;Holder with respect to the first taxable year of its holding period for the CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares in which CCXI is a PFIC, then the excess distribution regime discussed above will apply to certain dispositions of, distributions on and other amounts taxable with respect to, CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares, including in connection with the Domestication. Under current law, an MTM Election is not available with respect to warrants, including the CCXI Warrants. 
 The rules dealing with PFICs are very complex and are impacted by various factors in addition to those described above, including the application of the rules addressing overlaps in the PFIC rules and the Section&#160;367(b)&#160;rules and the rules relating to Controlled Foreign Corporations. All U.S.&#160;Holders of CCXI Securities are urged to consult their tax advisors regarding the consequences to them of the PFIC rules, including whether a QEF Election (or a QEF Election along with a purging election), an MTM Election or any other election is available and whether and how any overlap rules apply, and the consequences to them of any such election or overlap rule and the impact of any proposed or final PFIC Treasury Regulations. 
 Tax Effects to U.S.&#160;Holders of Exercising Redemption Rights 
 Generally 
 The U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences to a U.S.&#160;Holder of CCXI public shares that exercises its redemption rights with respect to its CCXI public shares will depend on whether the redemption qualifies as a sale of shares under Section&#160;302 of the Code. If the redemption qualifies as a sale of shares by a U.S.&#160;Holder, the tax consequences to such U.S.&#160;Holder are as described below under the section entitled &#8220; &#8212;&#160;Taxation of Redemption Treated as a Sale .&#8221; If the redemption does not qualify as a sale of shares, a U.S.&#160;Holder will be treated as receiving a corporate distribution with the tax consequences to such U.S.&#160;Holder as described below under the section entitled &#8220; &#8212;&#160;Taxation of Redemption Treated as a Distribution .&#8221; 
 Whether a redemption of shares qualifies for sale treatment will depend largely on the total number of shares of the Post -Closing Company common stock treated as held by the redeemed U.S.&#160;Holder before and after the redemption (including any shares treated as constructively owned by the U.S.&#160;Holder as a result of owning CCXI Warrants and any shares that a U.S.&#160;Holder would directly or indirectly acquire pursuant to the business combination) relative to all of the stock of the Post -Closing Company outstanding both before and after the redemption. The redemption generally will be treated as a sale of shares (rather than as a corporate distribution) if the redemption (1)&#160;is &#8220;substantially disproportionate&#8221; with respect to the U.S.&#160;Holder, (2)&#160;results in a &#8220;complete termination&#8221; of the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s interest in the Post -Closing Company or (3)&#160;is &#8220;not essentially equivalent to a dividend&#8221; with respect to the U.S.&#160;Holder. These tests are explained more fully below. 
 In determining whether any of the foregoing tests result in a redemption qualifying for sale treatment, a U.S.&#160;Holder takes into account not only shares actually owned by the U.S.&#160;Holder but also shares that are constructively owned by it under certain attribution rules set forth in the Code. A U.S.&#160;Holder may constructively own, in addition to shares owned directly, shares owned by certain related individuals and entities in which the U.S.&#160;Holder has an interest or that have an interest in such U.S.&#160;Holder, as well as any shares that the holder has a right to acquire by exercise of an option, which would generally include shares which could be acquired pursuant to the exercise of Post -Closing Company public warrants. Moreover, any shares that a U.S.&#160;Holder directly or constructively acquires pursuant to the business combination generally should be included in determining the U.S.&#160;federal income tax treatment of the redemption. 
 In order to meet the substantially disproportionate test, the percentage of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s outstanding voting stock actually and constructively owned by the U.S.&#160;Holder immediately following the redemption of shares must, among other requirements, be less than 80% of the percentage of CCXI&#8217;s outstanding voting stock actually and constructively owned by the U.S.&#160;Holder immediately before the redemption (determined based on reduction in voting power, and taking into account redemptions by other holders and possibly the Post -Closing Company common stock to be issued pursuant to the business combination). There will be a complete termination of a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s interest in the Post -Closing Company if either (1)&#160;all of the shares actually and constructively owned by the U.S.&#160;Holder are redeemed or (2)&#160;all of the shares actually owned by the U.S.&#160;Holder are redeemed and the U.S.&#160;Holder is eligible to waive, and effectively waives in accordance with specific rules, the attribution of stock owned by certain family members and the U.S.&#160;Holder does not constructively own any other shares (including any stock constructively owned by the U.S.&#160;Holder 
 

 155 
 Table of Contents 

 
 as a result of owning CCXI Warrants). The redemption will not be essentially equivalent to a dividend if the redemption results in a &#8220;meaningful reduction&#8221; of the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s proportionate interest in the Post -Closing Company. Whether the redemption will result in a meaningful reduction in a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s proportionate interest in the Post -Closing Company will depend on the particular facts and circumstances. However, the IRS has indicated in a published ruling that even a small reduction in the proportionate interest of a small minority stockholder in a publicly held corporation where such stockholder exercises no control over corporate affairs may constitute such a &#8220;meaningful reduction.&#8221; 
 If none of the foregoing tests is satisfied, then the redemption of shares generally will be treated as a corporate distribution to the redeemed U.S.&#160;Holder, and the tax effects to such a U.S.&#160;Holder will be as described below under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Taxation of Redemption Treated as a Distribution .&#8221; After the application of those rules, any remaining tax basis of the U.S.&#160;Holder in the redeemed shares will be added to the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in its remaining Post -Closing Company common stock or, if it has none, to the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in its Post -Closing Company public warrants or possibly in other Post -Closing Company common stock constructively owned by it. 
 U.S.&#160;Holders exercising redemption rights will be subject to the potential tax consequences of the Domestication (discussed further above). 
 U.S.&#160;Holders who actually or constructively own at least five percent by vote or value (or, if Post -Closing Company common stock is not then publicly traded, at least one percent by vote or value) or more of the total outstanding Post -Closing Company common stock may be subject to special reporting requirements with respect to a redemption of shares, and such holders should consult with their tax advisors with respect to their reporting requirements. 
 Taxation of Redemption Treated as a Distribution 
 If the redemption of a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s shares is treated as a corporate distribution, as discussed above under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Generally ,&#8221; the amount of cash received in the redemption generally will constitute a dividend for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes to the extent paid from the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s current or accumulated earnings and profits, as determined under U.S.&#160;federal income tax principles. 
 Distributions in excess of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s current and accumulated earnings and profits will constitute a return of capital that will be applied against and reduce (but not below zero) the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in its shares. Any remaining excess will be treated as gain realized on the sale of shares and will be treated as described below under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Taxation of Redemption Treated as a Sale .&#8221; 
 Taxation of Redemption Treated as a Sale 
 If the redemption of a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s shares is treated as a sale, as discussed above under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Generally ,&#8221; a U.S.&#160;Holder generally will recognize capital gain or loss in an amount equal to the difference between the amount of cash received in the redemption and the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in the shares redeemed. Any such capital gain or loss generally will be long -term capital gain or loss if the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for the shares so disposed of exceeds one year. Long -term capital gains recognized by non -corporate U.S.&#160;Holders generally will be eligible to be taxed at reduced rates. The deductibility of capital losses is subject to limitations. 
 U.S.&#160;Holders who hold different blocks of shares (including as a result of holding different blocks of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares purchased or acquired on different dates or at different prices) should consult their tax advisors to determine how the above rules apply to them. 
 ALL U.S.&#160;HOLDERS ARE URGED TO CONSULT THEIR TAX ADVISORS AS TO THE TAX CONSEQUENCES TO THEM OF AN EXERCISE OF REDEMPTION RIGHTS. 
 Tax Consequences of Ownership and Disposition of Post-Closing Company Securities 
 Taxation of Distributions 
 In general, distributions of cash or other property to U.S.&#160;Holders of Post -Closing Company common stock (other than certain distributions of the Post -Closing Company common stock or rights to acquire the Post -Closing Company common stock) generally will constitute dividends for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes to the extent paid from the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s current or accumulated earnings and profits, as determined under U.S.&#160;federal 
 

 156 
 Table of Contents 

 
 income tax principles. Distributions in excess of current and accumulated earnings and profits generally will constitute a return of capital that will be applied against and reduce (but not below zero) the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in its Post -Closing Company common stock. Any remaining excess generally will be treated as gain realized on the sale or other disposition of the Post -Closing Company common stock, as described below under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Gain or Loss on Sale, Taxable Exchange or Other Taxable Disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities .&#8221; 
 Dividends paid to a U.S.&#160;Holder that is treated as a taxable corporation for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes generally will qualify for the dividends received deduction if the requisite holding period is satisfied. With certain exceptions (including dividends treated as investment income for purposes of investment interest deduction limitations), and provided certain holding period requirements are met, dividends paid to a non -corporate U.S.&#160;Holder generally will constitute &#8220;qualified dividend income&#8221; subject to tax at reduced rates applicable to long -term capital gains. 
 Gain or Loss on Sale, Taxable Exchange or Other Taxable Disposition of Post-Closing Company Securities 
 Upon a sale or other taxable disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities (which, in general, would include a redemption of Post -Closing Company public warrants that is treated as a sale of such warrants as described below), a U.S.&#160;Holder generally will recognize capital gain or loss in an amount equal to the difference between the amount realized and the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in the Post -Closing Company Securities. Any such capital gain or loss generally will be long -term capital gain or loss if the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for the Post -Closing Company Securities so disposed of exceeds one year. Long -term capital gains recognized by non -corporate U.S.&#160;Holders may be eligible to be taxed at reduced rates. The deductibility of capital losses is subject to limitations. 
 Generally, the amount of gain or loss recognized by a U.S.&#160;Holder is an amount equal to the difference between (1)&#160;the sum of the amount of cash and the fair market value of any property received in such disposition and (2)&#160;the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in its Post -Closing Company Securities so disposed of. See the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Tax Effects of the Domestication to U.S.&#160;Holders &#8221; above for a discussion of a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in its securities following the Domestication. See the section entitled &#8220;&#8212; &#160;Exercise, Lapse or Redemption of Post -Closing Company Public Warrants &#8221; below for a discussion regarding a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in Post -Closing Company common stock acquired pursuant to the exercise of a Post -Closing Company public warrant. 
 Exercise, Lapse or Redemption of Post-Closing Company Public Warrants 
 A U.S.&#160;Holder generally will not recognize taxable gain or loss on the acquisition of Post -Closing Company common stock upon exercise of Post -Closing Company public warrants for cash. The U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in the shares of Post -Closing Company common stock received upon exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants generally will be an amount equal to the sum of the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in the Post -Closing Company public warrants and the exercise price. It is unclear whether the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for the Post -Closing Company common stock received upon exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants will begin on the date following the date of exercise or on the date of exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants; in either case, the holding period will not include the period during which the U.S.&#160;Holder held the Post -Closing Company public warrants. If any Post -Closing Company public warrants are allowed to lapse unexercised, a U.S.&#160;Holder generally will recognize a capital loss equal to such holder&#8217;s tax basis in the lapsed Post -Closing Company public warrants. 
 The tax consequences of a cashless exercise of Post -Closing Company public warrants are not clear under current tax law. A cashless exercise may not be taxable, either because the exercise is not a realization event or because the exercise is treated as a recapitalization for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes. If the cashless exercise is not taxable, a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s basis in the Post -Closing Company common stock received would equal the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s basis in the Post -Closing Company public warrants exercised therefor. If the cashless exercise were treated as not being a realization event, it is unclear whether a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period in the Post -Closing Company common stock would be treated as commencing on the date following the date of exercise or on the date of exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants; in either case, the holding period would not include the period during which the U.S.&#160;Holder held the Post -Closing Company public warrants. If the cashless exercise were treated as a recapitalization, the holding period of the Post -Closing Company common stock would include the holding period of the Post -Closing Company public warrants exercised therefor. 
 It is also possible that a cashless exercise could be treated in part as a taxable exchange in which gain or loss would be recognized. In such event, a U.S.&#160;Holder could be deemed to have surrendered a number of Post -Closing Company public warrants equal to the number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock having a value equal 
 

 157 
 Table of Contents 

 
 to the exercise price for the total number of Post -Closing Company public warrants to be exercised. In such case, the U.S.&#160;Holder would recognize capital gain or loss with respect to the Post -Closing Company public warrants deemed surrendered in an amount equal to the difference between the fair market value of the Post -Closing Company common stock that would have been received in a regular exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants deemed surrendered and the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in the Post -Closing Company public warrants deemed surrendered. In this case, a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s aggregate tax basis in the Post -Closing Company common stock received would equal the sum of the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in the Post -Closing Company public warrants deemed exercised and the aggregate exercise price of such Post -Closing Company public warrants. It is unclear whether a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for the Post -Closing Company common stock would commence on the date following the date of exercise or on the date of exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants; in either case, the holding period would not include the period during which the U.S.&#160;Holder held the Post -Closing Company public warrants. 
 Due to the absence of authority on the U.S.&#160;federal income tax treatment of a cashless exercise, including when a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period would commence with respect to the Post -Closing Company common stock received, there can be no assurance regarding which, if any, of the alternative tax consequences and holding periods described above would be adopted by the IRS or a court of law. Accordingly, U.S.&#160;Holders should consult their tax advisors regarding the tax consequences of a cashless exercise. 
 If the Post -Closing Company redeems Post -Closing Company public warrants for cash or if it purchases Post -Closing Company public warrants in an open market transaction, such redemption or purchase generally will be treated as a taxable disposition to the U.S.&#160;Holder, taxed as described above under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Gain or Loss on Sale, Taxable Exchange or Other Taxable Disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities .&#8221; 
 Possible Constructive Distributions 
 Consistent with the CCXI Warrants, the terms of each Post -Closing Company public warrant will provide for an adjustment to the number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock for which the Post -Closing Company public warrant may be exercised or to the exercise price of the Post -Closing Company public warrant in certain events. An adjustment which has the effect of preventing dilution generally is not taxable. A U.S.&#160;Holder of the Post -Closing Company public warrants would, however, be treated as receiving a constructive distribution from the Post -Closing Company if, for example, the adjustment increases the U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s proportionate interest in the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s assets or earnings and profits (for example, through an increase in the number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock that would be obtained upon exercise or through a decrease in the exercise price of the Post -Closing Company public warrant), which adjustment may be made as a result of a distribution of cash or other property, such as other securities, to the holders of shares of the Post -Closing Company common stock, or as a result of the issuance of a stock dividend to holders of shares of the Post -Closing Company common stock, in each case, which is taxable to the holders of such shares as a distribution. Such constructive distribution generally would be subject to tax as described above under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Taxation of Distributions &#8221; in the same manner as if the U.S.&#160;Holders of the Post -Closing Company public warrants received a cash distribution from the Post -Closing Company equal to the fair market value of such increased interest. 
 Information Reporting and Backup Withholding 
 Payments of dividends on and the proceeds from a sale or other disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities will be subject to information reporting to the IRS and such payments may also be subject to U.S.&#160;backup withholding. Backup withholding will not apply, however, to a U.S.&#160;Holder who furnishes a correct taxpayer identification number and makes other required certifications, or who is otherwise exempt from backup withholding and establishes such exempt status. 
 Backup withholding is not an additional tax. Amounts withheld as backup withholding may be credited against a U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s U.S.&#160;federal income tax liability, and the U.S.&#160;Holder generally may obtain a refund of any excess amounts withheld under the backup withholding rules by timely filing the appropriate claim for refund with the IRS and furnishing any required information.

 Non-U.S.&#160;Holders 
 As used in this proxy statement/prospectus, a &#8220;Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8221; is a beneficial owner (not including a partnership) of a CCXI Security or Post -Closing Company Security, as applicable, who or that for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes is, or is treated as: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; a non -resident alien individual, other than certain former citizens and residents of the United&#160;States subject to U.S.&#160;tax as expatriates; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; a foreign corporation; or 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; an estate or trust that is not a U.S.&#160;Holder. 
 Tax Effects of the Domestication to Non-U.S.&#160;Holders 
 The Domestication is not expected to result in any U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences to a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder of CCXI Securities unless the Domestication fails to qualify as an F Reorganization (and does not otherwise qualify as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; within the meaning of Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code) and such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder holds its CCXI Securities in connection with the conduct of a trade or business in the United&#160;States (and, if required by an applicable income tax treaty, is attributable to a permanent establishment or fixed base that such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder maintains in the United&#160;States) or is a nonresident alien individual who is physically present in the United&#160;States for at least 183&#160;days during that individual&#8217;s taxable year in which the Domestication occurs and meets certain other requirements. Non -U .S.&#160;Holders will own stock and warrants of a U.S.&#160;corporation, i.e., the Post -Closing Company, rather than a non -U .S.&#160;corporation, i.e., CCXI, after the Domestication. 
 Non -U .S.&#160;Holders exercising redemption rights will be subject to the potential tax consequences of the Domestication. All Non -U .S.&#160;Holders considering exercising redemption rights with respect to CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares are urged to consult with their tax advisors with respect to the potential tax consequences to them of the Domestication and exercise of redemption rights. 
 Tax Effects to Non-U.S.&#160;Holders of Exercising Redemption Rights 
 The U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences to a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder of CCXI Class&#160;A Ordinary Shares that exercises its redemption rights will depend on whether the redemption qualifies as a sale of the shares redeemed, as described above under &#8220; U.S.&#160;Holders&#160;&#8212;&#160;Tax Effects to U.S.&#160;Holders of Exercising Redemption Rights&#160; &#8212;&#160; Generally .&#8221; The U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences to the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder will be as described below under &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Tax Consequences of Ownership and Disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities&#160;&#8212;&#160;Sale, Taxable Exchange or Other Taxable Disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities .&#8221; If the redemption does not qualify as a sale of Post -Closing Company common stock, the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder will be treated as receiving a corporate distribution, the U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences of which are described below under &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Tax Consequences of Ownership and Disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities&#160;&#8212;&#160;Taxation of Distributions .&#8221; 
 Because it may not be certain at the time a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder is redeemed whether such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s redemption will be treated as a sale of shares or a corporate distribution, and because such determination will depend in part on a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s particular circumstances, the applicable withholding agent may not be able to determine whether (or to what extent) a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder is treated as receiving a dividend for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes. Therefore, the applicable withholding agent may withhold tax at a rate of 30% (or such lower rate as may be specified by an applicable income tax treaty) on the gross amount of any consideration paid to a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder in redemption of such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s Post -Closing Company common stock, unless (1)&#160;the applicable withholding agent has established special procedures allowing Non -U .S.&#160;Holders to certify that they are exempt from such withholding tax and (2)&#160;such Non -U .S.&#160;Holders are able to certify that they meet the requirements of such exemption (e.g., because such Non -U .S.&#160;Holders are not treated as receiving a dividend under the Section&#160;302 tests described above under the section entitled &#8220; U.S.&#160;Holders&#160;&#8212;&#160;Tax Effects to U.S.&#160;Holders of Exercising Redemption Rights&#160;&#8212;&#160;Generally &#8221;). However, there can be no assurance that any applicable withholding agent will establish such special certification procedures. If an applicable withholding agent withholds excess amounts from the amount payable to a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder, such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder generally may obtain a refund of any such excess amounts by timely filing an appropriate claim for refund with the IRS.&#160;Non -U .S.&#160;Holders should consult their own tax advisors regarding the application of the foregoing rules in light of their particular facts and circumstances and any applicable procedures or certification requirements.

 Tax Consequences of Ownership and Disposition of Post-Closing Company Securities 
 Taxation of Distributions 
 In general, any distributions (including constructive distributions, but not including certain distributions of the Post -Closing Company common stock or rights to acquire the Post -Closing Company common stock) made to a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock, to the extent paid out of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s current or accumulated earnings and profits (as determined under U.S.&#160;federal income tax principles), will constitute dividends for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes and, provided such dividends are not effectively connected with the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s conduct of a trade or business within the United&#160;States, the Post -Closing Company (or another applicable withholding agent) will be required to withhold tax from the gross amount of the dividend at a rate of 30%, unless such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder is eligible for a reduced rate of withholding tax under an applicable income tax treaty and provides proper certification of its eligibility for such reduced rate (usually on an IRS Form&#160;W -8BEN or W -8BEN-E ). In the case of any constructive dividend, it is possible that this tax would be withheld from any amount owed to a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder by the applicable withholding agent, including cash distributions on other property or sale proceeds from warrants or other property subsequently paid or credited to such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder. Any distribution not constituting a dividend will be treated first as reducing (but not below zero) the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in its shares of Post -Closing Company common stock and, to the extent such distribution exceeds the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s adjusted tax basis, as gain realized from the sale or other disposition of the Post -Closing Company common stock, which will be treated as described below under the section entitled &#8220; &#8212;&#160;Sale, Taxable Exchange or Other Taxable Disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities .&#8221; If the Post -Closing Company determines that it is likely to be classified as a &#8220;United&#160;States real property holding corporation&#8221; (see the section entitled &#8220; &#8212;&#160;Sale, Taxable Exchange or Other Taxable Disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities &#8221; below), the applicable withholding agent may be required to withhold 15% of any distribution that exceeds the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s current and accumulated earnings and profits. 
 The withholding tax generally does not apply to dividends paid to a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder who provides an IRS Form&#160;W -8ECI , certifying that the dividends are effectively connected with the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s conduct of a trade or business within the United&#160;States. Instead, the effectively connected dividends will be subject to regular U.S.&#160;federal income tax as if the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder were a U.S.&#160;resident, subject to an applicable income tax treaty providing otherwise. A Non -U .S.&#160;Holder that is treated as a foreign corporation for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes receiving effectively connected dividends may also be subject to an additional &#8220;branch profits tax&#8221; imposed at a rate of 30% (or a lower rate provided in an applicable tax treaty). 
 Sale, Taxable Exchange or Other Taxable Disposition of Post-Closing Company Securities 
 A Non -U .S.&#160;Holder generally will not be subject to U.S.&#160;federal income or withholding tax in respect of gain recognized on a sale, taxable exchange or other taxable disposition of its Post -Closing Company Securities, including an expiration or redemption of the Post -Closing Company public warrants as described below under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Exercise, Lapse or Redemption of Post -Closing Company Public Warrants ,&#8221; or a redemption of Post -Closing Company common stock that is treated as a sale of shares as described above under the section entitled &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Tax Effects to Non -U .S.&#160;Holders of Exercising Redemption Rights ,&#8221; unless: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; the gain is effectively connected with the conduct by the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder of a trade or business within the United&#160;States (and, if required by an applicable income tax treaty, is attributable to a permanent establishment or fixed base that such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder maintains in the United&#160;States); 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder is an individual who was present in the United&#160;States for 183&#160;days or more in the taxable year of such disposition (as such&#160;days are calculated pursuant to Section&#160;7701(b)(3)&#160;of the Code) and certain other requirements are met; or 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; the Post -Closing Company is or has been a &#8220;United&#160;States real property holding corporation&#8221; for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes at any time during the shorter of the five -year period ending on the date of disposition or the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for the applicable Post -Closing Company Security being disposed of. 
 

 160 
 Table of Contents 

 
 Unless an applicable treaty provides otherwise, gain described in the first bullet point above will be subject to tax at generally applicable U.S.&#160;federal income tax rates as if the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder were a U.S.&#160;resident. Any gains described in the first bullet point above of a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder that is treated as a foreign corporation for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes may also be subject to an additional &#8220;branch profits tax&#8221; imposed at a 30% rate (or a lower applicable income tax treaty rate). 
 If the second bullet point applies to a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder, such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder generally will be subject to U.S.&#160;tax on such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s net capital gain for such year (including any gain realized in connection with the redemption) at a tax rate of 30% (or a lower applicable tax treaty rate). 
 If the third bullet point above applies to a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder, subject to certain exceptions in the case of interests that are regularly traded on an established market, gain recognized by such holder will be subject to tax at generally applicable U.S.&#160;federal income tax rates, and a buyer of such Post -Closing Company Security or the Post -Closing Company may be required to withhold U.S.&#160;federal income tax at a rate of 15% of the amount realized upon such disposition or redemption. 
 Based on the nature of the business and activities of Agility, it generally is not expected that the Post -Closing Company would be a United&#160;States real property holding corporation after the Domestication or immediately after the business combination is completed. However, neither CCXI nor the Post -Closing Company has undertaken a formal analysis of the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s possible status as a United&#160;States real property holding corporation. Such determination is factual in nature and subject to change. Accordingly, no assurance can be provided as to whether the Post -Closing Company would be treated as a United&#160;States real property holding corporation in any taxable year. 
 Non -U .S.&#160;Holders should consult their tax advisors regarding the U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences to them in respect of any loss recognized on a sale, taxable exchange or other taxable disposition of its Post -Closing Company Securities. 
 Exercise, Lapse or Redemption of Post-Closing Company Public Warrants 
 A Non -U .S.&#160;Holder generally will not recognize taxable gain or loss on the acquisition of Post -Closing Company common stock upon exercise of Post -Closing Company public warrants for cash. The Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in the share of Post -Closing Company common stock received upon exercise of Post -Closing Company public warrants generally will be an amount equal to the sum of the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in such Post -Closing Company public warrants and the exercise price. It is unclear whether the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for the Post -Closing Company common stock received upon exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants will begin on the date following the date of exercise or on the date of exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants; in either case, the holding period will not include the period during which the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder held the Post -Closing Company public warrants. If any Post -Closing Company public warrants are allowed to lapse unexercised, a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder generally will recognize a capital loss equal to such holder&#8217;s tax basis in such lapsed Post -Closing Company public warrants and generally will be taxed as described above under &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Sale, Taxable Exchange or Other Taxable Disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities .&#8221; 
 Consistent with the CCXI Warrants, the Post -Closing Company public warrants may be exercised on a cashless basis in certain circumstances. The U.S.&#160;federal income tax characterization of a cashless exercise of Post -Closing Company public warrants are not clear under current tax law. A cashless exercise may not be a taxable exchange, either because the exercise is not a realization event or because the exercise is treated as a recapitalization for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes. If the cashless exercise is not taxable, a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in the Post -Closing Company common stock received would equal the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in the Post -Closing Company public warrants exercised therefor. If the cashless exercise were treated as not being a realization event, it is unclear whether a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period in the Post -Closing Company common stock would be treated as commencing on the date following the date of exercise or on the date of exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants; in either case, the holding period would not include the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for the Post -Closing Company public warrants exercised therefor. 
 If the cashless exercise were treated as a recapitalization, the holding period of the Post -Closing Company common stock would include the holding period of the Post -Closing Company public warrants exercised therefor. 
 It is also possible that a cashless exercise could be treated in part as a taxable exchange in which gain or loss would be recognized. In such event, a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder could be deemed to have surrendered a number of Post -Closing Company public warrants equal to the number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock having a value 
 

 161 
 Table of Contents 

 
 equal to the exercise price for the total number of Post -Closing Company public warrants to be exercised. In such case, the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder would recognize capital gain or loss with respect to the Post -Closing Company public warrants deemed surrendered in an amount equal to the difference between the fair market value of the Post -Closing Company common stock that would have been received in a regular exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants deemed surrendered and the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in the Post -Closing Company public warrants deemed surrendered. Any gain or loss recognized by a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder generally will be taxed as described above in &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Sale, Taxable Exchange or Other Taxable Disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities .&#8221; It is unclear whether a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for the Post -Closing Company common stock would commence on the date following the date of exercise or on the date of exercise of the Post -Closing Company public warrants; in either case, the holding period would not include the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period for the Post -Closing Company public warrants exercised therefor. 
 Due to the absence of authority on the U.S.&#160;federal income tax treatment of a cashless exercise, including when a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period would commence with respect to the Post -Closing Company common stock received, there can be no assurance regarding which, if any, of the alternative tax consequences and holding periods described above would be adopted by the IRS or a court of law. Accordingly, Non -U .S.&#160;Holders should consult their tax advisors regarding the tax consequences of a cashless exercise. 
 If the Post -Closing Company redeems Post -Closing Company public warrants for cash or if Post -Closing Company purchases Post -Closing Company public warrants in an open market transaction, such redemption or purchase generally will be treated as a taxable disposition to the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder, taxed as described above under &#8220;&#8212;&#160; Sale, Taxable Exchange or Other Taxable Disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities .&#8221; 
 Non -U .S.&#160;Holders should consult their tax advisors regarding the tax consequences of the exercise, lapse, or redemption of Post -Closing Company public warrants. 
 Possible Constructive Distributions 
 Similar to the CCXI Warrants, the terms of each Post -Closing Company public warrant will provide for an adjustment to the number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock for which the Post -Closing Company public warrant may be exercised or to the exercise price of the Post -Closing Company public warrant in certain events. An adjustment which has the effect of preventing dilution generally is not a taxable event. A Non -U .S.&#160;Holder of the Post -Closing Company public warrants would, however, be treated as receiving a constructive distribution from the&#160;Post -Closing Company if, for example, the adjustment increases the Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s proportionate interest in the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s assets or earnings and profits (for example, through an increase in the number of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock that would be obtained upon exercise or through a decrease in the exercise price of the Post -Closing Company public warrant), which adjustment may be made as a result of a distribution of cash or other property, such as other securities, to the holders of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock, or as a result of the issuance of a stock dividend to holders of shares of Post -Closing Company common stock, in each case, which is taxable to the holders of such stock as a distribution. Any constructive distribution treated as received by a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder generally would be subject to U.S.&#160;federal income tax (including any applicable withholding) in the same manner as if such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder received a corporate distribution from Post -Closing Company equal to the fair market value of such increased interest without any corresponding receipt of cash, the U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences of which are described above under &#8220; &#8212;&#160;Taxation of Distributions .&#8221; 
 Information Reporting and Backup Withholding 
 Information returns will be filed with the IRS in connection with payments of distributions and the proceeds from a sale or other disposition of Post -Closing Company Securities. A Non -U .S.&#160;Holder may have to comply with certification procedures to establish that it is not a U.S.&#160;person in order to avoid backup withholding requirements. The certification procedures required to claim a reduced rate of withholding under a treaty generally will satisfy the certification requirements necessary to avoid the backup withholding as well. 
 Backup withholding is not an additional tax. The amount of any backup withholding from a payment to a Non -U .S.&#160;Holder generally will be allowed as a credit against such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s U.S.&#160;federal income tax liability and may entitle such Non -U .S.&#160;Holder to a refund, provided that the required information is timely furnished to the IRS.

 Material U.S.&#160;Federal Income Tax Considerations of the Merger 
 The following is a discussion of the material U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences of the Merger to (i)&#160;Agility, (ii)&#160;CCXI, (iii)&#160;beneficial owners of CCXI public shares and (iv)&#160;Agility U.S.&#160;Holders and Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holders (each as defined below, and together, &#8220; Agility Holders &#8221;) who exchange in the Merger shares of Agility common stock for Post -Closing Company common stock. This summary is based upon current provisions of the Code, existing Treasury Regulations promulgated thereunder, judicial decisions, and published rulings and administrative pronouncements of the IRS, all in effect as of the date hereof and all of which are subject to differing interpretations or change. Any such change or differing interpretation, which may be retroactive, could alter the tax consequences from those discussed in the following summary. This discussion assumes that the Merger will be consummated in accordance with the Merger Agreement and as described in this proxy statement/prospectus. 
 This discussion applies only to Agility Holders who hold Agility common stock as a &#8220;capital asset&#8221; within the meaning of Section&#160;1221 of the Code (generally, property held for investment) and does not purport to address all U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences relevant to Agility Holders. In addition, it does not address consequences relevant to Agility Holders that are subject to particular U.S.&#160;or non -U .S.&#160;tax rules, including, without limitation, to Agility Holders that are: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; brokers, dealers or traders in securities; banks; insurance companies; other financial institutions; mutual funds;

 Definitions of &#8220;Agility U.S.&#160;Holder&#8221; and &#8220;Agility Non-U.S.&#160;Holder&#8221; 
 For purposes of this discussion, an &#8220;Agility U.S.&#160;Holder&#8221; is a beneficial owner of Agility common stock that for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes is, or is treated as: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; an individual who is a citizen or resident of the United&#160;States; 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; a corporation or any other entity taxable as a corporation created or organized in or under the laws of the United&#160;States, any state thereof, or the District of Columbia;

 General 
 Each of Agility and CCXI intends for the Merger to qualify as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; pursuant to Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code. Based on the terms of the Merger Agreement and the representations and covenants of the parties therein, although the matter is not free from doubt because there is no authority directly addressing the treatment of all of the particular facts of the Merger for U.S. federal income tax purposes, the Merger should qualify as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; within the meaning of Section 368(a) of the Code. Furthermore, in the Merger Agreement, each of Agility and CCXI agrees to (and cause their respective Subsidiaries and Affiliates to) use its reasonable best efforts to cause the Merger to qualify for such intended tax treatment and not take or cause to be taken any action, or fail to take or cause to be taken any action, which action or failure to act would reasonably be expected to prevent the Merger from so qualifying. Nevertheless, Agility and CCXI cannot guarantee that the IRS will not challenge the intended tax treatment of the Merger, and that such a challenge will not be successful. None of Agility, CCXI, or Merger Sub intend to obtain a ruling 
 

 164 
 Table of Contents 

 
 from the IRS with respect to the tax consequences of the Merger. Further, the closing of the Merger is not conditioned upon obtaining an opinion from counsel that the Merger will qualify as a reorganization. Accordingly, no assurance can be given that the IRS will not challenge the Merger&#8217;s qualification as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; within the meaning of Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code or that a court would not sustain such a challenge. Subject to the qualifications, assumptions and limitations set forth herein and in the U.S. federal income tax opinion filed as Exhibit 8.1 to this registration statement, the foregoing represents the opinion of Willkie Farr &amp; Gallagher LLP, counsel to CCXI, with respect to the material U.S. federal income tax consequences of the Business Combination. 
 Consequences to Agility U.S.&#160;Holders and Agility Non-U.S.&#160;Holders of Agility Common Stock if the Merger Qualifies as a Reorganization 
 Assuming the Merger qualifies as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; under Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code, the U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences of the Merger to Agility Holders are as follows: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Holders of Agility common stock generally will not recognize gain or loss upon the exchange of their Agility common stock for Post -Closing Company common stock. Holders of Agility common stock generally will obtain a basis in the Post -Closing Company common stock they receive in the Merger equal to their basis in the Agility common stock exchanged therefor; and 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; if a Holder of Agility common stock acquired different blocks of shares of Agility common stock at different times or at different prices, such Holder should consult its own tax advisor regarding the manner in which its basis and holding period should be allocated among its Post -Closing Company common stock in light of its specific circumstances. 
 Consequences to Agility U.S.&#160;Holders if the Merger Does Not Qualify as a Reorganization 
 If the Merger does not qualify as a reorganization within the meaning of Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code, then each Agility U.S.&#160;Holder will be treated as exchanging his, her or its Agility common stock in a fully taxable transaction in exchange for Post -Closing Company common stock. Agility U.S.&#160;Holders generally will recognize capital gain or loss in such exchange equal to the difference between (1)&#160;the fair market value of the Post -Closing Company common stock and (2)&#160;such U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in the Agility common stock surrendered in the Merger. Gain or loss must be calculated separately for shares of Agility common stock acquired by Agility U.S.&#160;Holders at different times for different prices and exchanged by such Agility U.S.&#160;Holder in connection with the Merger. Any gain or loss recognized generally would be long -term capital gain or loss if the Agility U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s holding period in a particular block of Agility common stock exceeds one year at the time of the Merger. Long -term capital gain of non -corporate Agility U.S.&#160;Holders (including individuals) generally is taxed at reduced U.S.&#160;federal income tax rates. The deductibility of capital losses is subject to limitations. The aggregate tax basis of an Agility U.S.&#160;Holder in the Post -Closing Company common stock will equal its fair market value at the Effective Time, and the holding period of Post -Closing Company common stock received in the Merger will begin on the&#160;day after the consummation of the Merger. 
 Consequences to Agility Non-U.S.&#160;Holders if the Merger Does Not Qualify as a Reorganization 
 If the Merger does not qualify as a reorganization under Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code, Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holders will generally not be subject to U.S.&#160;federal income tax in connection with the Merger, except to the extent described below. 
 If gain recognized upon the exchange of the Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s shares of Agility common stock for shares of Post -Closing Company common stock is effectively connected with the Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s conduct of a trade or business within the United&#160;States (and, if required by an applicable income tax treaty, the Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder maintains a permanent establishment in the United&#160;States to which such gain is attributable), such gain will be subject to U.S.&#160;federal income tax on a net income basis at the regular graduated rates applicable to U.S.&#160;Holders. An Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder that is a corporation also may be subject to a branch profits tax at a rate of 30% (or such lower rate specified by an applicable income tax treaty) on such effectively connected gain, as adjusted for certain items. If an Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder is a nonresident alien individual present in the United&#160;States for 183&#160;days or more during the taxable year of the Merger and certain other requirements are met, then any gain recognized by such Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder with respect to such Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s Agility common stock as a result of the Merger generally will be subject to U.S.&#160;federal income tax at a rate of 30% (or such lower rate specified by an applicable income tax treaty), which generally may be offset by U.S.&#160;source capital losses of such Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder (even though 
 

 165 
 Table of Contents 

 
 the individual is not considered a resident of the United&#160;States), provided such Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder has timely filed U.S.&#160;federal income tax returns with respect to such losses. In addition, if Agility is or has been a &#8220;United&#160;States real property holding corporation&#8221; for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes at any time during the shorter of the five -year period ending on the date of the Merger or the period that the Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder held Agility common stock, any gain recognized by such Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder with respect to such Agility Non -U .S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s Agility common stock as a result of the Merger would generally be subject to tax at applicable U.S.&#160;federal income tax rates and a U.S.&#160;federal withholding tax could apply. However, Agility believes that it is not, and has not been at any time since the five -year period ending on the date of the Merger, a United&#160;States real property holding corporation and neither Agility nor the Post -Closing Company expects to be a United&#160;States real property holding corporation immediately after the business combination is completed. However, Agility has not undertaken a formal analysis of its or the Post -Closing Company&#8217;s possible status as a United&#160;States real property holding corporation. Such determination is factual in nature and subject to change. Accordingly, no assurance can be provided as to whether Agility or the Post -Closing Company would be treated as a United&#160;States real property holding corporation in any taxable year. 
 Consequences to Agility, CCXI and CCXI Shareholders 
 Regardless of whether the Merger qualifies as a &#8220;reorganization&#8221; under Section&#160;368(a)&#160;of the Code, Agility and CCXI will not recognize any gain or loss for U.S.&#160;federal income tax purposes as a result of the Merger. In addition, beneficial owners of CCXI public shares who do not exercise their redemption rights will not be selling, exchanging, or otherwise transferring their CCXI public shares in the Merger and will therefore not be subject to any material U.S.&#160;federal income tax consequences as a result of the Merger. 
 Information Reporting for Agility U.S.&#160;Holders 
 Each Agility U.S.&#160;Holder who receives shares of Post -Closing Company common stock in the Merger is required to retain permanent records pertaining to the Merger, and make such records available to any authorized IRS officers and employees. Such records should specifically include information regarding the amount, basis, and fair market value of all shares of Agility common stock that are exchanged in the Merger, and relevant facts regarding any liabilities assumed or extinguished as part of such reorganization. Agility U.S.&#160;Holders who owned immediately before the Merger at least one percent (by vote or value) of the total outstanding stock of Agility or securities of Agility with a basis of $1.0&#160;million or more, are required to attach a statement to their tax returns for the year in which the Merger is consummated that contains the information listed in Treasury Regulations Section&#160;1.368 -3 (b). Such statement must include the Agility U.S.&#160;Holder&#8217;s tax basis in such Holder&#8217;s Agility common stock or securities surrendered in the Merger, the fair market value of such stock or securities, the date of the Merger and the name and employer identification number of each of Agility and the Post -Closing Company. Agility U.S.&#160;Holders are urged to consult with their own tax advisors to comply with these rules.

 Expected Accounting Treatment of the Transactions 
 The business combination is expected to be accounted for as a reverse recapitalization in accordance with GAAP because Agility has been determined to be the accounting acquirer under both the redemption scenarios presented. Under this method of accounting, CCXI, which is the legal acquirer, will be treated as the accounting acquiree for financial reporting purposes and Agility, which is the legal acquiree, will be treated as the accounting acquirer for financial reporting purposes. Accordingly, the consolidated assets, liabilities and results of operations of Agility will become the historical financial statements of the Post -Closing Company, and CCXI&#8217;s assets, liabilities and results of operations will be consolidated with Agility&#8217;s beginning on the acquisition date. For accounting purposes, the financial statements of the Post -Closing Company will represent a continuation of the financial statements of Agility with the business combination being treated as the equivalent of Agility issuing stock for the net assets of CCXI, accompanied by a recapitalization. The net assets of CCXI will be stated at historical costs, which are expected to approximate fair value, and no goodwill or other intangible assets will be recorded. Operations prior to the business combination will be presented as those of Agility in future reports of the Post -Closing Company.

 Regulatory Matters 
 Under the HSR Act and the rules that have been promulgated thereunder by the FTC, certain transactions may not be consummated unless information has been furnished to the Antitrust Division and the FTC and certain waiting period requirements have been satisfied. Complying with a Second Request can take a significant period of time. 
 Each of CCXI and Agility filed a Notification and Report Form&#160;with the FTC and the Antitrust Division in connection with the Transactions on July&#160;9, 2026. The initial 30 -day waiting period will expire at 11:59&#160;p.m., Eastern time, on August&#160;10, 2026.

Private parties may also seek to take legal action under the antitrust laws under certain circumstances.  Proposal&#160;No.&#160;2 &#8212;&#160;The Domestication Proposal 
 Unless the context otherwise requires, references in this section to &#8220;we,&#8221; &#8220;our&#8221; and &#8220;us&#8221; generally refer to CCXI prior to the business combination. 
 Overview 
 Assuming each of the business combination proposal, organizational documents proposal, advisory organizational documents proposal, stock issuance proposal, incentive plan proposal, ESPP proposal and director election proposal, is approved, CCXI is seeking shareholder approval of the domestication proposal on a non -binding advisory basis. The approval of the domestication proposal is a condition to the Closing under the Merger Agreement. If the domestication proposal is approved, but the business combination proposal is not approved, then neither the Domestication nor the business combination will be consummated. 
 Under the CCXI current articles of association, CCXI&#8217;s directors have the authority to resolve that CCXI be registered by way of continuation in a jurisdiction outside the Cayman Islands or such other jurisdiction in which it is for the time being incorporated, registered or existing (including, but not limited to, the approval of the organizational documents to be adopted by the Company in such other jurisdiction to the extent applicable). Accordingly, it is not necessary for CCXI to receive shareholder consent to the Domestication, and the domestication proposal and the organizational documents proposal are therefore being presented to CCXI shareholders on a non -binding advisory basis only. 
 As a condition to Closing, the CCXI Board has unanimously approved the Domestication, subject to shareholders approving the domestication proposal. To effect the Domestication, CCXI will file an application to deregister with the Cayman Islands Registrar of Companies, together with the necessary accompanying documents, and file the Proposed Certificate of Incorporation and a certificate of corporate domestication with the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware, under which CCXI will be domesticated and continue as a Delaware corporation. In connection with the Domestication and prior to the business combination, CCXI will be renamed &#8220;Agility Robotics, Inc.&#8221; 
 The domestication proposal, if approved, will authorize the transfer of the registration of CCXI by way of continuation from the Cayman Islands to the State of Delaware. Accordingly, while CCXI is currently governed by the Companies Act, upon the Domestication, Agility will be governed by the DGCL.&#160;CCXI encourages shareholders to carefully consult the information set out under &#8220; Comparison of Shareholder Rights. &#8221; 
 Reasons for the Domestication 
 The CCXI Board believes that it would be in the best interests of CCXI, in connection with the completion of the business combination, to effect the Domestication. Further, the CCXI Board believes that any direct benefit that the DGCL provides to a corporation also indirectly benefits its shareholders, who are the owners of the corporation. Because Agility will operate within the United&#160;States following the business combination, it is the view of the CCXI Board that Agility should be structured as a corporation organized in the United&#160;States. 
 The CCXI Board believes that there are several reasons why a reincorporation in Delaware is in the best interests of CCXI and its shareholders. 
 These additional reasons can be summarized as follows: 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Prominence, Predictability and Flexibility of Delaware Law .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;For many&#160;years, Delaware has followed a policy of encouraging incorporation in its state and, in furtherance of that policy, has been a leader in adopting, construing, and implementing comprehensive, flexible corporate laws responsive to the legal and business needs of corporations organized under its laws. Many corporations have chosen Delaware initially as a state of incorporation or have subsequently changed corporate domicile to Delaware. Because of Delaware&#8217;s prominence as the state of incorporation for many major corporations, both the legislature and courts in Delaware have demonstrated the ability and a willingness to act quickly and effectively to meet changing business needs. The DGCL is frequently revised and updated to accommodate changing legal and business needs and is more comprehensive, widely used and interpreted than other state corporate laws. This favorable corporate and regulatory environment is attractive to businesses such as ours. 
 

 169 
 Table of Contents 

 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Well -Established Principles of Corporate Governance . &#160; &#160;&#160;&#160; There is substantial judicial precedent in the Delaware courts as to the legal principles applicable to measures that may be taken by a corporation and to the conduct of a company&#8217;s board of directors, such as under the business judgment rule and other standards. Because the judicial system is based largely on legal precedents, the abundance of Delaware case law provides clarity and predictability to many areas of corporate law. We believe such clarity would be advantageous to the Post -Closing Company and its board and management to make corporate decisions and take corporate actions with greater assurance as to the validity and consequences of those decisions and actions. Further, investors and securities professionals are generally more familiar with Delaware corporations, and the laws governing such corporations, increasing their level of comfort with Delaware corporations relative to other jurisdictions. The Delaware courts have developed considerable expertise in dealing with corporate issues, and a substantial body of case law has developed construing Delaware law and establishing public policies with respect to corporate legal affairs. Moreover, Delaware&#8217;s vast body of law on the fiduciary duties of directors and officers provides appropriate protection for Agility&#8217;s stockholders from possible abuses by directors and officers. 
 &#8226; &#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; Increased Ability to Attract and Retain Qualified Directors .&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;Reregistration from the Cayman Islands to Delaware is attractive to directors, officers, and stockholders alike. The incorporation of the Post -Closing Company in Delaware may make Agility more attractive to future candidates for the board of the Post -Closing Company, because many such candidates are already familiar with Delaware corporate law from their past business experiences. To date, we have not experienced difficulty in retaining directors or officers, but directors of public companies are exposed to significant potential liability. Thus, candidates&#8217; familiarity and comfort with Delaware laws&#160;&#8212;&#160;especially those relating to director indemnification (as discussed below) &#8212;&#160;draw such qualified candidates to Delaware corporations. The CCXI Board therefore believes that providing the benefits afforded directors by Delaware law will enable Agility to compete more effectively with other public companies in the recruitment of talented and experienced directors and officers. 
 The frequency of claims and litigation pursued against directors and officers has greatly expanded the risks facing directors and officers of corporations in carrying out their respective duties. The amount of time and money required to respond to such claims and to defend such litigation can be substantial. While both Cayman Islands and Delaware law permit a corporation to include a provision in its governing documents to reduce or eliminate the monetary liability of directors for breaches of fiduciary duty in certain circumstances, we believe that, in general, Delaware law is more developed and provides more guidance than Cayman Islands law on matters regarding a company&#8217;s ability to limit director liability. As a result, we believe that the corporate environment afforded by Delaware will enable Agility to compete more effectively with other public companies in attracting and retaining new directors. 
 Reasons for the Name Change 
 The CCXI Board believes that it would be in the best interests of CCXI to, in connection with the Domestication and the business combination, change its corporate name to &#8220;Agility Robotics, Inc.&#8221; in order to more accurately reflect the business purpose and activities of Agility. 
 Regulatory Approvals; Third-Party Consents 
 CCXI is not required to make any filings or to obtain any approvals or clearances from any antitrust regulatory authorities in the United&#160;States or other countries in order to complete the Domestication. However, because the Domestication must occur in connection with the business combination, it will not occur unless the business combination can be completed, which will require the approvals as described under the section of this proxy statement/prospectus entitled &#8220; Proposal&#160;No.&#160;1 &#8212;&#160;The Business Combination Proposal .&#8221; CCXI must comply with applicable U.S.&#160;federal and state securities laws in connection with the Domestication. 
 The Domestication will not breach any covenants or agreements binding upon CCXI and will not be subject to any additional federal or state regulatory requirements, except compliance with the laws of the Cayman Islands and Delaware necessary to effect the Domestication.

 General Vote Required for Combinations with Interested Stockholders/Shareholders 
 
 &#160; 
 
 Generally, a corporation may not engage in a business combination with an interested stockholder for a period of three&#160;years after the time of the transaction in which the person became an interested stockholder, unless the corporation opts out of the statutory provision or the other statutory exceptions are met.

 Appraisal Rights 
 
 &#160; 
 
 Generally, a stockholder of a publicly traded corporation does not have appraisal rights in connection with a merger. Stockholders of a publicly traded corporation do, however, generally have appraisal rights in connection with a merger, if they are required by the terms of a merger agreement to accept for their shares anything except: (1)&#160;shares or depository receipts of the corporation surviving or resulting from such merger; (2)&#160;shares of stock or depository receipts that will be either listed on a national securities exchange or held of record by more than 2,000 holders; (3)&#160;cash in lieu of fractional shares or fractional depository receipts described in (1)&#160;and (2)&#160;above; or (4)&#160;any combination of the shares of stock, depository receipts and cash in lieu of fractional shares or fractional depository receipts described in (1), (2)&#160;and (3)&#160;above. 
 
 &#160; 
 
 Under the Companies Act and subject to certain exceptions, shareholders that dissent to a merger are entitled to be paid the fair market value of their shares, which, if necessary, may ultimately be determined by the courts of the Cayman Islands.

 Requirements for Stockholder/Shareholder Approval 
 
 &#160; 
 
 Subject to the certificate of incorporation, stockholder approval of mergers, a sale of all or substantially all the assets of the corporation, dissolution and amendments of constitutional documents generally require approval by a majority of the voting power of the outstanding shares; unless otherwise specified in the corporation&#8217;s certificate of incorporation or bylaws, most other stockholder approvals require the affirmative vote of a majority of the shares present and entitled to vote on the subject matter, provided a quorum is present. The Proposed Bylaws provide that, when a quorum is present at any meeting, in all matters other than the election of directors, the affirmative vote of a majority of the voting power of the shares present in person, by remote communication, if applicable, or represented by proxy at the meeting and entitled to vote on the subject matter shall be the act of the stockholders (or if there are two or more classes or series of capital stock entitled to vote as separate classes or series, then in the case of each such class or series, the holders of a majority of the voting power of the shares of capital stock of the class, classes or series present in person, by remote communication, if applicable, or represented at the meeting and entitled to vote on the subject matter), except when a different vote is required by applicable law, the Proposed Certificate of Incorporation, the Proposed Bylaws, or the rules of any stock exchange applicable to the Post -Closing Company. 
 
 &#160; 
 
 Certain matters must be approved by special resolution of the shareholders as a matter of Cayman Islands law, including alteration of the memorandum or articles of association, appointment of inspectors to examine company affairs, reduction of share capital (subject, in relevant circumstances, to court approval), change of name, authorization of a plan of merger (other than a merger between a parent and a subsidiary), authorization of a transfer by way of continuation to another jurisdiction or consolidation or voluntary winding up of the company. 
 The Companies Act requires that a special resolution be passed by a majority of at least two -thirds or such higher percentage as set forth in the memorandum and articles of association, of shareholders being entitled to vote and do vote in person or by proxy at a general meeting, or by unanimous written consent of shareholders entitled to vote at a general meeting. 
 The Companies Act defines &#8220;special resolutions&#8221; only. A company&#8217;s memorandum and articles of association can therefore tailor the definition of &#8220;ordinary resolutions&#8221; as a whole, or with respect to specific provisions. Under the CCXI current articles of association an ordinary resolution must be passed at a general meeting by a simple majority of shareholders who (being entitled to do so) vote in person or by proxy at that meeting. The expression includes a unanimous written resolution.
